## Commentary on the Saḷāyatanavagga
## Saṃyutta Nikāya
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One
## 1. Saḷāyatanasaṃyutta
## 1. Anicca Vagga
## 1. Explanation of the Ajjhattānicca Sutta
In the first sutta of the Saḷāyatanavagga, regarding 'eye' (cakkhu), there are two kinds: the eye of knowledge (ñāṇacakkhu) and the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu). Among these two, the eye of knowledge is of five types: the Buddha-eye (buddhacakkhu), the Dhamma-eye (dhammacakkhu), the all-seeing eye (samantacakkhu), the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), and the wisdom eye (paññācakkhu).

Among these five, the knowledge that knows the inclinations (āsaya) and underlying tendencies (anusaya) of beings, and the knowledge that knows the maturity or immaturity of the faculties (indriya), is called the Buddha-eye. Regarding this Buddha-eye, it is stated: "Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye." The three lower paths and the three lower fruits are called the Dhamma-eye. Regarding this Dhamma-eye, it is stated: "The dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose." Omniscience is called the all-seeing eye. Regarding this all-seeing eye, it is stated: "Having ascended the palace, O All-seeing One." The knowledge that arises through the pervasion of light (āloka-kasiṇa) is called the divine eye. Regarding this divine eye, it is stated: "With the divine eye, which is purified." The knowledge that discerns the Four Noble Truths is called the wisdom eye. Regarding this wisdom eye, it is stated: "The eye [of knowledge] arose."
2:
The fleshly eye is also of two kinds: the composite eye (sasambhāracakkhu) and the sensitive eye (pasādacakkhu). Among these two, the mass of flesh in the eye socket surrounded by the eyelids is called the composite eye. In that mass of flesh, there are briefly 13 components (sambhāra): the four great elements, color, smell, taste, nutritive essence, semen (sambhava), the life-faculty, the sex-faculty, eye-sensitivity, and body-sensitivity. In detail, however, these nine types of matter—the four great elements, color, smell, taste, nutritive essence, and semen—become 36 through the power of the four causes (kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment). When combined with the four kamma-produced matters—the life-faculty, the sex-faculty, eye-sensitivity, and body-sensitivity—there are 40 components. This is called the composite eye. Within that mass of flesh, the sensitive matter alone, which is situated in the pupil [lit. 'vision-circle'] within the black circle delimited by the white circle and which is capable of seeing forms, is called the sensitive eye. The detailed explanation of this sensitive eye and the others such as the ear, etc., has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Among those two kinds, referring to the sensitive eye, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, the eye is impermanent," and so forth. In that text, the detailed explanation such as "It is called impermanent because it has arising and passing away due to four causes" has already been shown below. "Ear" also refers only to the sensitive ear (pasādasota). Likewise, the nose, tongue, and body are also just sensitive matters (pasādarūpa). "Mind" (mano) refers to the consciousness that ranges over the three planes as the object of insight knowledge. Thus, this sutta was taught by showing the three characteristics in the six internal sense bases, according to the disposition of those who would realize the Four Noble Truths.

## 2-3. Explanation of the Ajjhattadukkha Sutta, etc.
2-3. In the second sutta, two characteristics are shown, and in the third sutta, one characteristic is shown; these were taught according to the disposition of those who would realize the Four Noble Truths. As for the remaining characteristics, they were taught with the intention that those persons had already noted them or would understand them through just this much teaching.

## 4-6. Explanation of the Bāhirānicca Sutta, etc.
4-6. In the fourth sutta, visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangible objects have four causes. Sounds have two causes. "Mental phenomena" (dhammā) refers to the mental objects occurring in the three planes. This sutta was also taught by showing the three characteristics in the six external sense bases, by the power of those who would realize the Four Noble Truths. In the fifth and sixth suttas, the method is the same as that stated in the second and third suttas.

## 7-12. Explanation of the Ajjhattāniccātītānāgata Sutta, etc.
7-12. The seventh sutta and those following were taught for the sake of neyya persons (those requiring guidance) who, having noted the characteristics of impermanence, etc., in the past and future eyes, etc. (where attachment through craving and views is not firm because those bases are not manifest), struggle with strong attachment to the present eyes, etc. (because those bases are manifest) when ascending the path of insight. The rest of the text follows the same method as stated below.

## The First Chapter: Anicca Vagga.

## 2. Yamaka Vagga

## 1-4. Explanation of the First Pubbesambodha Sutta, etc.
13-16. In the first and second suttas of the Yamaka Vagga, "internal" (ajjhattikānaṃ) refers to the six sense bases such as the eye, which are internal by way of the self (atta). Their state of being internal should be understood through the excessive strength of desire and lust (chandarāga). To explain, the six internal sense bases should be regarded like the interior of people's houses, and the six external sense bases like the surroundings of the house. Just as desire and lust are extremely strong for the interior of the house filled with children, spouse, wealth, and grain—where they do not allow anyone to enter and even at a slight sound of a vessel they are prone to ask, "What is that?"—similarly, there is extremely strong desire and lust for the six internal sense bases. Thus, because of this strength of desire and lust, those six bases are called "internal" (ajjhattika).

However, in the surroundings of the house, desire and lust are not so strong; they do not immediately stop people or four-footed animals walking there. Although they do not stop them, being unwilling, they do not allow even a handful of dust to be taken. Thus, they do not have extremely strong desire and lust for those forms, etc. Similarly, because there is no extremely strong desire and lust for forms and so forth, those six bases such as the form-base are called "external" (bāhira). The detailed discussion on internal and external has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. The rest of the wording in both suttas follows the method already stated below. The same applies to the third and fourth suttas.

## 5-6. Explanation of the First Nocēassāda Sutta, etc.
17-18. In the fifth sutta, "nissaṭā" means departed from the world. "Visamyuttā" means not connected by the defilements that cause bondage. "Vippamuttā" means not entering into or inclining towards the world. "Vimariyādīkatena cetasā" means with a mind made free from boundaries [of defilements]. To explain, if any group of defilements or the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) has not yet been abandoned, because of those unabandoned defilements and the round, the mind of trainees (sekha) is called a mind with boundaries.
4:
The mind of the trainees (sekhas) is called 'limited' (samariyādīkata) because of those defilements and the round of rebirth that have not yet been abandoned. Because those defilements and the round have been abandoned, the mind of the trainees is called 'unlimited' (vimariyādīkata) due to that abandonment. In this sutta, however, the meaning should be understood as: because defilements and the round have been abandoned in every way, they dwelt with a mind that has surpassed the limits of defilements and the round, having made it unlimited. In the sixth sutta, the method is the same. It should be known that in these six suttas, only the Four Noble Truths are taught.

## 7-10. Commentary on the Paṭhamābhinanda Sutta, etc.

19-22. In the four suttas beginning with the seventh, only the round (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught. Their sequential explanation should be understood according to the method already mentioned below.

## Yamaka Vagga, the Second.

## 3. Sabba Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Sabba Sutta

In the first sutta of the Sabba Vagga, regarding the phrase 'Sabbaṃ vo, bhikkhave' (All to you, O monks), what is called 'All' is fourfold: the All-inclusive All (sabba-sabba), the All of the Bases (āyatana-sabba), the All of the Individual Identity (sakkāya-sabba), and the Partial All (padesa-sabba). Among these four—

'There is nothing in this world that is not seen by that Buddha with his vision, nor is there anything unknown or that should not be known. Whatever knowable (ñeyya) thing exists, the Blessed One has known it all with higher knowledge; therefore, the Buddha is called the All-seeing (Samantacakkhu).'

This 'All' is called the All-inclusive All. The passage 'Monks, I will teach you the all; listen to that' is called the All of the Bases. The passage 'Monks, I will teach you the root sequence of all things' is called the All of the Individual Identity. The passage 'In all things, first the five-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana) arises; then mind, mentality, thought... the mind-consciousness element appropriate to that adverting arises' is called the Partial All.

Thus, the mere five objects are called the Partial All. The things belonging to the three planes of existence are the All of the Individual Identity. The things belonging to the four planes of existence are the All of the Bases. All knowable things are the All-inclusive All. The Partial All...
5:
The Partial All does not reach the All of the Individual Identity; the All of the Individual Identity does not reach the All of the Bases; the All of the Bases does not reach the All-inclusive All. Why? Because there is no such thing that is not an object of the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) (i.e., all things are indeed objects of Omniscient Knowledge). In this sutta, however, the All of the Bases is intended.

Paccakkhāya means 'having rejected'. Vācāvatthukam-evassa means 'it would be a mere matter of words'. Beyond these twelve bases, one would not be able to show that there is another such thing as an ultimate reality (sabhāva-dhamma). If asked, 'What is this other All?', one would not be able to fulfill the answer by saying, 'It is such and such a thing'. Vighātaṃ āpajjeyya means 'one would meet with distress'. In the passage 'Monks, in what is not the domain (avisaya)', the word 'taṃ' is a mere particle. 'Yathā' is a word expressing a cause, meaning 'because he was asked about what is not the domain'. In a matter that is not one's domain and cannot be carried out, only distress arises for beings. Just as it is not one's domain to swim in deep water while carrying a stone the size of a pinnacled house on one's head, and just as it is not one's domain to pull down the moon and the sun, and a person striving in such a domain that is not his own only meets with distress; similarly, in the matter of designating another 'All' which is not the domain, one would only meet with distress. This is the meaning.

## 2. Commentary on the Pahāna Sutta

In the second sutta, sabbappahānāya means for the sake of abandoning all things (by abandoning desire and lust). Cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ refers to the feeling (vedanā) that arises together with reception (sampaṭicchana), investigation (santīrana), determining (votthabbana), and impulsion (javana), having eye-contact as its root cause. Regarding the feeling associated with eye-consciousness, there is nothing to be said (as it is obvious that it has eye-contact as its root cause). The same method applies to the conditions of feeling arising at the ear-door, etc. Here, 'mano' (mind) refers to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). 'Dhammā' (objects) refers to the sense objects. 'Manoviññāṇaṃ' (mind-consciousness) refers to the impulsion-consciousness (javana-viññāṇa) together with adverting (āvajjana). 'Manosamphasso' (mind-contact) refers to the contact arising together with the life-continuum. 'Vedayitaṃ' (feeling) refers to the impulsion-feeling together with the adverting-feeling. Regarding the taking of the feeling associated with the life-continuum, there is nothing to be said. Alternatively, without separating adverting from the life-continuum, 'mano' should be understood as the life-continuum together with adverting. 'Dhammā' refers to the objects. 'Manoviññāṇaṃ' refers to the impulsion-consciousness. 'Manosamphasso' refers to the contact arising together with the life-continuum. 'Vedayitaṃ' refers to the feeling arising together with impulsion. The feeling arising together with the life-continuum along with adverting is also appropriate. The teaching which is an authoritative instruction in this sutta is called a designation (paññatti).

## 3. Abhiññāpariññāpahāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, the phrase "sabbaṃ abhiññā pariññā pahānāya" means for the purpose of knowing all (the sense bases such as the eye) with higher knowledge (abhiññā), fully understanding them through the three types of full understanding (pariññā) in their aspects such as impermanence, and then abandoning them completely through the full understanding of abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). The phrase "abhiññā pariññā pahātabbaṃ" means that which should be known with higher knowledge, fully understood as impermanent through the three types of full understanding, and then abandoned completely through the full understanding of abandoning. The remaining terms should be understood in the same manner as previously described.

## 4. Paṭhama Aparijānana Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, the phrase "anabhijānaṃ aparijānaṃ avirājayaṃ appajahaṃ" refers to one who does not know with higher knowledge, one who does not fully understand aspects such as impermanence through the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), one who is not free from lust, and one who does not abandon completely through the full understanding of abandoning. In this context, "avirājento" means one who does not act to become free from lust. Thus, in this sutta, all three types of full understanding (pariññā) are taught. Specifically, by the word "abhijānaṃ," the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā) is taught; by the word "parijānaṃ," the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā) is taught; and by the two words "virājayaṃ pajahaṃ," the full understanding of abandoning (pahāna-pariññā) is taught.

## 5. Dutiya Aparijānana Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, by the passage "cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā," the Buddha again refers to the same visual objects (rūpa) mentioned below (in the phrase "ye ca rūpā"). Alternatively, the previous mention refers to visual objects that have come into the range of the eye-sensitivity, whereas in this sutta, it refers to those that have not come into range. However, the conclusion here is: while the previous mention included both visual objects that have come into range and those that have not, in this sutta, the three aggregates (feeling, perception, and mental formations) associated with eye-consciousness are taken. Because these aggregates are known together with eye-consciousness, they are called "cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbā" (things to be known by eye-consciousness). The same method applies to the remaining terms.

## 6. Āditta Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, regarding "Gayāsīse": near the village of Gayā, there is a pond named Gayā, a river, and a large stone slab named Gayāsīsa which resembles the hump of an elephant. That stone slab has enough space for a thousand monks; the Blessed One stayed there. Therefore, it is said "at Gayāsīsa." The phrase "bhikkhū āmantesi" (addressed the monks) means that after selecting a Dhamma discourse suitable for those monks, he addressed them to preach that teaching.

In this regard, the chronological account is as follows: ninety-two aeons ago, there was a king named Mahinda. His eldest son was named Phussa. This Prince Phussa was a being in his last birth (pacchimabhavika) who had fulfilled the perfections. When his knowledge reached maturity, he ascended the Bodhi-maṇḍa and attained omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)...
7:
...and penetrated omniscience. The King's younger son became the Chief Disciple (Aggasāvaka) of that Buddha, and the son of the chaplain (purohita) became the Second Disciple. The King thought: "My eldest son has renounced the world and become a Buddha, my younger son has become the Chief Disciple, and the chaplain's son has become the Second Disciple." Thinking, "The Buddha is only ours, the Dhamma is only ours, the Saṅgha is only ours," he built and offered a monastery. From the monastery gate to the door of his own house, he fenced both sides of the path with bamboo walls. Above, he had a canopy fastened, adorned with gold stars and hanging fragrant garlands and flower wreaths. Below, he had silver-colored sand spread and flowers scattered, and he had the Blessed One travel by that path. The Blessed One would put on his robes only at the monastery and travel to the King's house with the community of monks inside a curtained enclosure. After finishing the meal, he would return also within the curtained enclosure. No one else was allowed to give even a spoonful of alms. Then the townspeople complained: "The Buddha has appeared in the world, yet we do not get the chance to perform meritorious deeds. Just as the sun and moon provide light to all, Buddhas appear for the benefit of all beings. But this King keeps the meritorious intentions of everyone within his own reach alone."

That King had three other sons. The townspeople joined together with those princes and consulted: "There is no way to contend legally with the royal family; let us use a stratagem." They incited thieves in the border regions and had a message brought saying, "Some villages have been looted and destroyed," and reported this to the King. The King summoned his sons and sent them, saying, "Dear sons, I am old; you go and suppress the thieves." The arranged thieves did not scatter here and there but came directly to the princes. The princes had them stay in uninhabited villages and returned, reporting to the King, "The thieves have been suppressed," and remained after paying homage to the King.

The King was delighted and said, "Dear sons, I grant you a boon." After accepting, the princes went and consulted with the townspeople: "The King has granted us a boon. What should we take?" The townspeople said, "Young lords, for you, things like elephants and horses are not difficult to obtain. However, the Buddha-treasure is rare; it does not appear at all times. Take only the boon of the right to serve and attend to your elder brother, Phussa Buddha." The princes replied to the townspeople, "We will do so."
8:
Having accepted the words of the people, they trimmed their beards, bathed, and anointed themselves with perfumes. They then went to the King and requested, "Great King, please grant us a boon." When asked, "Dear sons, what boon will you take?" they replied, "Great King, we have no need for elephants, horses, and such. Please grant us the boon of the opportunity to serve and honor our elder brother, the Phussa Buddha." The King stopped both his ears, saying, "I cannot grant this boon while I am alive." They spoke truthfully, saying, "Great King, we did not force you to give this boon; you gave it yourself out of your own pleasure. Great King, is it proper for the royal family to speak with two tongues?"

Being unable to retract his word, the King said, "Dear sons, I will serve Him myself for seven years, seven months, and seven days, and only then will I give Him to you." They replied, "Very well, Great King, please give us a guarantee." When asked, "Dear sons, what kind of guarantee should I give?" they requested, "Great King, give us a guarantee of immortality for that length of time." The King replied, "Dear sons, you ask for an improper guarantee. I cannot give such a guarantee. The life of beings is like a dewdrop on the tip of a blade of grass." They then asked, "Great King, if you do not give a guarantee and we die in the meantime, what merit will we be able to perform?" The King then said, "If so, dear sons, take Him for six years." They replied, "Great King, it is not possible." He then offered five years, four, three, two, and one year. Then seven months, six months... even half a month. But they still replied, "Great King, it is not possible." Finally, he said, "Then take Him for seven days." They agreed, saying, "Very well, Great King," and accepted the seven days. Within those seven days, the King performed all the honors and offerings that were meant to be done over seven years, seven months, and seven days.

Then, to escort the Teacher to his sons' residence, he had the main road, eight usabhas wide, decorated. He had the central area, four usabhas wide, trampled by elephants to make it as level as a kasiṇa-maṇḍala, then spread with sand and strewn with flowers. In various places, he had banana trees and full vessels (puṇṇaghaṭa) placed, and banners and flags raised. He had ponds dug at intervals of one usabha. Furthermore, he had shops for perfumes and flowers set up on both sides of the road. On the two-usabha-wide paths on either side of the decorated four-usabha-wide central road, he had stumps and thorns removed and lampstands erected. The princes also had the main road, sixteen usabhas wide, decorated in the same manner within the areas under their authority.
9:
The King went to the boundary of his domain (near the city of Ketumatī), paid homage to the Teacher, and weeping, said, "Dear sons, you go as if you were plucking out and taking away my right eye. Since you are taking Him away, serve the Buddhas in a fitting and proper manner. Do not live heedlessly like drunkards." The princes replied, "We understand, Great King." They escorted the Teacher, built and offered a monastery, and while serving the Teacher there, they would sometimes stand in the place of the senior elder, sometimes in the place of the middle elder, and sometimes in the place of the newly ordained monk. When they examined their offerings, the gifts of all three brothers were identical.

As the time for the rains retreat approached, they thought, "How can we truly capture the Teacher's heart?" Then the thought occurred to them: "Buddhas are those who honor the Dhamma, not material offerings. If we establish ourselves in virtue (Sīla), we shall be able to capture the Teacher's heart." Therefore, they summoned the people in charge of the offerings and instructed them, "Friends, continue the offerings by providing gruel, rice, and hard food in this same manner," and thus they cut off the anxiety (palibodha) of managing the offerings.

Then, the eldest brother took five hundred men, established himself in the ten precepts, wore two saffron-dyed robes, and lived using only allowable water. The middle brother did the same with three hundred men, and the youngest with two hundred men. These three brothers served the Teacher for the rest of their lives. The Teacher also attained parinibbāna in their presence.

After they passed away, they wandered from the human world to the deva world and from the deva world to the human world for ninety-two aeons. In the time of our Teacher, they passed away from the deva world and were reborn in the human world. The great minister who had been diligent in the alms-hall was reborn as Bimbisāra, the King of Aṅga and Magadha. The three princes were reborn into wealthy brahmin families in that same King's realm. The eldest brother was born as the eldest, and the middle and youngest brothers were born as the middle and youngest respectively. Those who were their attendants then were also born as their attendants now. When they reached maturity, the three of them took those thousand men, went forth as ascetics (tāpasas), and lived on the banks of the river in the Uruvelā forest. The inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha brought them great honors and offerings month after month.
10:
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having made the Great Renunciation and gradually attaining omniscience, set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion. After disciplining noble sons such as Yasa and others, he sent sixty Arahants to various regions to preach the Dhamma. He himself, taking his bowl and robes, went to the Uruvelā forest with the thought, "I shall discipline those three ascetic brothers." By means of many miracles, he destroyed their wrong views and ordained them as monks. The Blessed One, taking those one thousand monks who bore robes and bowls created by psychic power, went to the Gayāsīsa stone slab. While staying there surrounded by those monks, he reflected, "What kind of Dhamma discourse would be suitable for these monks?" He then decided, "These monks constantly worship fire, morning and evening. I shall preach to them by making the twelve bases appear as if they are burning intensely, as if they are ablaze on all sides. If I preach in this way, these monks will be able to attain the fruit of Arahantship."

Then, in order to preach the Dhamma to them in such a manner, he spoke this Ādittapariyāya Sutta. Therefore, it is said, "He addressed the monks," meaning he addressed them with the intention of preaching a Dhamma discourse that was suitable for them after selecting it. In that context, "āditta" (burning) means being intensely burnt and ablaze on all sides by the eleven fires, such as lust (rāga). The remaining terms are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained. Thus, in this Sutta, the characteristic of suffering (dukkhalakkhaṇa) is taught.

## 7. Addhabhūtasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh Sutta, "addhabhūta" means oppressed, overwhelmed, or greatly harassed. In this Sutta as well, only the characteristic of suffering is taught.

## 8. Samugghātasāruppasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth Sutta, "sabbamanyitasamugghātasāruppa" means a Dhamma suitable for the total uprooting of all conceivings through craving, conceit, and wrong view. "Here" means in this Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Buddha. "Does not conceive the eye" means he does not conceive the eye as "I", or as "mine", or as "another", or as "another's". "Does not conceive in the eye" means he does not conceive "I am in the eye", or "my oppressive impediment is in the eye", or "another is in the eye", or "another's oppressive impediment is in the eye". "Does not conceive from the eye" means he does not conceive "I have emerged from the eye", or "my oppressive impediment has emerged from the eye", or "another has emerged from the eye", or "another's oppressive impediment has emerged from the eye". In this manner, he does not conceive; the meaning is that he does not give rise to even one of the conceivings through craving, conceit, and wrong view. "Does not conceive: The eye is mine" means he does not conceive "my eye"; the meaning is that he does not give rise to the conceiving of craving which is the state of taking it as "mine". The remaining terms are clear. In this Sutta, insight (vipassanā) is taught, leading to the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship in forty-four instances.

## 9. Paṭhamasamugghātasappāyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth Sutta, "samugghātasappāya" refers to the Dhamma that is beneficial to the Noble Path which totally uproots (defilements). "Tato taṃ hoti aññathā" means that the object, such as the eye, which is the basis of that conceiving, becomes otherwise than the mode of impermanence, etc., that was conceived. "The world of beings, which is subject to change and attached to existence, delights only in existence" means that even though it is subject to becoming otherwise by arriving at a state different from the moment of arising, and by the transformation through aging and death, this world, being attached to existences, delights only in existence.

"Bhikkhus, as far as there are aggregates, elements, and bases" means, bhikkhus, all the aggregates, elements, and bases as far as they exist. "He does not conceive that aggregate, element, or base either" means that by grouping together the Dhamma already taken below through the method of aggregates, etc., he shows once again the object which is the basis of conceiving. In this Sutta, insight is taught, leading to the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship in forty-eight instances.

## 10. Dutiyasamugghātasappāyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth Sutta, by means of the three phrases "This is mine," etc., the graspings of craving, conceit, and wrong view are shown, and the discourse is given through the method of the three rounds. In sequence, however, in these three Suttas, the four paths are also taught along with insight.

## Sabbavagga, the Third.

## 4. Jātidhammavagga-vaṇṇanā
33-42. In the Jātidhammavagga, "jātidhamma" means a thing that has the nature of being born or the nature of arising. "Jarādhamma" means a thing that has the nature of aging. "Byādidhamma" means a thing that has the nature of sickness because it is the cause for the arising of illness. "Maraṇadhamma" means a thing that has the nature of death. "Sokadhamma" means a thing that has the nature of sorrow because it is the cause for the arising of sorrow. "Saṅkilesikadhamma" means a thing that has the nature of defilement. "Khayadhamma" means a thing that has the nature of reaching destruction. In "vayadhamma" and so on, the method is the same.

## Jātidhammavagga, the Fourth.
12:
## 5. Commentary on the Universal Impermanence Group (Sabba-anicca-vagga)

43-52. In the Impermanence Group (Anicca-vagga), the term "to be known by higher knowledge" (abhiññeyya) refers to the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā). It should be understood that the other two types of full understanding (full understanding by investigation and full understanding by abandoning) are also included. In the terms "to be fully understood" (pariññeyya) and "to be abandoned" (pahātabba), although only full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā) and full understanding by abandoning (pahāna-pariññā) are mentioned, it should be understood that the other two types are also included. "To be realized" (sacchikātabba) means to be made manifest. In the term "to be fully understood by higher knowledge" (abhiññā-pariññeyya), although full understanding by abandoning is not explicitly mentioned, it should be understood as included. "Assailed" (upadduta) means assailed in the sense of not being concentrated on a single object. "Oppressed" (upassaṭṭha) means oppressed in the sense of being afflicted. The rest is clear.

## The Fifth Group: Universal Impermanence.

## The First Fifty [Suttas].

## 6. Commentary on the Ignorance Group (Avijjā-vagga)

53-62. In the Ignorance Group, "ignorance" (avijjā) is non-knowledge (delusion) regarding the Four Noble Truths. "Knowledge" (vijjā) is the knowledge associated with the Path of Arahantship. In the phrase "for one who knows and sees as impermanent" (aniccato jānato passato), [defilements] are indeed abandoned for one who knows and sees by way of suffering and non-self as well. However, in this sutta, it is spoken in terms of impermanence according to the inclination of the person who can be enlightened by that method. This principle is the same in all the suttas. Furthermore, in these suttas, "fetters" (saṃyojanā) refers to the ten fetters. "Taints" (āsavā) refers to the four taints. "Underlying tendencies" (anusayā) refers to the seven underlying tendencies. "For the full understanding of all clinging" (sabbupādānapariññāya) means for the purpose of fully understanding all four types of clinging through the three types of full understanding. "For the exhaustion" (pariyādānāya) means for the purpose of ending [them]. The rest is clear in all places.

## The Sixth Group: Ignorance.

## 7. The Migajāla Group

## 1. Commentary on the First Migajāla Sutta

In the first sutta of the Migajāla Group, "cognizable by the eye" (cakkhuviññeyyā) refers to things that are to be seen by eye-consciousness. The same method applies to "cognizable by the ear," and so on. "Desirable" (iṭṭhā) means whether sought after or...
13:
(...whether sought after or not), they are objects that are desired. "Lovely" (kantā) means desirable. "Agreeable" (manāpā) means those that increase [the pleasure of] the mind. "Endearing" (piyarūpā) means those of a lovable nature. "Connected with sensual desire" (kāmūpasaṃhitā) means connected with sensual desire that arises by making [them] an object. "Arousing lust" (rajanīyā) means those that are the cause for the arising of lust. "Delight" (nandī) is the delight of craving. "Bond" (saṃyoga) is a fetter (saṃyojana). "Bound by the fetter of delight" (nandisaṃyojanasaṃyutta) means bound by the bond of delight.

"Forests and woodland haunts" (araññavanapatthāni) refers to forests and forest dwellings (remote by five hundred bow-lengths). Regarding the term "araññavanapatthāni," although in the Abhidhamma it is stated literally that "everything outside the city gate-post is a forest," here, however, it should be understood that only a forest dwelling that fulfills the factor of a forest-dweller, being "at least five hundred bow-lengths distant," is intended. "Woodland haunt" (vanapattha) is a place beyond the vicinity of a village, not frequented by people, and where there is no plowing or sowing. This has also been stated:

"Woodland haunt is a name for remote dwellings. Woodland haunt is a name for dwellings in a forest thicket. Woodland haunt is a name for frightening dwellings. Woodland haunt is a name for hair-raising dwellings. Woodland haunt is a name for dwellings on the outskirts. Woodland haunt is a name for dwellings not frequented by humans" (as stated in the Vibhaṅga).

Here, setting aside the single synonym "on the outskirts" (pariyantānaṃ) (because it is included in the term "remote" (pantāni)), woodland haunts should be understood by the remaining synonyms. "Remote" (pantāni) means very distant dwellings on the outskirts. "Quiet" (appasaddāni) means quiet due to the absence of sounds such as mortars, pestles, and children. "Few noises" (appanigghosāni) means having few sounds because of the absence of the loud noises and roars of various creatures. "Free from the breath of people" (vijanavātāni) means free from the physical heat and breath of people passing by. "Suitable for seclusion" (manussarāhasseyyakāni) means suitable for the private acts of humans. "Suitable for retreat" (paṭisallānasāruppāni) means suitable for seclusion and withdrawal.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Migajāla Sutta

In the second sutta, "with the cessation of delight comes the cessation of suffering" (nandinirodhā dukkhanirodho) means the cessation of the suffering of the round [of rebirths] through the cessation of the delight of craving.
14:
## 3-5. Commentary on the First Samiddhi Māra Pañhā Sutta, etc.

65-67. In the third sutta, "Samiddhi" is the name received because of the perfection (samiddhatā) of his physical form (attabhāva). It is said that the physical form of that Elder was beautiful and pleasing, like a raised basket of flowers or a decorated flower chamber, perfect in every aspect. Therefore, he was known as Samiddhi. "Māra" refers to the questioning about death. "Māra-paññatti" means the designation or name "Māra". In this context, it shows that there is either death itself or this name "death" (maraṇa). The fourth sutta is very clear in its meaning; likewise, the fifth sutta is also clear.

## 6. Commentary on the Samiddhi Loka Pañhā Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "Loka" (the world) is so called because of its nature of breaking up and disintegrating (lujjana-palujjana). Thus, from the Āyācana Sutta of Elder Migajāla onwards, in all five suttas, only the round of suffering and the cessation of the round (vaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 7. Commentary on the Upasena Āsīvisa Sutta

In the seventh sutta, "Sītavana" refers to the cemetery grove of that name. "Sappasoṇḍika-pabbhāra" refers to the mountain slope/cave named so because of its resemblance to a snake's hood. "Upasenassa" refers to Elder Upasena, the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta). "Āsīviso patito hoti" means a highly venomous snake fell. It is said that the Elder, having finished his meal, took his great robe and sat in the shade of a cave, being fanned by a gentle breeze coming from a window, and was sewing his double-layered undergarment. At that moment, two young snakes were playing on the roof of the cave. One of them fell and landed on the Elder's shoulder. That snake was of a highly poisonous kind. Therefore, from the spot where it fell, the venom spread through the Elder's body like a flame consuming a wick. The Elder, seeing the spread of the venom, although it had reached its limit just by falling, made a determination through his psychic power: "Let not this physical body perish inside the cave," and called the monks. "Before this body is scattered right here" means "Carry it outside before it disintegrates." "Aññathattaṃ" means change or alteration. "Indriyānaṃ vā vipariṇāmaṃ" refers to the [alteration] of the faculties such as the eye, ear, etc...
15:
...meaning the abandonment of the natural state of the faculties. "It scattered right there" means it disintegrated on the couch in the place where it was placed after being carried outside.

## 8. Commentary on the Upavāṇa Sandiṭṭhika Sutta

In the eighth sutta, "Rūpappaṭisaṃvedī" means one who experiences forms by distinguishing objects such as blue, yellow, etc., making the form known (through full understanding). "Rūparāgappaṭisaṃvedī" means one who makes the lust for forms known because of the presence of defilements. The meanings of terms such as "Sandiṭṭhika" should be understood as stated in the Visuddhimagga. "No ca rūparāgappaṭisaṃvedī" means one who does not make the lust for forms known because of the absence of defilements. In this sutta, the reflection (paccavekkhaṇā) of trainees (sekha) and non-trainees (asekha) is taught.

## 9. Commentary on the First Chaphassāyatana Sutta

In the ninth sutta, "Phassāyatanānaṃ" refers to the things that are the bases (causes) of contact. "Avusitaṃ" means that which has not been lived or practiced. "Āraka" means far away. "Venerable Sir, I have perished in this Dispensation; I am one who is lost," the monk said. The Blessed One thought, "This monk says, 'I am lost in this Dispensation'; does he have any application in other meditation subjects such as the elements (dhātu) or kasinas?" Not seeing any such application, He thought, "Which meditation subject would be suitable for him?" Then, seeing that "the meditation on the bases (āyatana) is suitable," He said, "What do you think, monk?" etc., wishing to teach that. "Sādhu" is an expression of joy and praise for his answer. "Esevanto dukkhassa" means this is the end or limit of the suffering of the round, meaning Nibbāna.

## 10. Commentary on the Second Chaphassāyatana Sutta

In the tenth sutta, "Anassasaṃ" means I have perished, I am lost. In the phrase "āyatiṃ apunabbhavāya," "non-becoming in the future" (apunabbhava) means Nibbāna; it means it will be abandoned for the sake of Nibbāna.
16:
## 11. Tatiya-chaphassāyatana-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, 'anassasaṃ' means destroyed. 'panassasaṃ' means utterly destroyed. The remaining terms should be understood in the manner already described.

## Migajālavaggo sattamo.

## 8. Gilānavaggo

## 1-5. Paṭhamagilānasuttādi-vaṇṇanā
74-78. In the first sutta of the Gilāna Chapter, 'amukasmim' means in such and such, or in this and that. There is also this reading. 'Appaññāto' means obscure, one who is not known by name or by virtues such as morality. Although there are newly ordained monks who are well-known, like the Elder Rāhula and the novice Sumana, this monk is both newly ordained and obscure. The remaining terms in this sutta are as already described. Likewise, the four suttas following this should be understood in the same way.

## 6. Paṭhama-avijjāpahāna-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, for one who knows impermanence, ignorance is indeed abandoned even if one knows through the power of suffering and non-self. However, the reason for teaching by showing the characteristic of impermanence in this sutta is according to the inclination (ajjhāsaya) of the person who will realize the Four Noble Truths.

## 7. Dutiya-avijjāpahāna-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the seventh sutta, 'all phenomena' (sabbe dhammā) refers to all phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence. 'Not fit to be adhered to' (nālaṃ abhinivesāya) means it is not proper to grasp them through the misapprehension of adherence such as permanence. 'All signs' (sabba-nimittāni) refers to all signs of conditioned things (the signs of the suffering of the round of rebirth). 'Sees in another way' means seeing through the aspect of non-self, which is different from the aspect of self seen by a person with uncomprehended adherence. Indeed, a person with uncomprehended adherence sees all signs of conditioned things as self. But a person with comprehended adherence (a wise person) sees them only as non-self and not as self. Thus, in this sutta, only the characteristic of non-self is taught.
17:
## 8. Sambahulabhikkhu-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eighth sutta, in the phrase 'idha no', the particle 'no' is merely an expletive. The remaining terms have clear meanings. Specifically, it should be understood that the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) is taught in this sutta.

## 9. Lokapañhā-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'lujjati' means it crumbles or breaks. In this sutta, the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) is taught.

## 10. Phaggunapañhā-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, 'chinnapapañca' means one who has cut through proliferation because craving-proliferation (taṇhā-papañca) has been cut. 'Chinnavatuma' means one who has cut the round because the path of the round of craving (taṇhā-vaṭuma) has been cut. The question 'What shall I ask?' refers to asking about the eye, ear, etc., which were handled by the Buddhas of the past. Alternatively, it is asking whether, even if the path is developed, the round of suffering of the eye, ear, etc., will increase in the future.

## Gilānavaggo aṭṭhamo.

## 9. Channavaggo

## 1. Palokadhamma-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Channa Chapter, 'palokadhamma' refers to phenomena that have the nature of crumbling. Thus, in this sutta, only the characteristic of impermanence is taught.

## 2. Suññataloka-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'attaniyena' means by the requisites that are one's own property. Thus, in this sutta, only the characteristic of non-self is taught.

## 3. Saṅkhittadhamma-sutta-vaṇṇanā
The third sutta should be understood in the same manner as described in the Ānandovāda Sutta of the Khandhavagga Saṃyutta.
18:
## 4. Channa-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'Channa' is the name of this Elder; he is not the Channa (the companion) who followed during the Great Renunciation. 'Paṭisallāna' refers to arising from the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). 'Gilānapucchaka' refers to those who attend to the sick (gilānupaṭṭhāka). Attending to the sick is an action praised by the Blessed One; therefore, he spoke thus. 'Sīsaveṭha' refers to pain in the head, and it means 'would give that headache'. 'Satthaṃ' refers to a weapon (knife) that takes away the life faculty (jīvitindriya). 'Nāvakankhāmi' means 'I do not desire'. 'Pariciṇṇo' means 'having been attended' (paricarita). 'Manāpena' means through bodily actions, etc., that increase the delight of the mind. Here, the seven types of learners (sekha) are called 'those who attend', the Arahant is called 'one who attends', and the Blessed One is called 'the one who is attended'.

'Friend, such an action is suitable for a disciple' means 'Friend, for one called a disciple, such an action is appropriate'. 'Anupavajja' means that which does not cause rebirth to occur again (appavattika, appaṭisandhika). 'Friend Sāriputta, ask; having heard, we shall know' is called the invitation (pavāraṇā) of the disciples. 'This is mine', etc., are taught by the power of grasping through craving, conceit, and views. 'Having seen cessation' means having known destruction and passing away. 'I see it as: this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self' means seeing it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. In these instances, Elder Channa answered the questions asked by Elder Sāriputta by placing them within the context of Arahantship. However, Elder Sāriputta, although knowing that Elder Channa was still a worldling (puthujjana), remained silent without saying 'you are a worldling' or 'you are one whose taints are destroyed'. But Elder Cunda, thinking 'I will make him realize his status as a worldling', gave him an exhortation.

In that exhortation, 'therefore' (tasmā) means: because he says 'I will take up a weapon' (I will kill myself) being unable to endure the pains of nearing death, therefore the venerable one is a worldling; it demonstrates 'therefore, you should also bear this in mind'. Or, because you say 'having seen the cessation of the six sense bases, I do not see the eye, etc., by the power of the three types of grasping (craving, conceit, and views)', therefore the venerable one should also bear in mind this teaching of the Blessed One; thus he speaks, demonstrating only the status of a worldling. 'Niccakappaṃ' means 'at all times'. 'Nissitassa' means for one who relies on craving, conceit, and views. 'Calitaṃ' means there is wavering. Just as for the venerable one who is unable to endure the arisen pain, there is now wavering for one whose grasping is not yet abandoned, thinking 'I feel, it is my pain'; by this also, he says to him, 'You are only a worldling'.
19:
Passaddhi means the tranquility of body and mind, which has the sense of the calming of defilements (kilesas). Nati refers to the inclination towards the object of craving (taṇhā). Asati means when there is no all-around clinging through attachment (ālaya) for a new existence or through desire (nikanti). 'No coming and going' (āgatigati) means there is neither 'coming' (āgati) by way of rebirth nor 'going' (gati) from this life by way of death. Cutūpapāta refers to 'falling away' (cuti) by way of passing away and 'reappearing' (upapāta) by way of being reborn. 'Neither in this world, nor in the next world, nor in between the two' means it does not occur in this present world, nor in the future world; thus, it means it does not exist in both the present and the future.

'This is the end of suffering' means the end, the limit, and the state of having the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) severed, specifically the suffering of the round and the suffering of defilements. This is the intended meaning in this context. As for those teachers who, taking the phrase 'in between the two,' desire an intermediate state (antarābhava), their words are without merit. The existence of an intermediate state has already been rejected in the Abhidhamma (Kathāvatthu). The word 'antarena' (in between) merely indicates another alternative (vikappa) from the previous one. Therefore, the meaning here is: neither in this world, nor in the next, nor in the other alternative, which is both.

'He took the weapon' means he took a life-ending weapon, such as a knife, and cut his throat. At that moment, the fear of death overcame the Elder Channa, and the sign of his destiny (gati-nimitta) appeared. Realizing his status as a worldling (puthujjana), he felt a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), established insight (vipassanā), and while contemplating conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāras), he attained Arahantship and passed away as a Samasīsī (one who simultaneously attains the end of defilements and the end of life). 'The declaration of being blameless even in the presence [of death]' means that although this declaration was made while the Elder was still a worldling, it was because of this very declaration that his Parinibbāna occurred without obstacles. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke by taking up that very declaration from his time as a worldling.

Upavajjakulāni refers to families that should be approached or visited. With these words, the Elder Sāriputta asks, showing the fault of associating with families during the preliminary stage of practice: 'Venerable Sir, while such male and female lay supporters exist, will that bhikkhu attain Parinibbāna in your Dispensation?' Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show the absence of entanglement with families, said: 'Sāriputta, these families exist,' and so on. In this context, the Elder's state of being unentangled with families became clear. The rest of the words are clear in meaning in all places.

## 5-6. Commentary on the Puṇṇa Sutta and Others

88-89. In the fifth sutta, 'tañca' refers to that eye and that form. 'From the arising of delight comes the arising of suffering' means that due to the combination of craving (taṇhā), which is the origin (samudaya), there is the collective arising of the suffering of the five aggregates.
20:
Thus, regarding the six sense doors, by saying 'from the arising of delight comes the arising of suffering,' He showed the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) by bringing it to its peak through the power of the two truths (Suffering and Origin). In the second method, by saying 'cessation is the path,' He showed the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa) by bringing it to its peak through the power of the two truths (Cessation and Path). 'In this way, you, Puṇṇa...' is a separate connection (anusandhi). Thus, having first established the teaching at the level of Arahantship through the power of the round and its ending, He now spoke the words 'In this way, you...' and so on, to make the Elder Puṇṇa roar his lion's roar (sīhanāda) in seven situations.

Caṇḍā means those who are fierce and loathsome. Pharusā means those who are harsh. 'They will abuse' means they will abuse with the ten grounds for abuse. 'They will threaten' means they will threaten by saying, 'Why are you called a monk? We will do this and that to you.' 'In such a place' means 'in such a situation of being threatened, my reflection will be thus.' 'With a staff' refers to a four-cubit staff, a staff made of khadira wood, or a club (muggara). 'With a weapon' refers to a single-edged weapon and so on. 'They will seek a life-ending weapon'—the Elder said this referring to the monks in the story of the third Pārājika who, after hearing the discourse on foulness (asubha-kathā), became disgusted with their own bodies and sought weapons to end their lives. In the phrase 'damūpasamena,' the name 'dama' is a name for sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara) and so on.

'One who is tamed by truth, endowed with dama (sense restraint), who has reached the end of the Vedas (knowledge), and has lived the holy life...'
In this context, sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara) is called 'dama.'

'If there exists in this world anything superior to truth, dama (wisdom), generosity, and patience...'
In this context, wisdom (paññā) is called 'dama.'

'By generosity, by dama (observing the Uposatha), by self-control, and by truthful speech...'
In this context, the act of observing the Uposatha (uposatha-kamma) is called 'dama.'

In this sutta, however, patience (khanti) should be understood as 'dama.' 'Upasama' is simply a synonym for that 'dama.'

'Then the Venerable Puṇṇa...'—In this context, who is this Puṇṇa, and why did he want to go there? He was indeed a native of the Sunāparanta country. However, having noticed that living in Sāvatthī was unsuitable, he wished to go to that Sunāparanta.
21:
In this context (regarding the term 'inhabitant of Sunāparanta'), this is the sequential account: It is said that in a certain merchant village in the country of Sunāparanta, there were these two brothers. Among these two brothers, sometimes the elder brother (Mahāpuṇṇa) would take five hundred carts to the countryside to bring back trade goods; sometimes the younger brother (Cūḷapuṇṇa) would do so. At this particular time, however, the elder brother, having left the younger brother at home and taking five hundred carts, was traveling through the countryside and eventually reached Sāvatthī. Having parked the caravan of carts not far from the Jetavana monastery and finished his morning meal, he sat in a suitable place surrounded by his attendants.

At that time, the inhabitants of Sāvatthī, having finished their morning meal, undertook the uposatha precepts. Wearing clean upper robes and carrying perfumes, flowers, and so on in their hands, they were inclined, leaned, and tended toward where the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha were. They exited through the south gate and went toward the Jetavana monastery. Mahāpuṇṇa, seeing them, asked a man, "Where are these people going?" The man replied, "Sir, do you not know? The three jewels—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—have appeared in the world. Therefore, this multitude of people is going to the presence of the Teacher to listen to the Dhamma talk." For Mahāpuṇṇa, the word "Buddha" pierced through his skin, flesh, and so on, and remained fixed reaching the bone marrow. Surrounded by his attendants, he went to the monastery along with that crowd. While the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma with a sweet voice, he stood at the edge of the assembly. Having heard the Dhamma, the thought of ordaining arose in him. Then, the Teacher, knowing the right time, dismissed the assembly. Mahāpuṇṇa approached the Teacher, paid homage, and invited Him for the next day's meal. On the second day, he had a pavilion built, prepared seats, and gave a great offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. After finishing his morning meal, he undertook the uposatha precepts, summoned his treasurer, and said, "This much wealth has been spent; this much wealth has not yet been spent," explaining everything. He handed over everything, saying, "Give this property to my younger brother." He then ordained in the presence of the Teacher and became one devoted to meditation (kammaṭṭhāna).

Then, while he was reflecting on the meditation subject, the meditation subject did not become clear to him. He then thought, "This countryside is not suitable for me. What if I take a meditation subject from the Teacher and go back to my own country?" Then, having wandered for alms in the morning and risen from seclusion in the evening, he approached the Blessed One, asked for a meditation subject to be taught, and after roaring words like the seven-fold lion's roar, he departed. For that reason, it is said (in the Pali text), "Then the Venerable Puṇṇa... lived..."
22:
Where did he stay? He stayed in four places. First, having entered the country of Sunāparanta and reached the mountain named Abbuhattha, he entered the merchant village for alms. Then, his younger brother Cūḷapuṇṇa recognized him, offered him alms-food, and made him promise, "Venerable sir, do not go elsewhere; please stay right here." Thus, he made him stay there.

From there, he went to the monastery named Samuddagiri. In that monastery, there was a walkway (caṅkama) demarcated with magnetic stones; no one was able to walk on that walkway. There, the ocean waves would come and strike the magnetic stones, making a loud noise. The Elder resolved, "May it be a pleasant stay for the monks who are reflecting on their meditation subjects," and he made the ocean silent.

From there, he went to the monastery named Mātulagiri. There, too, the flocks of birds were so numerous that the sound of birds was continuous day and night. The Elder reflected, "This place is not pleasant," and from there, he went to the monastery named Makulakārāma. That Makulakārāma monastery was neither too far from nor too close to the merchant village, easy to reach, secluded, and quiet. The Elder thought, "This place is pleasant," and having had night quarters, day quarters, and walkways prepared there, he entered the rains retreat (vassa). Thus, he stayed in these four places.

Then one day, during that very rains retreat, five hundred merchants, thinking "We shall go to the other side of the ocean," loaded trade goods onto a ship. On the day of boarding the ship, the Elder's younger brother, Cūḷapuṇṇa, fed the Elder, took the precepts in the Elder's presence, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, the ocean is untrustworthy and full of many dangers; please keep us in your thoughts." Having said this, he boarded the ship. As the ship was traveling with great speed, it reached a small island. The people went ashore on the island, thinking, "We shall have our morning meal." On that island, there were no other trees, but only a forest of sandalwood.

Then, one man struck a tree with an axe and, realizing it was red sandalwood (lohitacandana), said, "Friends, we are going to the other side of the ocean for the sake of gain, but there is no gain greater than what is on this island. Even a piece of sandalwood four inches long is worth a hundred thousand pieces of money. Therefore, let us discard the goods that should be discarded and fill the ship with sandalwood." Those merchants did exactly as he said.
23:
(The merchants) did so. The non-human beings (amanussa) dwelling in the sandalwood forest became angry and thought, "These people have destroyed our sandalwood forest; we shall kill them." Then they thought, "If we kill them right here on this island, the whole island will be filled with rotting corpses. We shall sink their ship in the middle of the ocean." When the merchants' ship had departed and traveled for just a moment, great waves arose, and those non-human beings revealed terrifying forms. The frightened people worshipped their respective deities. Cūḷapuṇṇa the householder, the younger brother of the Elder, stood worshipping the Elder (recalling the name Puṇṇa), saying, "May my elder brother be my refuge."

The Elder, too, reflecting at that very moment and knowing that they were facing destruction, flew into the sky and stood before the ship. As soon as the non-human beings saw the Elder, they said, "The Venerable Puṇṇa Thera has come," and they departed. The great waves also subsided. The Elder comforted them, saying, "Do not be afraid," and asked, "Where do you wish to go?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, we wish to go only to our own home." The Elder stepped onto the deck of the ship and made a resolution: "May they reach their desired destination." When the merchants reached their home, they told the news to their wives and children, saying, "Come, let us go to the Elder for refuge." Thus, the five hundred merchants, together with their five hundred wives, established themselves in the Three Refuges and declared themselves lay followers (upāsakas). Then, unloading the goods from the ship, they set aside one portion for the Elder and said, "Venerable Sir, this portion is for you." The Elder said, "I have no need for a separate portion. Have you ever seen the Buddha?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, we have never seen Him." "If so," the Elder said, "build a circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāla) for the Buddha with this portion of sandalwood. In this way, you shall see the Buddha." They agreed, saying, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and began to build the circular pavilion using that portion as well as their own portions.

The Buddha, it is said, made use of that pavilion from the time its construction began. The guards saw a light at night and thought, "There is a deity of great power." The lay followers completed the circular pavilion and the dwellings for the community of monks, prepared the offerings, and informed the Elder, "Venerable Sir, our task is finished; please invite the Buddha." In the evening, the Elder went to Sāvatthī by psychic power and requested the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, the villagers of Vāṇijagāma wish to see You..."
24:
"...please show compassion to them, Venerable Sir." The Buddha accepted. The Elder returned to his own place.

The Buddha then addressed the Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, tomorrow we shall wander for alms in the merchant village of Sunāparanta. Give the voting tickets (salāka) to four hundred and ninety-nine monks." The Elder replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and informed the community of monks, saying, "Let the monks who can travel through the air take the voting tickets." On that day, the Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna took the first ticket. The villagers of Vāṇijagāma, knowing that "Tomorrow the Buddha will arrive," built a pavilion in the middle of the village and prepared the alms-hall.

Early in the morning, the Buddha performed His bodily ablutions, entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), and sat down, entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). At that time, Sakka's Pandukambala stone throne became hot. Sakka reflected, "What is the reason for this?" and seeing the Buddha's journey to Sunāparanta, he called the celestial architect Vissakamma and ordered, "Dear son, today the Buddha will travel for alms a distance of about three hundred yojanas. Create five hundred peaked palatial vehicles (kūṭāgāra), and place them above the gateway of the Jetavana monastery, ready for departure."

Vissakamma did as Sakka commanded. The Buddha's palatial vehicle had four faces; those of the two Chief Disciples had two faces each, and the remaining ones had one face each. The Buddha emerged from the Fragrant Chamber and entered the foremost of the palatial vehicles arranged in order. Starting with the two Chief Disciples, the four hundred and ninety-nine monks also boarded their respective palatial vehicles. One palatial vehicle remained empty. All five hundred palatial vehicles then rose into the sky.

When the Buddha reached the Saccabandha Mountain, He caused the palatial vehicles to stop in the sky. On that mountain lived a wrong-viewed ascetic named Saccabandha, who was teaching wrong views to the people and had reached the pinnacle of gain and fame. However, within him, the potential (upanissaya) for the fruit of Arahatship was glowing like a lamp inside a jar. Seeing that potential, the Buddha went there to preach the Dhamma to him. At the end of the discourse, the ascetic attained Arahatship. Along with the Path, the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) also arrived. He became an "Ehi Bhikkhu" monk, and bearing the robes and bowl created by psychic power, he entered the empty palatial vehicle.
25:
The Blessed One, together with five hundred monks traveling in celestial mansions, went to the village of Vāṇijagāma. Having made the celestial mansions invisible, he entered Vāṇijagāma. The merchants offered a great donation to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and invited the Teacher to the Makulakārāma monastery (the Sandalwood monastery). The Teacher entered the monastery grounds. While the Teacher rested to dispel physical fatigue, the multitude of people had their morning meal, undertook the Uposatha precepts, and taking many perfumes and flowers, returned to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. The Teacher preached the Dhamma. For the multitude, there was liberation from bonds, and a great Buddha-uproar (Buddha-kolāhala) arose.

To favor the multitude, the Teacher stayed there for seven days; however, at dawn, he would always remain in the Great Fragrant Chamber (Mahāgandhakuṭī). At the end of the Dhamma teaching throughout those seven days, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya). Having stayed there for seven days and wandered for alms in Vāṇijagāma, he instructed the Elder Puṇṇa, saying, "You remain right here," and then proceeded to the bank of the river named Nammada, which lay on his journey. The Naga King Nammada welcomed the Teacher, invited him to the Naga realm, and made offerings to the Triple Gem. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to the Naga King and departed from the Naga realm. The Naga King requested, "Venerable Sir, please give me an object of worship to be constantly revered." The Blessed One showed a footprint-shrine (pādacetiya) on the bank of the Nammada River. That footprint is covered when the waves come and revealed when the waves recede. It became an object of great honor from various regions. The Teacher departed from there and went to Saccabandha Mountain, where he said to the Elder Saccabandha: "You have led many people down the path to the lower realms. Stay right here, make them abandon their wrong views, and establish them on the path to Nibbāna." That Elder Saccabandha also requested an object of worship. The Teacher showed a footprint-shrine on a solid stone slab, as if a seal were pressed into a lump of moist clay. From there, he proceeded to the Jetavana monastery. With reference to this matter, it is said, "tene'va antaravassena," and so forth.

"Parinibbāyi" means attaining Parinibbāna (extinguishment) through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). The multitude performed the funeral rites for the Elder's body for seven days, and after piling up many pieces of scented wood and cremating the body, they took the relics and built a stupa (cetiya). "Sambahulā Bhikkhū" refers to the monks standing at the Elder's cremation site. The remaining words are clear in every respect. The sixth (Bāhiya Sutta) is also clear in meaning.
