## 7-8. Commentary on the First Ejā Sutta and Others
90-91. In the seventh sutta, "ejā" means craving (taṇhā). It is called "ejā" because of its nature of trembling. That same craving is called a "disease" (roga) in the sense of oppressing, a "boil" (gaṇḍa) in the sense of destroying from within, and a "dart" (salla) in the sense of piercing and penetrating. "Therefore" means because craving is a disease, a boil, and a dart. The phrase "cakkhuṃ na maññeyya" (one should not conceive the eye) and so forth follows the method already explained; in this sutta as well, all the dhammas previously mentioned are shown in combination. The eighth sutta also follows the method already explained.

## 9-10. Commentary on the First Dvaya Sutta and Others
92-93. In the ninth sutta, "dvaya" means groups of pairs. In the tenth sutta, "itthetaṃ dvayaံ" means "thus these two dhammas." "Calañceva byathañca" means it both trembles and wavers because it cannot remain stable in its own nature. "Yo pi hetu yo pi paccayo" means the base (vatthu) and the object (ārammaṇa) of eye-consciousness are called both cause (hetu) and condition (paccayo). "Kuto niccaṃ bhavissati" means for what reason would it be permanent, or how could it be permanent? To give an example, just as a child born from the womb of a male slave and a female slave is certainly a slave, so too, a dhamma born of impermanent causes is certainly impermanent—this is the meaning. "Saṅgati" means occurring together. "Sannipāta" means meeting together. "Samavāya" means coming together in union. By the phrase "ayaṃ vuccati cakkhusamphasso," this combination of the three—saṅgati, sannipāta, and samavāya—is called eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa) because it arises due to the condition known as the meeting, the falling together, and the union.

"That cause also" refers to the base of contact, the object, and the three associated aggregates; these are the causes. Regarding "phuṭṭho," here the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative; it means that feeling experiences only the object touched by contact, volition performs its function, and perception marks it. Alternatively, "phuṭṭho" means the person endowed with contact experiences, performs, and marks only the object touched by contact through feeling and so forth. Thus, in this sutta, thirty aggregates are taught. How? In the eye-door, first, the base and the object are the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha); the feeling that "experiences upon touching" is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha); the volition that "performs" is the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha); the perception that "marks" is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha); and the consciousness that "cognizes" is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). The same method applies to the remaining doors. In the mind-door as well, the physical base is certainly the aggregate of matter; if the object is a material form, the object is also the aggregate of matter. Thus, there are six groups of five, making thirty. In brief, however, in those six doors...
27:
"Only the five aggregates exist" means that when the five aggregates, along with their causes, are taught in detail as impermanent, this sutta was taught according to the inclination of those beings who are capable of understanding.

## The Ninth Chapter: Channa.

## 10. The Saḷa Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Adanta-agutta Sutta

In the first sutta of the Saḷa Chapter, 'adantā' means (minds) that are untamed. 'Aguttā' means (minds) that are not made secure. 'Arakkhitā' means (minds) that are not protected by the protection of mindfulness. 'Asaṃvutā' means (minds) that are not closed off by the bolt of restraint. 'Dukkhādhivāhā honti' means they bring about excessive suffering characterized by hell and so forth. 'Sukhādhivāhā honti' means they bring about excessive happiness characterized by jhāna, path, and fruition. There is also a reading 'adhivahā', which has the same meaning.

'Saḷevā' means only the six. 'Asaṃvuto yattha dukkhaṃ nigacchati' means in whichever sense bases a person devoid of restraint reaches suffering. 'Tesañca ye saṃvaraṇaṃ avedisuṃ' means those who have obtained the protection of those sense bases. 'Viharantānavassutā' means they live without being moistened by defilements.

'Asāditañca sādum' means (an object) that is both delightful and sweet. 'Phassadvayaṃ sukhadukkhe upekkhe' means one should be equanimous towards these two touches: pleasant touch and painful touch; the meaning is that one should arouse only equanimity here. There is also a reading 'phassadvayaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ upekkho', meaning one who is equanimous towards the pleasure and pain born of touch should be one who is equanimous without arousing liking for pleasure or opposition to pain. 'Anānuruddho aviruddho kenaci' means one should be neither in agreement nor in opposition with anyone.

'Papañcasaññā' means having become what is called the perception of proliferation through the perception of defilements. 'Itarītarā narā' means low beings. 'Papañcayantā upayanti' means while proliferating defilements, they approach the round of rebirth. 'Saññino' means beings with perception. 'Manomayaṃ gehasitañca sabbaṃ' means all thoughts produced by the mind that are based on the home of the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Panujja' means having expelled or removed. 'Nekkhamma-sitaṃ irīyati' means a monk of noble birth conducts himself with behavior based on renunciation from sensual pleasures.
28:
"When it is well-developed in the six sense objects" means being well-developed in the six sense objects. "The mind does not tremble or shake in any object" means the mind of a monk who is touched by either a pleasant contact or a painful contact does not tremble or shake in any object. "Be those who reach the further shore of birth and death" means be those who go to Nibbāna, which is the further shore of birth and death.

## 2. Mālunkyaputtasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "Mālunkyaputta" refers to the son of the Brahmin woman Mālunkyā. With the words "in this (your request for instruction)," the Blessed One both rebuked and encouraged the Elder. How? It is said that this Elder Mālunkyaputta was negligent regarding visible forms and so on in his youth, and later, in his old age, he desired to live in the forest and requested a meditation subject. Then the Blessed One, with the intention of saying, "If you request instruction in your old age like this, what shall I say to the young monks? Should I say: 'Like the old monk Mālunkyaputta, you too should be negligent in your youth and only enter the forest to practice the Dhamma of a recluse when you are old'?", rebuked the Elder.

However, because the Elder desired to enter the forest and practice the Dhamma of a recluse even in his old age, the Blessed One, with the intention of saying, "Even though you are old, you request instruction; what shall I say to the young monks? I shall say: 'This Mālunkyaputta of ours, even in his old age, desires to enter the forest and practice the Dhamma of a recluse and requests a meditation subject; but you do not make an effort even in your youth'", encouraged the Elder.

"Yatra hi nāma" means "such as." In the Pali "kiñcāpāhaṃ," the words should be analyzed as "kiñcāpi ahaṃ." It is understood as "I am old." With the intention, "Even if I am old, I will be able to practice the Dhamma of a recluse; may the Blessed One, O Lord, teach me," he spoke thus, accepting his state of being old and desiring to praise the instruction.

"Those not seen before" means those not seen in this present existence, and also not seen before in the past. Visible forms known by eye-consciousness exist. "You do not see them now" means you do not see those visible forms even at this present time. "If you do not have the attention of wanting to see" means the Blessed One asks, "If you do not have such attention of wanting to see, would desire and affection for those visible forms arise in you?"

"In the seen, there will be only the seen" means when a visible form is seen by eye-consciousness, it will be only the seen. Eye-consciousness sees only the visible form in the visible form, not its nature such as permanence. Thus, the meaning is: "With the remaining consciousnesses, my mind will be only the seen in this visible form." Alternatively (atha)...
29:
Alternatively, in the seen, what is called 'the seen' is eye-consciousness, meaning the cognizing of a visible form in a visible form. 'Matta' means measure (extent). Because it has the measure of only the seen aspect, it is called 'diṭṭhamatta' (merely the seen). It means: 'My mind will be merely the measure of eye-consciousness.' The meaning is this: Just as eye-consciousness is not lustful, not hateful, and not deluded regarding a visible form that has come into range, in the same way, through the absence of lust and so on, the impulsion (javana) will be merely the measure of eye-consciousness; I will establish the impulsion only within the measure of eye-consciousness. Or else, 'the seen' (diṭṭha) is the visible form seen by eye-consciousness. 'Merely the seen' (diṭṭhamatta) in the seen refers to the three types of consciousness—receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), and determining (voṭṭhabbana)—that arise right there in that visible form. Just as those types of consciousness are not lustful, not hateful, and not deluded, in the same way, I will cause the impulsion to arise only within the measure of those types of consciousness like receiving and so on regarding a visible form that has come into range; I will not allow it to arise by way of lust and so on by exceeding that measure—this is the meaning here. The same method applies to the heard (suta) and the sensed (muta).

In the phrase 'in the cognized, there will be only the cognized' (viññāte viññātamattaṃ), 'the cognized' (viññāta) refers to the object cognized by mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana). 'Merely the cognized' in that cognized object refers to the measure of the adverting consciousness. Just as one is not lustful, not hateful, and not deluded when reflecting with the adverting consciousness, in the same way, I will establish the mind only within the measure of the adverting consciousness without giving it the opportunity to arise by way of lust and so on—this is the meaning here.

'Yato' means when. 'Tato' means then. 'Na tena' means one will not be lustful with that lust, hateful with that hatred, or deluded with that delusion. 'Mālukyaputta, then you are not in that' means when you are not lustful, hateful, or deluded by that lust, hatred, or delusion, then you will not be bound to, attached to, or established in that seen, heard, sensed, or cognized object. The phrases beginning with 'neither here' have the same meaning as already stated.

'Sati muṭṭhā' means the loss of mindfulness. 'Tañca ajjhosā' means having swallowed (clung to) that object. 'Abhijjhā ca vihesā ca' refers to covetousness and harming (vexation). Alternatively, it should be connected with the phrase 'tassa vaḍḍhanti', meaning these two states, covetousness and harming, also increase for him.

'Cittamassūpahanyatī' means his mind is oppressed by covetousness and harming. 'Ācinato' means for one who accumulates and increases (defilements). 'Ārā nibbāna vuccatī' means for a person of such a nature, Nibbāna is said to be far away. 'Ghatvā' means having smelled. 'Bhotvā' means having eaten (tasted, touched, or known).
30:
Having licked, having eaten. 'Phussa' means having touched. 'Paṭissato' means one who is endowed with mindfulness known as 'paṭissati'. 'Sevato cāpi vedanaṃ' refers to one who partakes in the supramundane feeling that has arisen, associated with the four paths. 'Khīyati' means it reaches destruction. What is destroyed? Both suffering and the collection of defilements. 'Aññataro' means one among the eighty great disciples. Thus, in this sutta, even through the verses, only the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## 3. Commentary on the Parihānadhamma Sutta
In the third sutta, 'parihānadhammaṃ' means the nature of decline. 'Abhibhāyatanāni' means the bases that are overcome. In the term 'sarasaṅkappā', they are called 'sara' because they run (saranti). Because those states both run and are thoughts (vitakka), they are called 'sarasaṅkappā'. 'Saṃyojaniyā' refers to states that are bound by fetters or are the cause of fetters. 'Tañce bhikkhū' refers to either that collection of defilements that has arisen or that object. 'Adhivāseti' means placing it in the mind and allowing it to dwell. 'Nappajahati' means not abandoning by way of abandoning desire and lust (chanda-rāga). In this way, it should be connected with all the terms. 'Abhibhāyatanñhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā' means the Blessed One taught this defilement as a base to be overcome. In this sutta, the Dhamma is shown by way of a person who questions and analyzes the Dhamma.

## 4. Commentary on the Pamādavihārī Sutta
In the fourth sutta, 'asaṃvutassa' refers to one who is not closed off by mindfulness but remains wide open. 'Byāsiñcati' means it especially pours over; it exists being moistened by defilements. 'Pāmojja' is weak rapture (pīti). 'Pīti' is strong rapture. 'Passaddhi' is the calming of distress. 'Dhammā na pātubhavanti' means the states of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) do not arise. In this sutta, the person is shown by way of the Dhamma that questions and analyzes the person.

## 5. Commentary on the Saṃvara Sutta
In the fifth sutta, regarding the words "Bhikkhus, how is there lack of restraint?", it should be understood that this is taught by way of explaining the state to be abandoned first, due to skill in teaching, just as one skilled in directions might say, "Leave the left path and take the right path," first mentioning the path to be avoided. In this sutta, the Dhamma is questioned and only the Dhamma is analyzed.
31:
## 6. Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta

In the sixth sutta, concentration (*samādhi*) refers to one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*). This sutta was taught because the Buddha saw monks declining in concentration and knew, "If these monks attain one-pointedness of mind, their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) will reach growth and prosperity."

## 7. Commentary on the Paṭisallāna Sutta

In the seventh sutta, seclusion (*paṭisallāna*) refers to bodily seclusion (*kāyaviveka*). This sutta was taught because the Buddha saw monks declining in bodily seclusion and knew, "If these monks attain bodily seclusion, their meditation subject will reach growth and prosperity."

## 8-9. Commentary on the First Natumhāka Sutta, etc.

101-102. The eighth sutta was taught according to the inclination of those who would understand easily when surrounded by similes. The ninth sutta was taught according to the inclination of those who would understand easily through plain teaching without similes. The meaning in both suttas should be understood in the same manner as stated in the *Khandhiya Vagga*.

## 10. Commentary on the Udaka Sutta

In the tenth sutta, in the phrase "udako suda," the word "suda" is merely a particle (*nipāta*) without its own meaning. "Udaka" is the name of that person. In the phrase "idaṃ jātu vedagū," "idaṃ" is merely a particle. Alternatively, it is said in this way to show, "Listen to these words of mine." "Jātu vedagū" means "I am certainly one who has reached the truths to be known through the knowledge (*ñāṇa*) called *veda*," or it means "I am a wise person who has attained the *veda*." "Sabbajī" means "I am one who stands having certainly conquered and overcome the entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*)." "Apaliikhataṃ gaṇḍamūlaṃ" refers to the unexcavated root of suffering. "Palikhani" means "I have dug all around; I am one who stands having dug it up."

"Mātāpettikasambhavassa" refers to the body produced from the semen and blood of both parents, born from both mother and father. "Odanakummāsūpacayassa" refers to the body that has grown and been nourished by boiled rice and bread/gruel. In the phrase "aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammassa," this body is of an impermanent nature (*aniccadhamma*) because it ceases to exist after having arisen. It is of a nature to be anointed (*ucchādanadhamma*) by applying perfumes to remove bad odors. It is of a nature to be massaged (*parimaddanadhamma*) by gentle rubbing to remove aches in the limbs.
32:
Also, in childhood, it is of a nature to be massaged through pulling and pressing to perfect the shape of various limbs that became distorted due to lying on the thighs or being in the mother's womb. Even when cared for and nourished in this way, it is of a nature to break and disintegrate (*bhedanaviddhaṃsanadhamma*); it both breaks and scatters. This is its nature—this is the meaning.

Among those terms, growth (*vaḍḍhi*) is taught by the words "born of parents," "nourished by rice and bread," and "massaged." Decline (*parihāni*) is taught by the words "impermanent," "breaking," and "disintegrating." Alternatively, arising (*samudaya*) is taught by the first three terms, and passing away (*atthangama*) is taught by the latter terms. In this way, the growth, decline, arising, and breaking of the body made of the four great elements are shown. The rest of the words have very clear meanings.

## The tenth, the Saḷa Vagga, is finished.

## The second Paṇṇāsaka is finished.

## 11. The Yogakkhemi Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Yogakkhemi Sutta

In the first sutta of the Yogakkhemi Vagga, "yogakkhemipariyāya" refers to the cause of being safe from the four bonds (*yoga*). "Dhammapariyāya" refers to the cause of the Dhamma (the cause of knowing the *pariyatti dhamma*). "He taught the yoga" means he taught the cause, which is the suitable means consisting of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). Regarding the word "Therefore," why? Is it because it was taught, or because it was abandoned? It is because it was abandoned. Indeed, one does not become "safe from bonds" (*yogakkhemi*) merely by the teaching.

## 2-10. Commentary on the Upādāya Sutta and others

105-113. In the second sutta, pleasure and pain as feelings (*vedanā*) are taught; those should be understood as resultant (*vipāka*) pleasure and pain. In the third sutta, "of suffering" refers to the suffering of the cycle (*vaṭṭadukkha*). In the fourth sutta, "of the world" refers to the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*). In the fifth sutta and those following, the words to be explained follow the method already stated in the *Khandhiya Vagga*.

## The eleventh, the Yogakkhemi Vagga, is finished.
33:
## 12. Lokakāmaguṇavagga
## 1-2. Commentary on the First Mārapāsa Sutta, etc.

114-115. In the first sutta of the Lokakāmaguṇavagga, 'āvāsagato' means one who has gone to a dwelling place. 'Mārassa vasaṃ gato' means falling under the power of the three kinds of Māra. 'Paṭimukkassa mārapāso' means that the snare of Māra, which is craving (taṇhā), is cast or placed around that person's neck. The second sutta is clear in its meaning.

## 3. Commentary on the Lokantagamana Sutta

In the third sutta, 'lokassa' refers to the world of space (okāsaloka), which is the universe (cakkavāḷa). 'Lokassa antaṃ' refers to the end of the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). 'Vihāraṃ pāvisi' (He entered the monastery) means that the Buddha thought: "When I enter the monastery, these monks will ask Ānanda about this brief teaching. Ānanda will then explain it to those monks in accordance with my Omniscient Knowledge. At that time, I will praise Ānanda. Upon hearing my praise, the monks will regard Ānanda as one who should be approached, whose words should be listened to, and who should be trusted. Such an occurrence will lead to the long-term welfare and happiness of those monks." Having thus reflected, without explaining in detail the meaning of the Dhamma taught in brief, he disappeared from his seat and appeared in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). Therefore, it is said, 'uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ pāvisi' (rising from his seat, he entered the monastery).

Because he is praised by the Teacher, it is said 'satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito'. The term 'viññūnaṃ' is in the genitive case with the sense of the instrumental (karaṇattha); it means being praised by wise fellow-practitioners. 'Pahoti' means he is able. 'Atikkammeva mūlaṃ atikkammeva khandhaṃ' means that essence (sāra) might reside in the root or the trunk; the meaning is surpassing even that root and trunk which contain the essence. 'Evaṃsampadamidaṃ' means possessing such success or attainment, or having such a nature. 'Atisitvā' means having surpassed. 'Jānaṃ jānāti' means he knows only that which is to be known. 'Passaṃ passati' means he sees only that which is to be seen. Otherwise, just as some people, though knowing, do not know correctly due to perversion, and though seeing, do not see correctly, the Blessed One is not like that. The Blessed One, being one who knows, truly knows; being one who sees, truly sees. That Blessed One is called 'Cakkhubhūta' (Become the Eye) because he leads to the right path. He is called 'Ñāṇabhūta' (Become Knowledge) because he performs what is to be known. He is called 'Dhammabhūta' (Become the Dhamma) because of his non-perverted nature, or because he brings forth the Pariyatti Dhamma, having thought it with his mind and expressed it with his speech. He is called 'Brahmabhūta' (Become the Sublime) because of his excellence. Alternatively, he is called 'Cakkhubhūta' because he has become like an eye. In this way, the meaning of these terms should be understood.
34:
Because he teaches the Dhamma, he is called 'Vattā' (the Speaker). Because he sets the Dhamma in motion, he is called 'Pavattā' (the Proclaimer). Because he is capable of repeatedly drawing out and showing the meaning, he is called 'Ninneta' (the Extractor of meaning). Because he teaches the practice for attaining the Deathless Nibbāna, he is called 'Amatassa dātā' (the Giver of the Deathless).

'Agaruṃ karitvā' refers to making it burdensome. One who makes another person ask repeatedly is said to make it burdensome. Teaching in a way that is difficult to understand—as if picking sand from the foot of Mount Sineru—while remaining within one's own trainee's analytical insight (sekkhapaṭisambhidāñāṇa), is also called making it burdensome. The request means: "Without doing that, and without making us ask repeatedly, please teach us so that it is easy to understand."

'Yaṃ kho vo' refers to that which is yours. In the statement, "Friends, in the world, one is a perceiver of the world and a conceiver of the world through the eye," the reason is that an uninstructed worldling (puthujjana) with unabandoned views perceives and conceives the world in terms of the world of beings (sattaloka) or the universe (cakkavāḷaloka). Apart from the twelve bases (āyatana) such as the eye, such perception or conceit cannot arise for that worldling. Therefore, it is said, "Friends, in the world, one is a perceiver of the world and a conceiver of the world through the eye." It is not possible to know, see, or reach the end of this world by traveling. However, it should be understood that because it has the nature of crumbling (lujjana), without reaching the end of that world of formations—consisting of the eye and so forth—which is called Nibbāna, there is no such thing as making an end of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha).

Having thus answered the question, he now says "Ākaṅkhamānā pana..." and so forth, wishing to urge them: "Do not have doubts just because a disciple has taught the question; this Blessed One sits holding the great scale of Omniscient Knowledge. If you wish, approach that Blessed One and be free of doubt."

'Imehi ākārehi' refers to these reasons: the reasons for the lack of an end to the universe and the reasons for reaching the end of the world of formations. 'Imehi padehi' refers to these words, which are combinations of syllables. 'Byañjanehi' refers to the individual syllables.

'Paṇḍito' means being endowed with wisdom. One is called wise (paṇḍita) through four reasons: skill in elements (dhātu), skill in bases (āyatana), skill in dependent origination (paccayākāra), and skill in what is and is not a cause (kāraṇākāraṇa). 'Mahāpañño' means [possessing wisdom regarding] great meanings and great dhammas...
35:
He is endowed with great wisdom because of his ability to grasp great meanings, great teachings, great philology, and great eloquence. "As Ānanda answered" refers to the meaning that Venerable Ānanda explained in detail. It means, "Just as Ānanda explained that meaning in detail, I too shall explain it in the same way."

## 4. Kāmaguṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "ye me" means those five cords of sensual pleasure of mine. "Cetaso samphuṭṭhapubbā" means previously experienced by the mind. "Therein my mind would frequently go" indicates that the mind would arise many times regarding those five cords of sensual pleasure previously experienced in the three types of palaces and three seasons. "Or in the present" shows that while practicing austerities for six years, the mind would arise many times regarding present pleasant objects of sensual pleasure seen or heard, such as flocks of birds in a well-blossomed forest. "Or slightly in the future" shows that the mind would arise only slightly regarding future cords of sensual pleasure, such as "The Buddha named Metteyya will arise, the Cakkavatti King named Saṅkha will arise, the royal capital named Ketumatī will arise," and so on. "Therein, I, for my own benefit" means I, who desire my own welfare, regarding those five cords of sensual pleasure experienced in the past. "Appamāda" (diligence) is the constant exertion in wholesome states and not letting the mind loose in the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Sati" (mindfulness) is the mindfulness that grasps the object. "Ārakkho" (protection) shows that it occurred to me that this diligence and mindfulness should be made the protection of the mind. It means these two states should be practiced for the sake of protection.

"Therefore, monks, that base (āyatana) should be known" means that because diligence and mindfulness must be practiced to protect the mind, and because once that base called Nibbāna is known, there is nothing more to be done with diligence or mindfulness, therefore that base (Nibbāna) should be known; that cause should be known. "Saḷāyatananirodha" (cessation of the six sense bases) is spoken with reference to Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the six sense bases. This is because in Nibbāna, the sense bases such as the eye and the perceptions of forms (rūpasaññā) etc., cease. The rest is as previously explained.
36:

118-119. In the fifth sutta, "diṭṭheva dhamme" means in this very existence. "Parinibbāyanti" means they are extinguished through the extinction of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna). "Tannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ hoti" refers to the arising of kamma-consciousness dependent on craving. "Tadupādānaṃ" means it is consciousness accompanied by the grasping of craving. The sixth sutta is clear in its meaning.

In the seventh sutta, "santānessati" means he will strive; he will not allow the opportunity for the severance of his application (yoga-viccheda) to be reached.

## 8. Rāhulovādasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "vimuttiparipācaniyā" means they are called "ripening for liberation" because they cause the fruit of Arahatship to ripen. "Dhammā" refers to the fifteen states; these should be understood by their power to purify the faculties such as faith (saddhindriya). It has also been said:

"The faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is purified by these three factors: avoiding faithless persons, associating with and serving faithful persons, and reflecting on inspiring discourses (suttantas). The faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) is purified by these three factors: avoiding lazy persons, associating with and serving energetic persons, and reflecting on the Right Efforts (Sammappadhāna). The faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) is purified by these three factors: avoiding muddled/forgetful persons, associating with and serving mindful persons, and reflecting on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna). The faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) is purified by these three factors: avoiding unconcentrated persons, associating with and serving concentrated persons, and reflecting on the jhanas and liberations (vimokkha). The faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) is purified by these three factors: avoiding unwise persons, associating with and serving wise persons, and reflecting on the states that are the range of profound knowledge. Thus, by avoiding these five types of persons and associating with these five types of persons..."
37:
...associating [with noble friends], and reflecting on the five discourses; for these fifteen reasons, it is said (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga) that these five faculties are purified.

There are another fifteen things that ripen liberation (Arahattaphala). They are: the five faculties starting with faith, the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā), the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of abandonment (pahānasaññā), the perception of dispassion (virāgasaññā)—these five perceptions leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya)—and the five things such as good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā) taught to the Elder Meghiya. At what time did this thought occur to the Blessed One? It occurred while he was surveying the world at the time of dawn.

'Many thousands of deities' (anekāni devatāsahassāni) refers to the deities who made an aspiration together with the Venerable Rāhula when he made his aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Padumuttara during his time as the Naga King Palita. Among those deities, some were earth-bound, some were sky-bound, some were of the Cātumahārājikā realm, some were in the [other] deva realms, and some were born in the Brahma realm. On this day, however, all of them gathered in one place in the Andhavana forest. Referring to those deities, he said, 'Many thousands of deities.' 'Dhamma-eye' (dhammacakkhu) in this discourse should be understood as the four paths and the four fruits. Among those deities, some became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), Non-returners (Anāgāmī), and Arahants. There is no limit to the number of those deities. The remaining words are clear in every respect.

## 4-5. Commentary on the Bhāradvāja Sutta, etc.

127-128. In the fourth sutta, he is called "Piṇḍola" because he went forth as a monk while seeking alms. He was once a Brahmin whose wealth had been exhausted. Then, seeing the gains and honors of the Saṅgha of monks, he went forth from the household life for the sake of alms. He wandered carrying a large bowl like a shard of a pot. With that bowl, he drank a bowlful of gruel, ate a bowlful of snacks, and consumed a bowlful of rice. Then, they reported his gluttonous nature to the Blessed One. The Blessed One did not yet allow a bowl-case for his bowl. He would place the bowl upside down under the couch. When placing it, he would push it while rubbing it against the ground; when taking it, he would pull it while rubbing it against the ground. As time passed, due to the rubbing, that large bowl became a small bowl that could hold only a single measure of rice. When they reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One allowed a bowl-case for him. Later, that Elder developed the faculties and was established in the supreme fruit, Arahantship. Thus, he is called "Piṇḍola" because he went forth for alms, and "Bhāradvāja" by lineage; combining both, he is called "Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja."

"He approached" (upasaṅkami) means he approached surrounded by very high-ranking ministers. It is said that one day, after wandering for alms in Sāvatthī and finishing his meal, the Elder thought, "I will take a daytime rest in a cool place during the heat of the summer," and went through the air to King Udena's garden named "Udapāna" on the bank of the Ganges. Entering there, he sat at the foot of a certain tree for his daytime rest, being fanned by the cool water-breeze.

King Udena, after drinking and making merry for seven days, had the garden cleaned on the seventh day and went to the garden surrounded by a great crowd, lying down on a bed spread upon an auspicious stone slab. A female attendant sat massaging his feet, and the King gradually fell asleep. When he fell asleep, the dancing women thought, "The King for whom we would perform songs and so on has fallen asleep; we should not make loud noises while he sleeps," and putting down their instruments, they wandered through the garden. While wandering, eating various fruits and wearing flowers, they saw the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. They warned each other not to make noise, paid homage, and sat down. The Elder preached a suitable Dhamma talk to those women. The woman massaging the King's feet then shook the King's feet to wake him. When the King asked, "Where have those women gone?", she replied, "They are sitting surrounding a monk."
39:
Saying that loud noises should not be made while [the King] was sleeping, they left their musical instruments behind and departed for the garden. While those women were wandering about here and there, eating various fruits and wearing flowers, they saw the Elder. They cautioned one another, saying, "Do not make any noise," and after paying homage, they sat down. The Elder then preached a suitable Dhamma discourse to those ladies, using methods such as "Envy should be abandoned, stinginess should be dispelled."

That woman who was sitting and massaging the King's feet moved his feet and woke him up. The King asked, "Where have they gone?" She replied, "What do you have to do with them? They are sitting around a certain monk." The King became angry and, making a crackling sound like salt thrown into a furnace, he stood up and thought, "I will have him bitten by red ants." As he went, he saw a nest of red ants on an Asoka tree. Although he tried to pull it down with his hand, he could not catch the branch. The ant nest broke and fell onto the King's head. His entire body became as if sprinkled with rice husks or burned by torches. The Elder, knowing the King's malicious intent, flew into the air by psychic power. Those women also stood up, went to the King, and while pretending to wipe his body, they picked up the ants that had fallen on the ground and threw them onto the King's body. They mocked him, saying, "What is this? Other kings, upon seeing monks, pay homage and ask questions. But this king has become one who wants to break an ant nest over his head."

The King, realizing his mistake, summoned the gardener and asked, "Who is this monk? Does he usually come here on other days?" The gardener replied, "Yes, Your Majesty, he does." The King commanded, "Inform me on the day he comes." After a few days, the Elder came again and sat at the foot of a tree. When the gardener saw him, he thought, "This is a great gift for me," and went quickly to inform the King. The King stood up, stopped the sounds of musical instruments such as conch shells and drums, and went to the garden with high-ranking ministers. Regarding that going, it is said, "Upasaṅkami" (he approached).

"Anikīḷitāvino kāmesu" means those whose sensual desires have never been played with or enjoyed in sensual pleasures. "Addhānañca āpādenti" means they bring about a lineage; they cause a continuous connection for a long time. "Mātumattīsu" means among women who are like mothers. In the world, these three—mother, sister, and daughter—are objects of respect...
40:
...showing that the mind, bound by the rope of mindfulness established on a respected object, cannot be released, he spoke thus. Furthermore, seeing that the King's mind did not enter into [the meaning of] that question in the ninth section (navakavāra), the Elder preached the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dwattimsākāra kammaṭṭhāna), which was taught by the Blessed One for the purpose of binding the mind through the power of reflecting on the repulsive.

"Abhāvitakāyā" refers to those whose bodies, specifically the five sense doors, have not been developed for the purpose of increasing meditation. For such people, it is very difficult to develop that meditation on the foul (asubha kammaṭṭhāna). Thus, knowing that the King's mind still did not enter into [the meaning] even through this problem, he preached the virtue of sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara-sīla). In the virtue of sense restraint, the mind bound by the rope of mindfulness cannot be harassed. Having heard that virtue of sense restraint, the King's mind entered into it, and he said, "Venerable Bhāradvāja, it is wonderful!" and so on.

In the phrases such as "with an unprotected body," not protecting the body means playing with the hands and feet or looking here and there by turning the neck. Not protecting speech means speaking various kinds of coarse words. Not protecting the mind means thinking thoughts of sensual desire and so on. In the phrases such as "with a protected body," the meaning should be understood as the opposite of what was just said.

"At that time, states of greed greatly oppressed me" means that at that time, greed overcame and arose within me. "With established mindfulness" means by well-establishing mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) such as the hair and so on. "Not so to me at that time" means that greed does not overcome and arise as it did before. The word "pari-sahanti" (oppress) also has the meaning of "arise." Thus, in this Sutta, three types of "body" (kāya) are mentioned. How? In the phrase "this very body," the physical body (karaja-kāya) is mentioned. In "developed body," the body of the five sense doors is mentioned. In "with a protected body," the moving body (copana-kāya) is mentioned, which is bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). The fifth Sutta is quite clear in its meaning.

## 6. Ghosita Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth Sutta, "pleasant forms also" means that pleasant forms exist. "Eye-consciousness also" means that eye-consciousness exists. "Contact to be experienced as pleasant" refers to the contact associated with eye-consciousness which, by way of decisive support (upanissaya), is the cause of pleasant feeling at the time of the impulsion (javana). "Pleasant feeling" means that a pleasant feeling arises by way of impulsion depending on a single contact. In the remaining terms, this same method should be applied.
41:
In this way, twenty-three elements (dhātus) are taught in this sutta. How? To explain in detail: in this sutta, eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) is called the eye element (cakkhu-dhātu); its object is the visible-form element (rūpa-dhātu); eye-consciousness is the consciousness element (viññāṇa-dhātu); and the three aggregates arising together with the eye-consciousness element are the mental-object element (dhamma-dhātu). Thus, in the five doors, there are twenty elements by way of four for each. In the mind door, the adverting consciousness (āvajjana-citta) is taken as the 'mind element' (mano-dhātu); both the object and the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) are called the mental-object element (dhamma-dhātu); and there is the mind-consciousness element (mano-viññāṇa-dhātu) which depends on the base. Thus, there are twenty-three elements. In this way, it is shown that the Blessed One taught the diversity of elements by way of these twenty-three elements.

## 7-8. Commentary on the Hāliddikāni Sutta, etc.

130-131. In the seventh sutta, the phrase 'He understands "this is pleasant and desirable"' means that he sees a certain visible form that increases the pleasure of the mind, and he understands it specifically as 'this visible form is indeed pleasant.' The phrase 'dependent on eye-consciousness and the contact that is the cause of pleasant feeling' means that dependent on eye-consciousness and the contact which is a condition for pleasant feeling—whether by way of decisive support (upanissaya), proximity (anantara), immediate proximity (samanantara), or association (sampayutta)—pleasant feeling arises. This method applies in all cases. Thus, it should be understood that in these two suttas, either the functional mind-consciousness element (kiriya-manoviññāṇadhātu) which performs the function of adverting, or the mind element (mano-dhātu) itself, is spoken of by the name 'mind element.' The eighth sutta is clear in its meaning.

## 9. Commentary on the Lohicca Sutta

In the ninth sutta, 'in Makkarakata' means in the city of that name. 'In a forest hut' (arañña-kuṭikāyaṃ) means in a separate hut built in the forest, not a hut at the edge of a monastery. 'Young brahmins' (māṇavakā) refers to those who, even if they were elderly, are called 'young brahmins' because they were students even in their old age. 'They approached' (tenupasaṅkamiṃsu) means that after learning their arts in the morning, they entered the forest in the evening to fetch firewood for their teacher, and while wandering, they approached the place where that hut was located. 'Around the hut' (parito parito kuṭikāya) means all around that hut. 'Seleyyakāni' refers to the playing of games while walking to and fro, such as jumping over each other's backs while holding on.
42:
In the words such as 'muṇḍakā' (shavelings), they spoke of them as 'shavelings' and 'contemptible ascetics' (samaṇakā) because they wished to revile them. 'Ibba' refers to householders. 'Kaṇha' means those of dark complexion. In the term 'bandhupādāpaccā,' 'Bandhu' refers to Brahmā. The brahmins address that Brahmā as 'Grandfather.' 'Pādāpaccā' means offspring from the feet, referring to those born from the soles of Brahmā's feet. Their doctrine is: 'Brahmins came out from Brahmā's mouth, Khattiyas from his chest, Vessas from his navel, Suddas from his knees, and ascetics (samaṇas) from the soles of his feet.' 'Bharatakānaṃ' refers to householders who are called 'Bharata' because they support the country. These youths said 'bharatakānaṃ' because they wished to show contempt.

'Leaving the monastery' means: inside a pleasant courtyard surrounded by bricks made at night, with sand spread evenly like a silver sheet, they were playing excessively—tying bundles of wood and throwing them, stirring the sand, and holding each other's hands while circling the leaf-roofed hut, shouting repeatedly, 'These shavelings are the objects of worship for these wretched householders!' They did not even realize that there were monks in the monastery. Thinking, 'I will show these youths that there are monks here,' [the monk] came out from the leaf-roofed hut.

'In the past, only the virtuous were supreme' means that by speaking of the virtues of those with merit, the lack of virtue in those without merit will become clear; thus, he spoke of the virtues of the ancient brahmins. Therein, 'sīluttamā' refers to those who regard virtue as foremost. For them, virtue alone was supreme, not birth or lineage. 'Those who remember the ancient Dhamma' are those who remember the ancient brahminical Dhamma. Having overcome anger, their sense-doors were well-guarded and well-protected. They delighted in the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakamma-patha) and the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti).

After thus speaking of the virtues of the ancient brahmins, wishing to humble the pride of the brahmins of the present day, he said the words beginning with 'Having deviated from these Dhammas, we recite.' Therein, 'vokkamma' (having deviated) means having moved away from those virtues such as virtue. The meaning is: thinking themselves to be brahmins merely by saying 'We recite and study the Vedas,' they become intoxicated by their lineage and behave unrighteously, performing unrighteous bodily actions and so forth.
43:
"Puthuattadaṇḍā" means those who carry various kinds of weapons or sticks, or those who have taken up various kinds of weapons.

"Sataṇhātataṇhesu" means among those with craving and those without craving.

"Aguttadvārassa bhavanti moghā" indicates that all the undertaken practices of one who does not guard the sense-doors are in vain.

How so? Just as the various treasures like rubies and pearls obtained by a man in a dream are in vain because he sees nothing upon waking, similarly, those practices are in vain.

"Anāsakā" refers to those who go without food for one or two days, and so on.

"Thaṇḍilasāyikā" means sleeping on the ground covered with green kusa grass.

"Pāto sinānañca tayo ca vedā" means descending into the water early in the morning to bathe and reciting the three Vedas.

"Kharaājinaṃ jaṭā paṅko" refers to rough-textured antelope skins, matted hair, and dirt. "Paṅka" (dirt) specifically refers to the tartar on teeth.

"Mantā sīlabbataṃ tapo" refers to mantras, virtue (sīla) known as goat-virtue or cow-virtue, and observances (vata) known as goat-observance or cow-observance. This means these are the practices of Brahmins nowadays.

"Kuhanā vaṅkadaṇḍā ca" means deception that hides faults like a covered pit, and a crooked staff taken from one of the trees: Udumbara, Palāsa, or Beḷuva.

"Udakācamanāni ca" means washing the face with water.

"Vaṇṇā ete brāhmaṇānaṃ" shows that these deceptions, crooked staffs, etc., are the outward appearances and requisites of Brahmins.

"Katakiñcikkhabhāvanā" means they are done to obtain a small amount of material gain (āmisa). Or, this is the reading itself, meaning it is done to increase the small benefit of material gain.

Having thus humbled the pride of the Brahmins of today, he spoke "Cittañca susamāhitaṃ" and so on, to describe the virtues of the ancient Brahmins. Therein, "susamāhitaṃ" shows that the minds of those ancient Brahmins were well-concentrated through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi).

"Akhilaṃ" means gentle and not harsh.

"So maggo brahmapattiyā" means that quality is the path to reaching the sublime. To show "Why then are you called Brahmins?", he said this.

"Āgamaṃsu nu khvidha" should be resolved as "Āgamaṃsu nu kho idha".

"Adhimuccati" means being excessively greedy through the power of defilements.

"Byāpajjati" means the occurrence of a corrupt mind through the power of ill-will.

"Parittacetaso" means having a limited mind with a defiled mind due to the lack of established mindfulness.

"Cetovimutti" refers to the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala-samādhi).

"Paññāvimutti" refers to the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala-paññā).

"Appamāṇacetaso" means having an immeasurable mind with a mind free from defilements due to established mindfulness.

## 14. Devadaha-vagga

## 1. Devadahasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first Sutta of the Devadaha-vagga, "Devadaha" is a market town (nigama) that has received its name in the neuter gender. "Manoramā" means pleasing to the mind, having a delightful meaning. "Amanoramā" means not delightful.

## 2. Khaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second Sutta, there are no separate hells named "Chaphassāyatanika" (Six-fold Sense-base Hells). Indeed, in all thirty-one great hells, there is the designation of the six-door sense-bases. However, this statement is made with reference to the Avīci Great Hell. Here, "Saggā" (Heavens) also refers only to the city of Tāvatiṃsa. In the sense-sphere heavens (kāmāvacara-devaloka), there is no single heaven where the designation of the six-fold sense-bases does not exist.

What is shown by this? In hell, because of being subject to absolute suffering, and in the heaven realm, because of being endowed with absolute happiness and negligence arising from absolute play and delight, one is unable to live the holy life of the Path. The human realm, however, is a mixture of happiness and suffering; in this very human realm, both the lower realms and the heavens are evident. This human realm is called the "field of action" (kammabhūmi) for the holy life of the Path, and you have obtained that realm. Therefore, these human aggregates you have obtained are a great gain for you. This human existence you have obtained, and the opportunity and time (khaṇa-samaya) you have obtained to live the holy life, are a great gain for you. Regarding this, the ancient teachers said:

"This human realm is the field of action; here the Path is developed,
Many are the stirring places here;
In the objects that cause stirring,
One who is stirred should strive wisely."
45:
## 3. Commentary on the First Rūpārāma Sutta

In the third sutta, "rūpasammuditā" refers to those who have reached joy in form, those who possess joy. "Dukkhā" refers to those who have suffering. "Sukho" refers to one who is happy with the bliss of Nibbāna. "Kevalā" refers to all (the aggregates). "Yāvatatthīti vuccati" means as many (dhammas) as there are, it is said. In the phrase "ete vo," the word "vo" is merely a particle (nipāta). "Paccanīkamidaṃ hoti, sabbalokena passataṃ" means that the vision of the wise who see clearly is contrary to the entire world; it is opposed (viruddha). This is because the world considers the five aggregates as permanent, pleasant, self, and beautiful. The wise, however, see them as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and not beautiful. "Sukhato āhū" means they say it is pleasant. "Sukhato vidū" means they know it is pleasant. All these words are spoken solely with reference to Nibbāna.

"Sammūḷhettha" means they are confused in this Nibbāna. "Aviddasū" refers to fools. Indeed, all ninety-six types of sectarians (pāsaṇḍas) have the perception, "We shall reach Nibbāna," yet they do not even know, "Nibbāna is this unconditioned Dhamma (asaṅkhata-dhamma)." "Nivutānaṃ" refers to those who are shrouded and enveloped by the hindrance of defilements (kilesa-nīvaraṇa). "Andhakāro apassataṃ" means for those who do not see, it is total darkness. What is it that is thus? It is Nibbāna or the Noble Path that sees Nibbāna. For the fools who do not see, Nibbāna and the vision of Nibbāna are always like the moon's disk covered by dark clouds, or like an alms-bowl covered by an overturned large pot; it becomes only gloom and darkness.

"Satañca vivaṭaṃ hoti, āloko passatāmiva" means for the virtuous Noble Ones who see with the eye of wisdom, Nibbāna is open like light. "Santike na vijānanti, magā dhammassa akovidā" means Nibbāna is near because it is to be attained immediately after discerning any one part of one's own body, such as hair of the head or hair of the body, or because it is the path to the cessation of one's own aggregates. Even though it is thus near, common people who have gone astray do not know it, as they are unskilled in what is the path and what is not, or in the Dhamma of the Four Truths.

"Māradheyyānupannehi" refers to those who repeatedly follow the cycle of the three realms, which is the dwelling place of Māra. "Ko nu aññatra ariyebhi" means who else besides the Noble Ones is worthy to know the state of Nibbāna? "Sammadññāya parinibbanti" means having known rightly through the wisdom of Arahatship, they immediately become taintless and are extinguished through the extinguishing of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna). Or, having known rightly and becoming taintless, they are finally extinguished through the extinguishing of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna).

## 4-12. Commentary on the Second Rūpārāma Sutta, etc.

137-145. When the fourth sutta was taught purely in verse, it was spoken according to the disposition (ajjhāsaya) of those who would understand. The fifth sutta and others were also spoken according to the disposition of those who would understand in such and such a way. The meaning of those suttas is quite clear.

## 15. Navapurāṇa Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Kammanirodha Sutta

In the first sutta of the Navapurāṇa Vagga, "navapurāṇāni" refers to new kammas and old kammas. In the statement, "Monks, the eye is old kamma," the eye itself is not old; only the kamma that produced that eye is the old kamma completed in a past life. However, because it arises due to kamma which was the cause in a past life, it is called "old kamma" by the name of its cause (paccaya). "Abhisaṅkhata" means conditioned and constructed by the harmonious combination of causal factors. "Abhisañcetayita" means willed or intended by volition (cetanā). "Vedaniyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ" means it should be seen as the basis (vatthu) of feeling. "Touching liberation through cessation" means reaching liberation (the fruition of Arahatship) through the cessation of these three types of kamma. "It is thus said" means that the cessation (Nibbāna) which is the object of that liberation is called the cessation of kamma (kammanirodha). Thus, in this sutta, preliminary insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā) is taught.

## 2-5. Commentary on the Aniccanibbānasappāya Sutta, etc.

147-150. In the second sutta, "nibbānasappāya" refers to the practice that is helpful and conducive to Nibbāna (upakāra-paṭipadā). The same method applies to the third sutta and others. In sequence, the four paths along with insight are taught in all four of these suttas.

## 6-7. Commentary on the Antevāsika Sutta, etc.

151-152. In the sixth sutta, "anantevāsika" means being free from the defilements that dwell within like pupils. "Anācariyaka" means being free from the defilements that instruct and command like teachers. "They dwell within" means the defilements stick and reside within that person. "Those defilements command that person" means those defilements overwhelm and dominate that person, or they instruct, saying, "Perform medical work in this way, perform the work of a messenger in this way." Because of this sense of commanding, which is called instructing, those defilements are called "teachers."
47:
Because of those teachers (defilements), one is called 'one who has a teacher' (one who has a bad teacher). The remaining words in this sutta should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The seventh sutta is just as described previously.

## 8. Atthinukhopariyāyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma" means depending on which cause. "Aññatreva saddhāya" means apart from faith or excluding faith. Here, faith (saddhā) is not the direct realization (paccakkha-saddhā). It refers to the state of belief that arises upon hearing another say, "It is said to be thus, it is said to be thus."

In the terms such as ruci (preference), the state of noting "this reason should exist" after making oneself pleased by one's own will is called ruci. Hearing repeatedly "it will be thus" is called anussava (oral tradition). To one who sits quietly and reflects on a certain logical reason, that logic becomes manifest; when it becomes manifest, taking it as "this logic exists" is called ākāraparivitakka (reasoned reflection), meaning reflection on the cause. To one who reflects on the cause, a wrong view may arise; the state of accepting that view as "this view exists" is called diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti (acceptance of a view after reflection). "Aññaṃ vyākareyya" means declaring the fruit of Arahantship, setting aside these five factors such as faith. In this sutta, the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā) of trainees (sekha) and non-trainees (asekha) is taught.

## 9-10. Indriyasampannasutta-vaṇṇanā

154-155. In the ninth sutta, "indriyasampanna" means one who is endowed with the faculties. In that term, whoever contemplates the six faculties and reaches the fruit of Arahantship is called indriyasampanna because they are endowed with those faculties that are free from defilements. Or, one is called paripuṇṇindriya (one with complete faculties) because they are endowed with the faculties such as faith (saddhā) that arise in one who contemplates the six faculties such as the eye (cakkhu). With reference to that meaning, the Blessed One expanded the teaching in the manner beginning with "also in the eye faculty" and said, "Bhikkhu, to this extent one is indriyasampanna." The tenth sutta is just as described previously.

156-159. 168-227. Immediately following that Nandikkhayavagga is the chapter named Saṭṭhipeyyāla; its meaning is quite clear. The sixty suttas taught in this chapter [concerning] desire...
49:

## 18. Samudda Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the First Samudda Sutta

In the first sutta of the Samudda Vagga, the phrase "Monks, the eye of a man is an ocean" means that the eye is called an ocean either because it is difficult to fill or because of the sense of 'casting down' (samuddana). For, even if objects such as blue and so forth, from the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm, were to gather and enter that eye, they could not make it full; thus, it is called an ocean in the sense of being difficult to fill. The eye also moves towards various objects like blue and so forth, casting down faults upon them and proceeding in a repulsive manner. When it enters [objects] without restraint, it acts as a cause for the arising of defilements, and because it proceeds with faults, it is called an ocean in the sense of 'casting down' (samuddana). 

"Its current consisting of forms" means that just like the immeasurable current of waves in the ocean, the immeasurable current of forms should be understood in the eye-ocean, by way of the various objects like blue and so forth that gather and enter it. "He who endures that current consisting of forms" means the person who does not give rise to defilements such as lust (rāga) for pleasant forms, hatred (dosa) for unpleasant forms, and delusion (moha) for those not properly investigated, but endures them with equanimity.

In the words beginning with "sa-ūmiṃ" (with waves): it is called "with waves" because it is accompanied by the waves of defilements. It is called "with whirlpools" (sāvaṭṭaṃ) because it is accompanied by the whirlpools of defilements. It is called "with sharks and crocodiles" (sagāhaṃ) because it is accompanied by the sharks of defilements. It is called "with demons" (sarakkhasaṃ) because it is accompanied by the demons of defilements. Alternatively, it is called "with waves" by way of anger (kodha) and despair (upāyāsa). For it was said: "Monks, 'fear of waves' (ūmibhaya) is a designation for anger and despair." It is called "with whirlpools" by way of the cords of sensual pleasure. For it was said: "Monks, 'the whirlpool' (āvaṭṭagāha) is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure." It is called "with sharks" and "with demons" by way of women (mātugāma). For it was said: "Monks, 'the shark and the demon' (gāharakkhasa) is a designation for women." In the remaining sections, the method is the same.
50:
The same method applies to the rest. "He has crossed over this ocean with its dangers, difficult to cross" means he has transcended this ocean which is accompanied by dangers such as waves and is difficult to cross. "Lokantagū" means one who has reached the end of the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*). "Pāragato" is said to mean one who has reached Nibbāna.

## 2-3. Dutiyasamuddasuttādi-vaṇṇanā

229-230. In the second sutta, "ocean" is so called in the sense of *samuddana*, meaning the sense of moistening or wetting with defilements. "Mostly" (*yebhuyyena*) means excluding the noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*). "Samunnā" means those who are moistened, soaked, or submerged. The phrases beginning with "tantākulakajāta" (tangled like a ball of thread) have been explained in detail below. "Maccujaho" means one who stands having abandoned the three kinds of death (*maccu*). "Nirupadhī" means one who is free from acquisitions by way of the three types of acquisitions (*upadhi*). "For the sake of non-becoming again" means for the sake of Nibbāna. "Bewildered the King of Death" means he went having bewildered the King of Death so that the King of Death could not know his destination (*gati*). The third sutta follows the same method as already stated.

## 4-6. Khīrarukkhopamasuttādi-vaṇṇanā

231-233. In the fourth sutta, "there is" is said in the sense of not being abandoned. Therefore, it is said, "that thing is not abandoned." "Paritta" (small/limited) means that even a visible form as large as a mountain is called *paritta* if it is undesirable and not lust-inducing. This is intended to show that even such visible forms can overwhelm the mind. What then to say of "superior" (*adhimatta*) objects? What is there to say in the case where a desirable, lust-inducing object overwhelms the mind? In this context, even a lust-inducing object the size of a fingernail, such as pearls or gems, should be understood as a "superior object" (*adhimattārammaṇa*). The three terms beginning with "dahara" (young) are synonyms of each other. "Ābhindeyya" means should strike or break. In the fifth sutta, "tadubhayaṃ" means both of them. The sixth sutta is clear in its meaning.

## 7. Udāyīsutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "anekapariyāyena" means through various reasons. "Itipāyaṃ" means "thus also this [person]." In this sutta, the characteristic of non-self (*anatta*) is taught by way of the aspect of impermanence (*anicca*).

## 8. Ādittapariyāyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "grasping signs by way of minor features" (*anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho*) means grasping signs through minor features such as "the hands are beautiful, the feet are beautiful." "Nimittaggāho" means...
51:
Indeed, grasping by combining parts such as hands and feet (as a woman, a man, etc.) is called nimittaggāha (grasping at the sign); grasping by distinguishing parts is called anubyañjanaggāha (grasping at the details). Nimittaggāha is like a crocodile that seizes everything at once. Anubyañjanaggāha is like a leech that seizes specific parts such as hands and feet by distinguishing them. These two types of grasping (gāha) are found even in a single javana-vāra (impulsive process); it goes without saying that they occur in different javana-vāras.

'Nimittassādagathita' means bound or connected by the enjoyment of the sign. 'Viññāṇa' refers to kamma-viññāṇa (kamma-consciousness). Regarding the phrase "should one pass away at that time," there is no such thing as passing away with a defiled mind. All beings pass away only with the bhavaṅga (life-continuum). However, this was spoken to show the terrifying danger of defilements. Alternatively, it was said by way of the time of death. When an object comes into the path of the eye-door, a mind of lust, hatred, or delusion experiences the taste of the object and then descends into the bhavaṅga; staying in that bhavaṅga, one passes away. For one who passes away at such a time, only two destinations (gati) are possible (hell or the animal realm); it was said in reference to this situation.

"Monks, I (see) this danger" means that because He clearly saw the suffering to be experienced in hell for many hundreds of thousands of crores of years, He said, "I would rather have my eyes pierced with a red-hot iron rod," and so on. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all places. 'Ayosaṅku' means an iron spike. 'Sampalimaṭṭha' means severely tormented by piercing both ear-holes and striking them into the ground.

In the third instance, 'sampalimaṭṭha' means severely tormented by inserting a nail-cutter, lifting it, and cutting it off along with the skull bone. In the fourth instance, 'sampalimaṭṭha' means severely tormented by cutting off the root of the tongue. In the fifth instance, 'sampalimaṭṭha' means severely tormented by tearing out the body-sensitivity (kāyapassāda) with a sharp spear. In the context of 'sattiyā' (with a spear), it should be understood as a large spear with a long handle. 'Sotta' means falling into sleep. By the words "under the influence of such wrong thoughts, one might cause a schism in the Saṅgha," it is shown that wrong thoughts can lead to evil deeds as grave as saṅghabheda (causing a schism in the Saṅgha). The remaining words are clear.
52:
## 9-10. Commentary on the First Hatthapādopama Sutta, etc.

236-237. In the ninth sutta, "Monks, when there are hands" means when hands are clearly present. In the tenth sutta, the statement "does not occur" was spoken according to the inclination of those who will realize the Four Noble Truths. In both these suttas, by showing only the resultant happiness and resultant suffering, the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.

## The Samudda-vagga is finished.

## 19. Āsīvisavagga

## 1. Commentary on the Āsīvisopama Sutta

In the first sutta of the Āsīvisavagga, "He addressed the monks" means He addressed the meditating monks (yogāvacara) who were sitting around Him—those who practice alone, in pairs, threes, fours, or fives; those with similar conduct; those performing the task of meditation; those constantly striving in meditation; and those whose meditation subject is the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa). This sutta was spoken according to the inclinations of individuals. Among individuals, it was spoken for the sake of the vipañcitaññū (those who understand through elaboration) who reside in various regions, who meditate on the characteristic of suffering, and who arrived at the time of the assembly to sit surrounding the Teacher. Even though it was spoken for the vipañcitaññū, this sutta is a supporting cause for all four types of individuals, starting with the ugghaṭitaññū.

The ugghaṭitaññū individual (one of quick intuition) will reach Arahantship just by the presentation of the table of contents (mātikā) of this sutta. The vipañcitaññū will reach Arahantship through the detailed explanation of the mātikā. The neyya individual (one who needs guidance) will reach Arahantship by reciting this very sutta, inquiring about it, attending to it wisely, and associating with, following, and serving good friends. For the padaparama individual (one for whom the word is the maximum), this sutta will become a good latent tendency (vāsanā) for the future. Knowing that it is thus beneficial to all individuals, the Blessed One began this Āsīvisopama Sutta with great effort—as if lifting Mount Sineru, as if expanding the sky, and as if shaking the Cakkayāḷa mountains—saying, "Monks, suppose..."

In that sutta, the four vipers are: the kaṭṭhamukha (wood-mouth), the pūtimukha (rot-mouth), the aggimukha (fire-mouth), and the satthamukha (weapon-mouth). Among them, the entire body of one bitten by a kaṭṭhamukha becomes stiff like dry wood; in the joints, there is unbearable intense pain as if an iron spike has been driven in. The entire body of one bitten by a pūtimukha reaches a state where putrid pus flows out, like a ripe, rotten jackfruit...
53:
The body of a person bitten by a Pūtimukha snake leaks fluid continuously, like water poured into a sieve. The body of a person bitten by an Aggimukha snake, being burnt by the venom, crumbles and scatters like a handful of ashes or a handful of chaff. The body of a person bitten by a Satthamukha snake is torn and destroyed, like a place struck by lightning or like the opening of a joint carved by a large chisel. Thus, by the power of their venom, the āsīvisa snakes are divided into four types.

Furthermore, by the power of the variation in the intensity of the venom, these become sixteen types. The Kaṭṭhamukha snake has four varieties: one whose venom is through biting (daṭṭhavisa), one whose venom is through sight (diṭṭhavisa), one whose venom is through touch (phuṭṭhavisa), and one whose venom is through the wind (vātavisa). Whether that snake bites, looks, touches, or strikes with its wind, the body becomes stiff and rigid as previously described. The same method applies to the remaining snakes. Thus, by the power of the variation in the intensity of the venom, there are sixteen types.

Again, by the power of individual designation (puggalapaṇṇatti), there are sixty-four types. How? Among the Kaṭṭhamukha snakes, first, the one whose venom is through biting has four varieties: one whose venom comes quickly but is not fierce (āgatavisa no ghoravisa), one whose venom is fierce but does not come quickly (ghoravisa no āgatavisa), one whose venom both comes quickly and is fierce (āgatavisa ceva ghoravisa ca), and one whose venom neither comes quickly nor is fierce (nevāgatavisa na ghoravisa).

Among those four, the venom of a snake that rises quickly like the flame of a fiercely burning grass torch and reaches the state of seizing the eyes, shoulders, and head, is like the venom of the jewel-snake (maṇisappa) and others. However, by merely reciting a mantra, blowing air into the ear, or striking with a stick, the venom descends and remains only at the site of the bite. This snake is called 'one whose venom comes quickly but is not fierce' (āgatavisa no ghoravisa).

The venom of a snake that rises slowly, and in every place it rises, feels cool like cold water, is like the venom of water-snakes and others. Even after twelve years, it becomes evident through boils or pustules on the temples, shoulder blades, and so on. Even when treatments such as reciting mantras are performed, it does not descend quickly. This snake is called 'one whose venom is fierce but does not come quickly' (ghoravisa no āgatavisa).

The venom of a snake that rises quickly but does not descend quickly is like the venom of pythons (aneḷakasappa) and others. This snake is called 'one whose venom both comes quickly and is fierce' (āgatavisa ceva ghoravisa ca).

The venom of a snake that is weak and descends easily when the venom is being lowered is like the venom of the green snake (nīlasappa), the dhammanisappa snake, and others. This snake is called 'one whose venom neither comes quickly nor is fierce' (nevāgatavisa na ghoravisa). In this same manner, the daṭṭhavisa and others should be understood in the Kaṭṭhamukha snake, and the daṭṭhavisa and others in the Pūtimukha snake and so on. Thus, by the power of individual designation, there are sixty-four types.
54:
Among those sixty-four snakes, if each is divided into four types by the power of the four modes of birth (yoni), such as 'egg-born snakes' (aṇḍaja nāgā) (as mentioned in the Saṃyutta Nikāya), there are two hundred and fifty-six (256) types. If those snakes are multiplied by two, being water-born and land-born, there are five hundred and twelve (512) types. If those same snakes are further multiplied by two, being those that can change their appearance at will and those that cannot, they number one thousand and twenty-four (1024). Again, if summarized by reversing the above method, there are only the four types such as Kaṭṭhamukha. Referring to those four types, the Blessed One said, 'Monks, suppose there were four fierce snakes.' These four types are taken by the power of their species.

In that passage, they are called 'āsīvisa' because they have venom that is poured (āsittavisa), or because whatever food they eat becomes venom (asitavisa), or because they have venom like a sword (asisadisavisa). 'Āsittavisa' means the venom is full as if poured into their own entire body and the bodies of others; it means they have venom that is poured into the bodies of others and their own. 'Asitavisa' means whatever they eat or consume turns only into venom; therefore, they are āsīvisa because their food (asita) becomes venom (visa). 'Asisadisavisa' means they are called āsīvisa because they have venom that is sharp like a sword (asi) and capable of severely cutting flesh. Thus should the meaning of the words be understood here. 'Uggatejā' means having fierce power or strong power. 'Ghoravisā' means having venom that is difficult to subdue with mantras or medicine.

'They might say thus' is said for the purpose of having them looked after. Indeed, kings have fierce snakes caught, thinking, 'We will have such criminal thieves bitten and killed by these snakes, or we will throw them into the enemy's army when the city is besieged. If we are unable to crush the enemy's force, we will eat good food, ascend a noble bed, and have ourselves bitten by these snakes so that we may die according to our own wish without falling into the power of the enemies.' Thus they have the fierce snakes looked after. When those kings do not wish to kill a thief immediately, but desire that 'he shall die after suffering for a long time by being bitten by a snake,' they say to that man, 'Look here, man, these are four fierce snakes for you.'

In that passage, 'kālena kālaṃ' means at all times (from time to time). 'Saṃvesetabbā' means they should be made to lie down. 'Aññataro vā aññataro vā' means any one among the snakes such as the Kaṭṭhamukha. 'Look here, man, do what you must do'—this should be understood as the word of one who performs a beneficial service. It is said that after handing over the snakes to that man in this way, they inform the snakes kept in the four baskets, 'This man is your attendant.' Then, one snake comes out and, following the man's right foot...
55:
(One snake) came out and, climbing up by way of the man's right foot, wrapped itself around his right arm starting from the wrist. It then spread its hood at the base of his right ear and lay there making a 'hissing' sound. Another snake climbed up by way of the left foot and, in the same manner, wrapped itself around the left arm, spread its hood at the base of the left ear, and lay there making a 'hissing' sound. The third snake came out and, climbing up from the front, wrapped itself around the belly, spread its hood at the base of the throat, and lay there making a 'hissing' sound. The fourth snake climbed up from the back, wrapped itself around the neck, placed its hood upon the top of the head, and lay there making a 'hissing' sound.

While these four venomous snakes were thus positioned on his body, a man who sought his welfare saw him and asked, "O man, what have you obtained?" Then that man replied, "Friend, the King has granted me these special ornaments: like bracelets on my hands, like armlets on my arms, like a waist-cloth around my belly, like ear-ornaments on my ears, like a pearl necklace around my neck, and like a head-ornament on my head."

That person said, "O fool, do not think thus: 'The King, being pleased with me, has granted these ornaments.' You are but a thief who has offended the King. These four venomous snakes are difficult to attend to and difficult to care for. When one snake wishes to rise, another wishes to bathe; when one wishes to bathe, another wishes to eat; when one wishes to eat, another wishes to lie down. Among those snakes, if the desire of any one snake is not fulfilled, it will bite you right there and cause your death." The man asked, "O sir, if that is so, is there any way of safety?" The other replied, "Yes, knowing the time when the King's men are distracted and fleeing is the only way of safety," and he would say, "Do what you must do."

Hearing those words, when that man saw the moment of negligence of the four venomous snakes and that the King's men were absent, he used his left hand to wrap around his right hand, and while appearing to stroke the body of the sleeping snake, he gently removed the hood from his right ear-ornament. By this same means, he removed the remaining snakes and fled in fear of them. As he fled, those snakes would follow him, saying, "This man was given to us by the King as an attendant." With reference to this meaning, it was said: "Then, bhikkhus, that man, being afraid, fled from the four venomous snakes... and so on."

While that man was fleeing in great haste, looking back again and again at the path he had come, the King heard that "The man has fled," and while searching for who would be able to follow and kill him, he sent those who were his enemies...
56:
Having obtained five men who were enemies, (the King) would dispatch them, saying, "Go, pursue him and kill him." Then, men who sought his welfare, knowing of that matter, would inform him. That man would then flee in even greater haste, being exceedingly terrified. With reference to this meaning, it was said: "They would speak to him thus," and so forth.

"The sixth executioner who dwells within" means: Previously, when pursued by the snakes, he fled, deceiving them here and there. Now, when pursued by the five enemies, he flees even more. It is not possible to capture him with such speed; he can only be captured through enticement. Therefore, the ministers suggested, "Send an executioner who has been familiar with him since childhood, who has eaten and drunk together with him, and who dwells within (his circle) to kill him." Thus, it refers to the internal executioner whom the King searched for and dispatched.

"He would see an empty village" means: That man, fleeing without rest, looks back and sees the four venomous snakes, the five enemy executioners, and the sixth internal executioner following his tracks with great speed. Seeing them coming and saying, "O friend, do not flee; you shall live happily enjoying sensual pleasures with your wife and children," he flees with even greater speed to whatever direction he can. He would then see an empty village of only six houses at the border of the country. "He would enter it as something empty" means he enters it as something void because it is devoid of wealth, grain, couches, stools, and so on. "Tucchakaṃ suññakaṃ" (hollow and empty) are synonyms for this. "He would grope about" means he would open pots and vessels and put his hand inside to feel around, thinking, "If there is water, I shall drink; if there is food, I shall eat."

"They would speak to him thus" means: Having found nothing in any of the six houses, he goes to a well-shaded tree in the middle of the village. Seeing a curved wooden bench spread there, he thinks, "I will sit here for a while." While he sits there, enjoying the slight peace as if being fanned by a gentle breeze, some men seeking his welfare, knowing the situation outside, would arrive and speak to him thus: "O man, now..." is the meaning. "Robbers who plunder the village" refers to the six village-plundering robbers who have come with the intent: "Whatever we find here, we shall take or we shall kill."
57:
"Udakaṇṇava" refers to water that is both deep and wide. Indeed, water that is deep but not wide, or wide but not deep, is not called "aṇṇava" (ocean/expanse of water); only that which is both deep and wide is called by this name. "Sāsaṅkaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ" (suspicious and dangerous) refers to being full of apprehension and danger by way of the four poisonous snakes, the five executioners, the sixth internal traveler, and the six village-plundering robbers. "Khemaṃ appaṭibhayaṃ" (safe and secure) refers to being free from danger and peaceful due to the absence of those snakes and so forth, resembling a city of devas with excellent diverse gardens and abundant food and drink. "Na cassa nāvā santāraṇī" means there would be no ferry boat stationed with the intention, "I will go from this shore to the further shore by this boat." "Uttarasethu vā" means there would be no bridge for crossing, whether a log bridge, a footbridge, or a cart bridge. In the phrase "The Brahmin stands," this person is not actually a [birth] Brahmin. Why is he called a Brahmin? He is called so because he has warded off (bāhita) so many enemies, or because [the Buddha] wished to conclude the teaching by showing an Arahant Brahmin.

When that person has thus crossed over, the four poisonous snakes think, "Alas, we did not catch you; today we should have chewed up your life into tiny pieces and discarded it." The five enemies think, "Alas, we did not catch you; today we should have surrounded you, cut off your limbs and members, and gone to the king to receive a hundred or a thousand [pieces of gold]."
