The sixth internal person thinks, "I did not catch you; today I should have cut off your head with a sword as bright as crystal, and having obtained the position of general, I would have enjoyed prosperity." The six robbers think, "We did not catch you; today we should have made you undergo various tortures and made you bring much wealth." Thinking thus, being unable to descend into the expanse of water, and being unable to go further because of their fear of the king's command, they would wither away and die right there.

In the phrase "upamā kho myāyaṃ," the correlation of the simile and the thing illustrated should be understood from the beginning. Kamma (action) should be seen as the King. The worldling (puthujjana) dependent on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) is like the man who has committed an offense against the king. The four great elements (mahābhūta) are like the four poisonous snakes. The time when the king handed over the four poisonous snakes to that man is like the time when kamma gives the four great elements to the worldling at the very moment of rebirth-linking. The words, "At the moment when these snakes are negligent and the king's men are absent, go out and do what you must do, O man," which mean "Flee!", are like the time when the Teacher taught the meditation on the great elements to this monk and said, "Be repelled by these four great elements."
58:
The time when the Teacher taught the meditation on the Great Elements and said, "Be weary of these four Great Elements, be dispassionate; thus you will be liberated from the round of rebirth," is like when that man, hearing the words of the well-wisher, escapes at a moment when the four snakes are negligent and the king's men are absent, and flees to whatever place he can. Similarly, this monk, having received the meditation subject from the Teacher, flees with the "flight of wisdom" (ñāṇapalāyana) to be liberated from the snakes that are the Great Elements.

Now, the discussion of the four Great Elements beginning with "This is a designation for the four Great Elements: the earth element, the water element," etc., as well as the discussion of the five aggregates of clinging and the sense bases, should be understood according to the method detailed in the Visuddhimagga. Here, the earth element (pathavīdhātu) should be seen as the Kaṭṭhamukha snake. The remaining elements should be seen respectively as the Pūtimukha snake, the Aggimukha snake, and the Satthamukha snake. To elaborate: just as the entire body of one bitten by a Kaṭṭhamukha snake becomes stiff and rigid, so it is through the disturbance of the earth element. Just as the body of one bitten by the Pūtimukha and other snakes festers, burns, and is cut, so it is through the disturbance of the water element, fire element, and air element. Therefore, the Teachers of the Commentaries said:

"The body becomes rigid when bitten by a Kaṭṭhamukha snake; through the disturbance of the earth element, it becomes just like [one bitten by] a Kaṭṭhamukha."

"The body becomes putrid when bitten by a Pūtimukha snake; through the disturbance of the water element, it becomes just like [one bitten by] a Pūtimukha."

"The body becomes scorched when bitten by an Aggimukha snake; through the disturbance of the fire element, it becomes just like [one bitten by] an Aggimukha."

"The body becomes lacerated when bitten by a Satthamukha snake; through the disturbance of the air element, it becomes just like [one bitten by] a Satthamukha."

Thus, the specific similarities among these four Great Elements should be understood. In a general sense, their similarity to snakes should be understood through these reasons: habitat (āsaya), the transformation caused by the force of venom (visavegavikāra), bringing about harm (anatthaggahaṇa), being difficult to maintain (durupaṭṭhāna), being dangerous to approach (durāsada), ingratitude (akataññuta), lack of discrimination (avisesakāri), and having endless faults and dangers (anantadosūpaddava). Among these, "by way of habitat" (āsaya) means: the habitat of snakes is an anthill; they live right there. The habitat of the Great Elements is also the "body-anthill"; the Great Elements live right there. Furthermore, the habitats of snakes are tree hollows, grass, leaves, and places where refuse is discarded; they tend to live in such places. The habitat of the Great Elements is also the body, which is like a tree hollow...
59:
Dwelling place (Āsaya). The hollows of trees, grass, leaves, and places where rubbish is discarded are also dwelling places for snakes. Indeed, those snakes live in these places. For the great elements (mahābhūta), the body which is like a hollow tree, the body which is like grass and leaves, and the body which is like a place where rubbish is discarded is the dwelling place. Thus, first, the similarity in terms of dwelling place should be understood.

Regarding similarity through the transformation of toxic intensity (visavegavikāra): Snakes are of four types according to their lineage, such as Kaṭṭhamukha and so on. Among those four, when each is classified by the transformation of venom, there are four types each, such as the venom of the bite (daṭṭhavisa) and so on. The great elements are also four, such as earth (pathavī) and so on, by way of their individual characteristics. Among these great elements, each is of four types by way of its origin from kamma and so on. Thus, the similarity through the transformation of toxic intensity should be understood.

Regarding similarity through the grasping of harm (anatthaggahaṇa): Those who handle and grasp snakes grasp five harms. They grasp bad smell, impurity, disease, poison, and death. Those who grasp the great elements also grasp five harms. They grasp bad smell, impurity, disease, aging, and death. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"Whoever grasps a snake, smeared with dung and highly poisonous,
Those who delight in snakes in the world grasp five harms.
Bad smell, impurity, disease, poison, and fifthly, death—
These five are the harms in a snake smeared with dung.
In the same way, the unskilled, blind worldlings,
Delighting in being born in existence, grasp five harms.
Bad smell, impurity, disease, aging, and fifthly, death—
These five are the harms in a snake smeared with dung."

Thus, the similarity through the grasping of harm should be understood.

Regarding similarity through being difficult to serve (duruupaṭṭhāna): Those snakes are difficult to serve. When one wants to rise, another wants to bathe; when that one wants to bathe, another wants to eat; when that one wants to eat, another wants to sleep. Among those snakes, if the desire of any one is not fulfilled, it bites right there and kills. The elements are even more difficult to serve than these snakes. For when medical treatment is applied to the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), the water element (āpo-dhātu) becomes disturbed; while performing medical treatment for that water element...
60:
...the fire element; thus, while medical treatment is performed for one element, another element becomes disturbed and ruined. Thus, the similarity in terms of being difficult to attend should be understood.

In terms of similarity through being difficult to approach: Snakes are difficult to approach. If they see a snake in the front part of the house, they flee through the back; if they see it in the back, they flee through the front; if they see it in the middle of the house, they enter the inner chamber; if they see it in the inner chamber, they climb onto the couch or bench. The great elements are even more difficult to approach than those snakes. When such transformation occurs, the ears, nose, etc., of one afflicted by leprosy and such diseases fall off; the body breaks out severely and bluebottles swarm around; the body odor strikes even from afar. Even if that person is reviling or weeping, people are unable to approach, whether out of anger or out of compassion; they avoid that person even from afar, closing their noses and spitting. In the same way, this meaning should be understood through the power of other diseases such as fistula, stomach ailments, and wind ailments, which produce a loathsome appearance. Thus, the similarity in terms of being difficult to approach should be understood.

In terms of similarity through ingratitude: Snakes are ungrateful; even if they are bathed, fed, honored with perfumes and garlands, or carried around in a basket, they only seek an opportunity to bite. Wherever they get an opportunity to bite, they bite right there and cause death. The great elements are even more ungrateful than snakes. For there is no such thing as a favor done to these great elements; even if they are bathed with cold or hot pure water, honored with perfumes and garlands, attended to with soft clothes, beds, and vehicles, fed with excellent food, or given excellent drinks to drink, they only seek an opportunity to destroy. Wherever they get an opportunity to destroy, they become disturbed right there and lead to ruin and destruction. Thus, the similarity in terms of ingratitude should be understood.

In terms of similarity through acting without discrimination: Snakes do not make a distinction, thinking, 'This person is a Khattiya, a Brahmin, a Vessa, a Sudda, a householder, or a monk'; they bite and kill whoever happens to come. The great elements also do not make a distinction, thinking, 'This person is a Khattiya, a Brahmin, a Vessa, a Sudda, a householder, a monk, a deva, a human, Mara, Brahma, one without virtue, or one with virtue.' If those great elements [thought], 'This person is virtuous'...
61:
If these great elements were to have shame, they would feel shame before the Tathāgata, the supreme person in the world including the devas. Furthermore, if these great elements were to have shame, thinking, "This venerable one is of great wisdom, this venerable one is of great psychic power, this venerable one is a speaker of truth," and so on, they would feel shame before the great elders such as the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta. Furthermore, if these great elements were to have fear, thinking, "This person is devoid of virtue, cruel, and harsh," they would feel fear toward Devadatta, who is the foremost among the virtueless, harsh, and cruel in the world including the devas, or toward the monk Channa, or toward the great heretical teachers. However, these great elements feel neither shame nor fear; when provoked, they simply cause some form of ruin or disaster. Because they act without discrimination in this way, their similarity to snakes should be understood.

Regarding the term "anantadosūpaddavato" (having infinite harm and danger), there is no limit to the dangers and harms that arise depending on snakes. For those snakes, by biting, cause blindness, hunching, lameness, or squinting of one eye; thus they display immeasurable types of deformity. Similarly, when the great elements are disturbed, there is no deformity such as blindness that they do not cause; they certainly cause them. The danger and harm of these great elements are immeasurable. Because they possess such immeasurable danger and harm, their similarity to snakes should be understood.

At this point, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be explained by way of the four great elements up to the attainment of Arahantship; that meditation subject has already been explained in the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga), in the section on the Definition of the Four Elements (Catu-dhātu-vavatthāna-niddesa).

In the statement, "Monks, 'five murderous enemies' is a designation for the five aggregates of clinging," the similarity of the aggregates to murderous enemies should be understood in two ways. Indeed, the aggregates murder one another, and when those aggregates exist, what is called 'murder' is manifest. How do they murder one another? First, materiality (rūpa) murders materiality and also murders mentality (arūpa). Likewise, mentality murders mentality and also murders materiality. How? When this earth element breaks down, it breaks down only after taking the other three elements with it. The same method applies to the water element and so on. In this way, materiality first murders materiality itself. Furthermore, when the aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha) breaks down, it breaks down only after taking the four mental aggregates (arūpakkhandha) with it. In this way, materiality murders mentality as well. The aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), when it breaks down, breaks down only after taking the aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness with it. The same method applies to the aggregate of perception and so on. In this way, mentality murders mentality itself. At the moment of death (cuti-khana), however, when the four mental aggregates break down, they break down only after taking the physical base (vatthu-rūpa) with them. In this way, mentality murders materiality. Because they murder one another in this way, they are called murderers (vadhaka). Alternatively, wherever the aggregates exist, there occur cutting, breaking, killing, binding, and so on, and not elsewhere. Thus, because murder is manifest only when the aggregates exist, they are called murderers.
62:
Now, having divided the five aggregates into two groups (the truth of suffering) by way of materiality and mentality, the meditation subject should be explained starting from the grasping of materiality, either by way of materiality or by way of mentality, up to the attainment of Arahantship. That meditation subject has also already been explained in the Visuddhimagga.

In this Pali passage, "Monks, 'the sixth internal prowling murderer with a raised sword' is a designation for delight and lust (nandīrāga)," the similarity of delight and lust to a murderer with a raised sword should be understood in two ways: because it cuts off the head of wisdom (paññā) and because it leads to a mode of birth (yoni). How? When a desirable object comes into range at the eye-door, greed arises depending on that object; by the mere occurrence of this greed, the head of wisdom is said to have fallen. The same method applies to the ear-door and so on. Thus, first, its similarity should be understood because it cuts off the head of wisdom. Furthermore, this delight and lust leads one to the four modes of birth, such as the egg-born and so on. The twenty-five great fears and thirty-two types of torture, which have their root in entering those modes of birth, inevitably follow. Thus, its similarity to a murderer with a raised sword should also be understood because it leads to a mode of birth.

In this way, the meditation subject for a monk has also been explained by way of delight and lust. How? This delight and lust is the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Having defined it as the aggregate of mental formations, the feeling associated with it is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the perception is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), the mind is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), and their physical base and object are the aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha). In this way, one defines the five aggregates. Now, having defined those five aggregates by way of mentality and materiality, and having developed insight (vipassanā) starting from the search for their causes, one eventually reaches Arahantship. Thus, the meditation subject is explained by way of delight and lust.

The similarity of the six internal sense bases (ajjhattikāyatana) to an empty village appears in the Pali text itself. The method of meditation here is as follows: Just as six thieves enter an empty village of six houses and, prowling from one house to another, find nothing and thus have no desire for that village; even so, a monk, having established insight and investigating the six internal sense bases, sees nothing that can be grasped as "I" or "mine" and thus has no desire for those bases. Thinking, "I will begin insight," he grasps eye-sensitivity and so on by way of the meditation on derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) and defines them as "this is the aggregate of materiality." He defines the mind-base (manāyatana) as "the aggregate of mentality." Thus, having defined all these as materiality and mentality by way of mentality-materiality, and having searched for their causes, [he develops] insight...
63: A monk who develops insight and contemplates conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) gradually becomes established in the fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala). This aforementioned teaching is the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) for a certain monk until he reaches Arahatship. Now, wishing to show how the external sense bases are like village-raiding thieves, the Buddha said "Corā gāmaghātakā" and so on. In that phrase, "manāpāmanāpesu" is used in the locative case with the instrumental sense of "manāpāmanāpehi", meaning "by means of pleasant and unpleasant sights, etc." In that simile, there are five tasks when thieves raid a village. First, the thieves surround the village, set it on fire, and make a "kaṭakaṭa" sound. Then, people take their valuable possessions and flee outside. After that, they engage in physical struggle with those thieves because of their goods. Among them, some receive blows, and some fall at the place where they were struck. The remaining healthy people are bound, taken to the thieves' dwelling place, tied with ropes, and used as slaves. In that simile, the burning of the fire when the village-raiders surround the village should be understood as the burning of the heat of defilements (kilesa) when an object comes into range at the six doors. Fleeing outside with valuables should be understood as abandoning wholesome states and being possessed by unwholesome states at that moment. Engaging in physical struggle because of goods should be understood as the time of committing offenses such as Dukkhaṭa, Dubbhāsita, Pācittiya, and Thullaccaya. Receiving a blow should be understood as the time of committing a Saṅghādisesa offense. Falling at the place of the blow should be understood as the time of committing a Pārājika offense and ceasing to be a monk. Binding the remaining people, taking them to the dwelling place, and using them as slaves should be understood as the time of disrobing and returning to the lay life, having destroyed the Small, Middle, and Great Morality (Cūḷasīla, Majjhimasīla, Mahāsīla) even in the sight of all people, depending on that very object. For such a person who has become a layman and is supporting a wife and children, the mass of suffering experienced in the present life should be understood, as well as the mass of suffering in the future life after death, being reborn in the woeful states (apāya). These external sense bases were also taught as a meditation subject for a certain monk. Here, the four such as visible objects are derived matter (upādārūpa). The tangible object base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana) consists of three elements (earth, fire, air). In the mental object base (dhammāyatana), when those three elements are combined with the water element (āpodhātu), they become the four elements. These four elements are the great primary elements (mahābhūta). By way of delimiting them, there is the space element (ākāsadhātu). There are also lightness (lahutā) and so on. Thus, all primary and derived matter is the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). The four aggregates such as feeling (vedanā) that take that form as an object are the four mental aggregates (nāmakkhandha). Therein, the aggregate of form is "form" (rūpa), and the four...
64: ..."mental aggregates" (arūpino khandhā nāma). For one who defines mind and matter (nāmarūpa) and practices according to the previous method, the meditation subject is taught until the attainment of Arahatship. In the word "Ogha" (Flood), the meaning of "flood" is that which is difficult to cross. These four floods are called "Ogha" in the sense of being difficult to cross because they can only be crossed by one who arouses the intention, "I will fulfill the restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara) and reach Arahatship," relies on a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), and strives rightly; or because they are difficult for anyone to cross. These floods were also taught as a meditation subject for a certain monk. Indeed, these four are just the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). The rest should be expanded by applying the method mentioned under "delight and lust" (nandīrāga). "Sakkāyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ" means that "identity" (sakkāya) is like the near shore of a great river. Just as the near shore of a river is dangerous because of snakes and so on, so too identity is fearful and dangerous because of the four great elements. This identity was also taught as a meditation subject for a certain monk. Identity refers to the five aggregates belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka). These five aggregates, in brief, are just mind and matter (nāmarūpa). Thus, starting from the definition of mind and matter in this identity, the meditation subject should be expanded until Arahatship. "Nibbānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ" means that Nibbāna is like the far shore of a great river, a place of safety and freedom from dangers caused by the four great elements and so on. In the phrase "Vīriyārambhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ", for the purpose of showing the mental effort, the aforementioned "effort" (vāyāma) is taken as "energy" (vīriya). "Tiṇṇo pāraṅgato" means one who has crossed over and reached the other shore. In that text, one who stays on the dangerous near shore and wishes to cross the great river should not delay for a few days, slowly preparing a boat or raft as if playing in the water, without boarding the boat. One who does so will meet with disaster before even boarding. Similarly, one who wishes to cross the ocean of defilements should not procrastinate, thinking, "I am still young; I will construct the raft of the Eightfold Path when I am old." One who does so may meet with destruction before reaching old age, or even if he reaches it, he may not be able to do it. Remembering the Bhaddekaratta Sutta and others, one should quickly construct this raft of the Noble Path (Ariyamagga). Just as one who constructs a raft desires completeness of hands and feet—for a person with a crippled or twisted foot cannot stand, and those with severed hands cannot grasp grass and leaves—similarly, for one who constructs this raft of the Noble Path, the feet of virtue (sīla) and the hands of faith (saddhā) are desired to be complete. A person without virtue or lacking faith cannot stand in the Dispensation (sāsana) and, because of not believing in the holy life, cannot construct the raft of the Noble Path. Just as a person with hands and feet but who is weak cannot construct a raft, whereas only one endowed with strength can, similarly, a person who has virtue and faith but is lazy cannot construct this raft of the Noble Path; only one with aroused energy (vīriya) can. Therefore, one who wishes to construct this raft of the Noble Path should have energy along with faith and so on. That person, striving out of fear of danger, constructs the raft, stands on the bank, sees the league-wide river, and resolves his mind, "I shall cross this great river by relying on human effort." Similarly, the monk who wishes to practice meditation clearly descends and this...
65:
The fulfillment of the hand of faith (saddhā) is also to be desired. To speak of the fault: one who is deficient in virtue and lacking in faith cannot remain established in the Dispensation (sāsana); being faithless toward the noble practice, one is unable to construct the raft of the Noble Path (ariya-magga). Just as a person, though possessing hands and feet, cannot build a raft if they are weak and oppressed by disease, but only one endowed with strength can; similarly, even if one has pure virtue and faith, if one is lazy and indolent, one cannot build this raft of the Noble Path; only one with aroused energy (viriya) can. Therefore, one who wishes to build this raft must be one with aroused energy. Just as that man, having built the raft and standing on the shore, resolves in his mind regarding the great expanse of water a league wide: 'I must cross this great expanse by relying on my own human effort'; in the same way, the yogi monk, descending from the walking path (caṅkama), should resolve with a firm mind: 'Today, I shall cross the vast ocean of defilements (kilesa) to be destroyed by the four paths and establish myself in the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala).'

As that man, relying on the raft, crosses the ocean of the current and reaches a distance of one gāvuta, he looks back and knows: 'I have passed one part; three other parts remain.' Reaching another distance of one gāvuta and looking back, he knows: 'I have passed two parts; two parts remain.' Reaching another distance of one gāvuta and looking back, he knows: 'I have passed three parts; one part remains.' Having passed that remainder and looking back, he knows: 'All four of my parts have been passed.' He then treads on that raft with his foot, casts it into the current, and having crossed over, stands on the bank.

Similarly, this monk, relying on the raft of the Noble Path, crosses the ocean of defilements. Having crossed the defilements to be abandoned by the first path through the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), and standing in the fruition (phala) immediately following the path, he looks back with reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) and knows: 'Of the defilements to be abandoned by the four paths, one part of mine has been abandoned; the other three parts remain.' Again, in the same way, by combining the faculties (indriya), powers (bala), and factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and contemplating formations (saṅkhāra), he crosses the defilements to be abandoned by the second path through the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga). Standing in the fruition immediately following the path, he looks back with reviewing knowledge and knows: 'Of the defilements to be abandoned by the four paths, two parts of mine have been abandoned; the other two parts remain.' Again, in the same way, by combining the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, and contemplating formations, he crosses the defilements to be abandoned by the third path through the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga). Standing in the fruition immediately following the path, he looks back with reviewing knowledge and knows: 'Of the defilements to be abandoned by the four paths, three parts of mine have been abandoned; one part remains.' Again, in the same way, by combining the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, and contemplating formations...
66: ...[the three parts of defilements] have been abandoned; one part remains. Again, in the same way, by combining the faculties (indriya), powers (bala), and factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and contemplating formations (saṅkhāra), he crosses the defilements to be abandoned by the fourth path through the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). Standing in the fruition (phala) immediately following the path, he reviews with reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) and knows: 'All my defilements have been abandoned.' Just as that man, having let the raft float away in the current, climbs to the dry land, enters the city, and reaching the top of a noble palace, sits with a concentrated and joyful mind, thinking: 'Indeed, I am now free from such great danger'; in the same way, the monk, sitting in that very place or in any other place for the night or day, enters the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) with Nibbāna as the object, and sits with a concentrated and joyful mind, thinking: 'Indeed, I am now free from such great danger.' Monks, 'The Brahmin has crossed over, has reached the far shore, and stands on dry land'—this is a designation for an Arahant. It is with this meaning in mind that this was said. In this way, various meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) have been taught in this sutta. However, they should all be combined and shown as one. Even when shown as one, they should be presented by way of the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha). How? Herein, the four internal great elements (mahābhūta), the five internal bases (āyatana), the five external bases, and the fifteen types of subtle matter (sukhuma-rūpa) included in the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) constitute the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), which is a portion of identity (sakkāya). The mind base (manāyatana) is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). The four floods (ogha) and other portions of identity included in the base of mental objects are the remaining four immaterial aggregates (nāma-khandha). Therein, the aggregate of form is 'form' (rūpa), and the four immaterial aggregates are 'name' (nāma). This is 'name-and-form' (nāmarūpa). Its causes are delight and lust (nandī-rāga), the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), the flood of existence (bhavogha), and portions of the base of mental objects and identity. Thus, he defines name-and-form together with its causes. Having defined name-and-form with its causes, he applies the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), develops insight (vipassanā), and by contemplating formations, reaches the fruit of Arahantship. This is the door of deliverance (niyyāna-mukha) for a monk. Among those things, the four great elements, the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), the eleven internal and external bases, a portion of the base of mental objects, the flood of views (diṭṭhogha), the flood of ignorance (avijjogha), and a portion of identity are the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). Delight and lust, a portion of the base of mental objects, the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, and a portion of identity are the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca).
67:
Nibbāna, which is called the "further shore," is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca); the Noble Path is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Among these Four Noble Truths, two truths belong to the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and two to the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa); two are mundane (lokiya) and two are supramundane (lokuttara). Thus, these Four Noble Truths should be shown as divided into sixteen aspects and sixty thousand methods. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred monks who were "those who understand through detailed explanation" (vipañcitaññū) were established in the Fruit of Arahatship. This sutta, however, was taught by way of the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa).

## 2. Rathopama Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "abounding in happiness and joy" (sukha-somanassa-bahulo) means that for that person, bodily happiness (kāyika-sukha) and mental joy (cetasika-somanassa) are abundant. "His cause is accomplished" (yoni cassa āraddhā hoti) means that for that monk, the causal conditions are indeed complete. "For the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khayāya) means that in this sutta, the Path of Arahatship is intended as the dhamma that exhausts the taints; it means for the sake of that Path of Arahatship. "A goad placed crosswise" (odhastapatodo) refers to a goad placed across the middle of the chariot. "Wherever he wishes" (yenicchakaṃ) means towards whichever direction he desires. "Whatever he wishes" (yadicchakaṃ) means towards whatever journey he desires. "He would drive" (sāreyya) means he would urge [the horses] forward. "He would drive back" (paccāsāreyya) means he would turn back. "For protection" (ārakkhāya) means for the purpose of guarding. "For restraint" (saṃyamāya) means for the purpose of suppressing the momentum [of the senses]. "For taming" (damāya) means for the purpose of becoming disciplined by not indulging in opposites. "For tranquility" (upasamāya) means for the purpose of calming the defilements.

In the phrase "Even so" (evameva kho), by way of a simile: just as when an unskilled charioteer yokes untamed Sindh horses and drives the chariot on an uneven road, the wheels break, the axle breaks, and the hooves of the Sindh horses also break; he himself meets with ruin and disaster, and he cannot drive according to his wish. In the same way, a monk who has unguarded doors in the six sense faculties is unable to experience the delight of a recluse (samaṇa-rati)—namely, the bliss of Samatha, Vipassanā, the Path, and the Fruit—as he desires. Just as a skilled charioteer yokes tamed Sindh horses, brings the chariot down to a level piece of ground, takes the reins, keeps mindfulness on the horses' hooves, takes the goad, and by making them disciplined, drives them wherever he wishes; even so, a monk who has guarded doors in the six sense faculties experiences the delight of a recluse in this Dispensation as he desires. If he wishes to direct his knowledge towards the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), his knowledge goes towards that. In the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā) and so forth, the same method should be understood.

"Moderation in eating" (bhojane mattaññū) means knowing the measure in food. In that regard, there are two kinds of measures: the measure in receiving (paṭiggahaṇa) and the measure in consuming (paribhoga). Among these two, the measure in receiving should be known by way of the donor's wish, by way of the gift itself, and one should also know one's own capacity. To speak in detail, a monk who knows these three, even if the gift is abundant, if the donor wishes to give only a little, he receives only a little according to the donor's wish. Even if the gift is small, if the donor wishes to give much, he receives only a little according to the measure of the gift. If the gift is abundant and the donor also wishes to give much, he knows his own capacity and receives in a suitable measure. A monk who knows the measure in receiving in this way brings about gain that has not yet arisen and makes firm the gain that has already arisen. He is like the young novice, seven years of age, during the time of King Dhammika Tissa. To the King...
68:
(In receiving an offering,) one should know the donor's wish, one should know the measure of the gift, and one should also know one's own capacity. To speak in detail, a monk of such a nature, even if the gift is abundant, if the donor wishes to give only a little, he receives only a little according to the donor's wish. If the gift is small and the donor wishes to give much, he receives only a little according to the measure of the gift. If the gift is abundant and the donor also wishes to give much, he knows his own capacity and receives in a suitable measure. Such a monk, being one who knows the measure in receiving, brings about gain that has not yet arisen and makes firm the gain that has already arisen. He is like the young novice, seven years of age, in the time of King Dhammika Tissa.

It is heard that five hundred carts of molasses were brought to the King. The King said, "This is a delightful gift; I do not wish to eat it without the Venerable Ones," and he sent two hundred and fifty carts to the Mahāvihāra monastery. He himself went there after having his breakfast. When the drum was struck as a signal, twelve thousand monks assembled. The King, standing in a suitable place, called the monastery attendant and instructed: "In a king's gift, a full bowl is the measure. Fill the vessel they have brought and give it. If anyone, standing firm in knowing the measure of receiving, does not accept it, report it to me."

At that time, a Great Elder, thinking, "I will worship the Great Bodhi Tree and the Great Stupa," came from Cetiyapabbata. Upon entering the monastery, he saw the monks receiving molasses at the great pavilion and said to the novice following behind him, "Do you have a need for molasses?" The novice replied, "Yes, Bhante, I have no need." [The Elder said,] "Novice, we are tired from the journey; a single lump of molasses the size of a wood-apple (kapittha) fruit will be enough for us." The novice took out a vessel and stood according to the Elder's seniority. The attendant filled the vessel he had taken up to the brim, but the novice moved his finger to stop him. "Dear novice, in the gift of royal families, a full vessel is the measure. Accept a full vessel," he said. "Lay follower, it is true that kings have great intentions, but for our preceptor, only this much is needed," the novice said.

The King, hearing this conversation, asked, "Friends, what is the novice saying?" and went to the novice. The attendant said, "Sire, the novice's vessel is small, and he does not take much." The King said, "Bhante, please accept a full measure in the vessel you have brought." "Great King, it is true that kings have great intentions and wish to give a full vessel, but for our preceptor, only this much is needed," he said. The King thought, "This novice is only seven years old; even now he is not yet free from the smell of milk. (Others) might say they will take it, fill small and large pots, and eat it tomorrow or the day after. For the sake of preserving the Buddha's Dispensation..."
69:
...they were so, wishing to give only after filling the vessel; however, they said, 'We only need this much for our preceptor.' The King thought, 'This boy is only seven years old; even now the smell of milk has not left his mouth. He does not say, "I will take these goods, fill small and large jars, and eat them tomorrow or the day after." The Buddha's Dispensation can be supported by such as these.' He then commanded his men, 'Sirs, I am devoted to this novice (sāmaṇera). Bring the other two hundred and fifty carts as well and offer them to the Saṅgha.'

That same King, on one occasion, desiring to eat partridge meat, thought, 'If I tell another that I wish to eat partridge meat cooked on embers, they will cause the destruction of partridges within a league's (yojana) radius.' Thus, enduring the arising craving, he let three years pass. Then, pus formed in the King's ears. Being unable to endure it, he asked, 'Sirs, is there any attendant lay follower (upāsaka) of ours who guards his virtue (sīla)?' They replied, 'Yes, Your Majesty, there is one named Tissa who guards his virtue unbroken.' Then, wishing to test him, the King had him summoned. Tissa came, paid homage to the King, and stood there. Then the King asked him, 'Dear son, is your name Tissa?' 'Yes, Your Majesty,' he replied. 'Then go,' said the King.

When he had left, the King had a chicken brought and commanded a man, 'Go, tell Tissa: "Cook this chicken in three ways and serve it to us."' The man went and spoke accordingly. Tissa said, 'Sir, if this chicken were already dead, I would cook and serve it as I know how. However, I do not commit the taking of life (pāṇātipāta).' The man returned and informed the King. The King sent him again, saying, 'Go once more.' The man went and said, 'Sir, serving the King is a heavy burden; do not do this. Virtue can be undertaken again later; cook this chicken.' Then Tissa said, 'Sir, in this existence, death is certain but once. I will not commit the taking of life.' The man informed the King again. Although the King sent him a third time, Tissa did not accept. So the King had him summoned and questioned him himself. He gave the same answer to the King. Then the King commanded his men, 'This man violates the King's order. Go, place him on the executioner's block and cut off his head.'
70:
The King also gave a secret sign to the executioners: 'Threaten this man and take him away; place his head upon the executioner's block, and then come and report to me.'

The executioners made him lie on the executioner's block and placed the chicken in his hands. He held the chicken to his chest and said, 'Dear one, I give my life for yours; I take your life [as my own]. Go without fear,' and he released it. The chicken flapped its wings, flew through the air, and perched on a banyan tree. The place where the chicken was granted safety became known as Kukkuṭagiri.

When the King heard of this event, he summoned the minister's son, adorned him with all kinds of ornaments, and said, 'Dear son, I tested you for this very purpose. Three years have passed since I first desired to eat partridge meat. Can you prepare and serve me partridge meat that is pure in three respects (ti-koṭi-parisuddha)?' 'Great King, this task is indeed my duty,' he replied. He went out and, while standing in the doorway, saw a man entering early in the morning carrying three partridges. He gave him two kahāpaṇas, took the partridges, cleaned them, seasoned them with cumin and other spices, cooked them well over embers, and served them to the King. While seated upon the auspicious throne on the upper floor of the palace, the King took one, broke off a little, and put it in his mouth. At that very moment, the flavor spread through his seven thousand taste nerves.

At that time, remembering the Saṅgha of monks, he thought, 'Even a King who is the lord of the earth like me could not obtain partridge meat for three years. Where will the Saṅgha of monks, who do not cook for themselves, obtain it?' Thinking thus, he spat out the piece of partridge meat he had put in his mouth onto the ground. The minister's son knelt down and caught it with his mouth. The King said, 'Dear son, move aside. I know you are without fault. It is only for this reason that I have discarded this partridge meat.' He then added, 'Keep the remainder well-preserved just as it is.'

On the following day, the Elder who regularly frequented the royal palace entered for alms. Seeing the Elder, the minister's son took his bowl and invited him into the palace. Another man who had ordained in old age followed behind the Elder as if he were his attendant monk. The Elder, thinking, 'He must be a monk invited by the King,' remained unconcerned. The minister's son also, thinking, 'He must be the Elder's attendant,' remained unconcerned. Having seated them, they offered them rice gruel. After the gruel was finished, the King served the partridge meat. The Elder took one,
71:
The other elderly monk also took one. The king thought, "There is still a remaining portion; it is not proper to eat without asking," and so he asked the Mahāthera. The Mahāthera covered his hand, but the elderly monk accepted it. The king, becoming displeased, took the bowl of the Mahāthera who had finished his meal and, following behind him, said, "Venerable Sir, when coming to a family home, it is proper to bring a monk who has mastered the monastic duties (vatta)." At that moment, the Mahāthera realized, "This elderly monk was not invited by the king."

On the following day, he entered [the palace] taking his attendant novice (sāmaṇera) with him. At that time, after the king had served the rice gruel, he offered partridges. The Mahāthera took one, but the novice gestured with his finger to have it cut in the middle and took only a single portion. The king offered that portion to the Mahāthera. The Mahāthera covered his hand, and the novice also covered his hand. The king sat nearby and, while eating the pieces he had cut, said, "By relying on the venerable ones who have mastered the duties, I have gained the opportunity to eat one and a half partridges." At the very moment the king finished eating the meat, pus flowed from both his ears. Then, after washing his mouth, he approached the novice and said, "Dear child, I am very much inspired; I offer you eight permanent meals (dhuvabhatta)." The novice replied, "Great King, I give them to my preceptor (upajjhāya)." The king said, "I shall offer another eight." The novice replied, "I give those eight to our teacher (ācariya)." The king said, "I shall offer another eight as well." The novice replied, "I give those eight to my fellow monks (samānupajjhāya)." The king said, "I shall offer another eight as well." The novice replied, "I give those eight to the Saṅgha of monks." When the king said, "I shall offer another eight as well," the novice accepted them. In this way, one who knows the measure in receiving (paṭiggahanapamāṇa) can cause unarisen gains to arise and can make arisen gains endure. This is called the measure in receiving.

Among those [measures], the measure in consumption (paribhogapamāṇa) is beneficial for reflection (paccavekkhaṇā). Because reflecting and consuming with the thought, "I consume this food for this purpose," is the only beneficial way, it is called the measure in consumption; it is this paribhogapamāṇa that is intended here. For this reason, the Buddha taught "Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso..." and so on. Other [types of knowing the measure] are also proper.

## In this term 'Sīhaseyyā' (Lion's Sleep), there are four types of sleep: the sleep of the sensualist (kāmabhogiseyyā), the sleep of the hungry ghost (petaseyyā), the sleep of the lion (sīhaseyyā), and the sleep of the Tathāgata (tathāgataseyyā). Among these, the sleep mentioned as "Monks, for the most part, sensualists sleep on their left side" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.246) is called kāmabhogiseyyā. For among those sensualists, there is generally no one who sleeps on their right side.
72:
"Monks, for the most part, hungry ghosts (petas) sleep lying on their backs" (as stated in Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.246); this is the sleep of the hungry ghost (petaseyyā). Because hungry ghosts have very little flesh and blood and are merely a collection of bones, they cannot sleep on one side and only sleep on their backs.

"Monks, for the most part, the lion, the king of beasts, places its tail between its thighs and sleeps on its right side"; this is the sleep of the lion (sīhaseyyā). The powerful lion king places its two front paws in one place and its two hind paws in another, tucks its tail between its thighs, and after noting the positions where the front paws, hind paws, and tail are placed, it sleeps with its head resting upon its front paws. Even after sleeping the whole day, when it wakes up, it does so without being startled. It raises its head and observes the positions where its front paws and other limbs were placed. If any limb has moved from its original position, it becomes displeased, thinking, "This is not suitable for your birth and your bravery," and continues to lie right there; it does not go out for food. However, if the limbs remain unmoved, it becomes joyful, thinking, "This is suitable for your birth and your bravery," and after getting up, it stretches in the manner of lions, shakes its mane, roars three times, and then departs to seek food.

Sleeping in the fourth jhāna is called the sleep of the Tathāgata (tathāgataseyyā). Among these four types of sleep, the sleep of the lion (sīhaseyyā) is described in this Sutta. This sleep is called the noble sleep because it is a posture of great power.

"Foot on foot" (pāde pādaṃ) means placing the left foot upon the right foot. "Overlapping" (accādhāya) means placing it slightly beyond. This is because if the ankles or the knees touch each other, painful sensations constantly arise, the mind cannot become one-pointed, and the sleep is uncomfortable. If placed slightly beyond so they do not touch, pain does not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the sleep is comfortable. Therefore, one should sleep in this manner.

"Mindful and clearly comprehending" (sato sampajāno) means being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom. How can one who is asleep be mindful and clearly comprehending? It is possible by not abandoning mindfulness and clear comprehension. This monk, having purified his mind from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) throughout the day and the first watch of the night, descends from the walking path at the end of the first watch and, even while washing his feet, does so without abandoning his primary meditation subject (mūlakammaṭṭhāna). Without abandoning that primary meditation subject...
73:
He opens the door, sits on the couch, and enters sleep without abandoning the original meditation subject. Upon waking, he wakes up while grasping the original meditation subject. Even though he enters sleep in this way, he is one possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension. The former teachers did not approve of this being called ñāṇadhātuka (the element of knowledge).

By the method mentioned, that monk purifies his mind, and at the end of the first watch, thinking, "I will rest this kammically acquired (upādinnaka) body by sleeping," he descends from the walking path (caṅkama), washes his feet without abandoning the original meditation subject, and opens the door. However, when sitting on the couch, he lets go of the original meditation subject and reflects on the lodging, thinking, "Only aggregates strike against aggregates, only elements strike against elements," and gradually enters sleep. Upon waking, he wakes up while grasping the original meditation subject. It should be understood that even though he enters sleep in this way, he is one possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension.

Thus, in this sutta, only the preliminary stage of insight (vipassanā) consisting of three factors is spoken of. Without stopping at just this much, the monk combines the faculties (indriya), powers (bala), and enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) that arise at that moment of insight, develops insight, and reaches the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala). Thus, the teaching should be explained up to the Fruit of Arahantship.

## 3. Commentary on the Kummo-pama Sutta

In the third sutta, kummo means a tortoise with bones. Kacchapa is a synonym for that same tortoise. Anunadītīre means near the bank of a river. Gocarapasuta means one who is diligent, concerned, and attached to seeking food, thinking, "If I should get some fruit, large or small, I shall eat it." Samodahitvā means drawing [limbs] into one's own shell, like putting something into a chest. Saṅkhasāyati means he stays. Samodahanti means while drawing in the limbs, or keeping them in. This is the intended meaning: Just as a tortoise, by drawing its limbs into its shell, does not give an opportunity to the jackal, and the jackal cannot harm it; even so, a monk, by drawing his thoughts into the shell of his meditation object, does not give an opportunity to the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra), and Māra cannot harm him.

Anissita means not relying on the supports of craving and views. Aññamaheṭhayāna means not harming any other person. Parinibbuta means extinguished through the extinction of defilements. Nūpavadeyya kañci means he should not disparage any other person, either through their failure in virtue (sīlavipatti) or failure in conduct (ācāravipatti), with the desire to exalt himself...
74:
...or with the desire to despise another. He should not disparage them. Rather, having established five qualities within himself, he dwells with a mind established in the nature of uplifting [others], thinking: "I will speak at the right time, not at the wrong time; I will speak what is true, not what is false; I will speak gently, not harshly; I will speak what is beneficial, not what is unbeneficial; I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hate."

## 4. Commentary on the Paṭhama-dārukkhandhopama Sutta

In the fourth sutta, addasa (he saw) means he saw while sitting on the noble Buddha-seat prepared near the bank of the Ganges River. Vuyhamānaṃ (being carried along) refers to a log that was squared and planed, placed in a mountain cleft, well-dried by the wind and sun, and then, when the early rains fell, was floated by the water and gradually fell into the current of the Ganges River and was being carried along by that current. Bhikkhū āmantesi (he addressed the monks) means he addressed them with the desire to teach the Dhamma, thinking, "By using this log as a simile, I will show a son of good family who has gone forth out of faith in my Dispensation." Regarding the words "that great log being carried along by the current of the Ganges River," he began to show the other eight faults that hinder the arrival at the ocean of a log that has entered the current and is free from the [first] eight faults.

The freedom of that log from the eight faults should be understood thus: Indeed, one kind of log grows at the foot of a mountain not far from the Ganges River, becomes entwined with various creepers, reaches the state of having yellow leaves, and being eaten by termites and so on, perishes in that very place without even being called a "log." This log, having descended into the Ganges, cannot enjoy the beauty of the emerald-colored surface of the waves upon reaching the ocean while sporting in the winding places.

Another kind of log grows on the bank of the Ganges with its roots outside and its branches inside. Although this log occasionally touches the water with its hanging branches, because its roots are outside, it cannot enjoy the beauty of the emerald-colored surface of the waves upon reaching the ocean while sporting in the winding places after descending into the Ganges.

Another kind of log grows in the middle of the Ganges, well-established with firm roots. Its crooked branches extending outward are also firmly bound by various creepers. This log also, because of its firm roots and because of being firmly bound by creepers on the outside, cannot enjoy the beauty... after descending into the Ganges.
75:
Another log, covered by sand at the very place it fell, falls into decay. That log also, though descending into the Gaṅgā, [is unable to] enjoy itself in the winding places and reach the ocean to grace the surface of the emerald-colored waves.

Another log, because it grew between two large rocks, remains motionless as if firmly planted, splitting every incoming current into two. This log, because it is well-established between the rocks, though descending into the Gaṅgā... does not get the opportunity.

Another log remains in the open air, rising towards the sky and firmly bound by creepers. Only after one or two years have passed, when a heavy flood arrives, does it get wet once or twice. This log also, because it stands rising towards the sky and because it only gets wet once or twice after one or two years, though descending into the Gaṅgā... does not get the opportunity.

Another log grew on a small island in the middle of the Gaṅgā, having a soft trunk and branches. When the current comes, it lies down along the flow, and when the water recedes, it raises its head and stands as if dancing. Regarding that soft tree, it is as if the Ocean says to the Gaṅgā: "O Gaṅgā, you bring me various precious woods such as the heartwood of sandalwood and the heartwood of pine (salala), but you do not bring this soft log." The Gaṅgā river acknowledges, "Lord, this log is easy to obtain; I shall see to it next time." The next time, although she comes embracing it with reddish waters, that soft tree, just as before, lies down along the flow and, when the water recedes, raises its head and stands as if dancing. This tree, because of its own softness, though descending into the Gaṅgā... does not get the opportunity.

Another log has fallen crosswise in the Gaṅgā river and, being covered with sand, has become like an intermediate bridge, serving many people. Trees such as bamboo, rattan, karañja, and kudhā from both banks float down and get stuck at that very log. Likewise, various bushes, as well as floating rotten carcasses of pestles, winnowing trays, snakes, dogs, elephants, horses, and so on, get stuck there. Even the great Gaṅgā, upon hitting that log, splits into two and flows on. Fish, turtles, crocodiles, and makaras also make their home right there. This log, because it has fallen crosswise and serves the multitude, though descending into the Gaṅgā and enjoying itself in the winding places, does not get the opportunity to reach the ocean and grace the surface of the emerald-colored waves.

Thus, the Blessed One, in order to show the other eight faults that obstruct the reaching of the ocean by the log floating in the current, being free from these aforementioned eight faults, said:

In showing those eight faults, "na thale ussakkharissati" means it will not go up onto the dry land. "na manussaggāho gahessati" means that people crossing by raft, seeing this log floating in the great current, will not take it for the purpose of rafters and so on. "na amanussaggāho gahessati" means that deities and spirits (amanussa) will not take it, thinking, "This sandalwood heartwood is very precious; we shall place it at the door of our mansion." Similarly, in the phrase "evaṃ kho," the comparison between the simile and the thing signified should be understood along with the eight external faults in the following manner. To speak in detail, like a log that grew on a mountain peak near the Gaṅgā and decayed right there due to being eaten by termites, etc., leaving not even a name, so should a person with wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi) such as "there is no fruit of giving" be understood. Indeed, this person with such views, being far from the Dispensation (Sāsana), [cannot descend] into the Noble Path...
76:
The Blessed One spoke the words beginning with, "This great log is being carried along by the current of the river Gaṅgā." In showing those eight faults, "It will not be stranded on high ground" means it will not ascend onto the dry land. "Humans will not seize it" means that humans, seeing "Indeed, this log is very large," will not go by raft and take it for the purpose of rafters and so on. "Non-humans will not seize it" means that non-humans (amanussa) will not take it, thinking, "This sandalwood heartwood is very precious; we shall place it at the door of our mansion."

In the phrase "Even so," the comparison of the simile should be understood along with the eight external faults in this manner: Like a log that grew on the high ground of a mountain peak near the Gaṅgā and reached a state of being beyond designation, having decayed right there from being eaten by termites and so on, so should a person be understood who is possessed of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) such as "There is no fruit of giving." Indeed, this person, because of being far from the Dispensation (Sāsana), is unable to descend into the journey of the Noble Path, board the raft of concentration (samādhi), and reach the ocean of Nibbāna.

Like a tree growing on the bank of the Gaṅgā with roots on the outside and branches leaning towards the inside, so should the person who is a "monk-householder" (samaṇakuṭumbika) with unbreakable worldly ties be regarded. This monk-householder [thinks], "This mind is indeed unstable; even while saying 'I am a monk,' one becomes a householder; even while saying 'I am a householder,' one becomes a monk. Who can know? What will happen?" Even when ordaining at an old age, he does not let go of his householder ties. For those who ordain when old, there is no such thing as fulfillment. If that elderly monk receives a robe, he receives only one with torn edges, or one that is worn out and discolored. If he receives a lodging, he receives only a leaf-hut or a pavilion at the edge of the monastery. Even when wandering for alms, he has to walk behind children who are the age of his own sons and grandsons, and he has to sit in the furthest seat. For that reason, he is miserable and dejected, and with tears flowing, he thinks, "I have wealth belonging to my family; is it allowable for me to live by using that wealth?" and asks an expert in the Vinaya (Vinayadhara): "Venerable Teacher, is it allowable to manage and use one's own property, or is it not allowable?" "There is no fault in this; it is allowable," [the Vinayadhara replies]. That monk, taking some difficult and ill-behaved monks who attend on him, goes into the village in the evening, stands in the middle of the village, has the villagers called, and says, "To whom do you give the revenue and produce arising from our efforts?" The villagers say, "Venerable sirs, you have become monks; to whom should we give it?" Saying, "What? Is one's own property not allowable for monks?" he takes a hoe and a basket, and performing various tasks such as building embankments for the fields...
77: That monk lives as a wealthy monastic householder, collecting grain and various fruits, having them cooked and consuming them as he pleases during the cold, hot, and rainy seasons. For this monk, only a wife—a foot-servant—along with a young son with five top-knots is missing (otherwise, he is just like a householder). Although this person provides physical service to the monks at the courtyard of the stupa or the Bodhi tree, like a tree inside a river touching the water with its hanging branches, he is unable to enter the Noble Path and reach the ocean of Nibbāna while sitting on the raft of concentration, because he has not cut the bonds of a layman and is rooted outside the Dispensation. One should recognize a person of broken livelihood who lives depending on the property of the Saṅgha, like a crooked tree growing in the middle of a river, firmly bound by creepers from the outside. Some people, though they renounce the bonds of a layman and ordain, do not obtain ordination in a suitable place. Indeed, this ordination is like taking rebirth. Just as humans learn the customs of the families in which they are reborn, so too monks learn the customs of the teachers in whose presence they ordain. Therefore, some, having ordained in an unsuitable place, remain outside of advice, instruction, recitation, and inquiry. Early in the morning, they take a pot without a rim and go to the watering place. They place the alms-bowl on their shoulder for the sake of their teachers' and preceptors' food and go to the refectory. They play various games with difficult-to-discipline novices and live in association with the children of the park-keepers. In his youth, that monk goes to the Saṅgha's land with other young monks and park-keepers who are like him, saying, 'This is the Saṅgha's land received by the Noble Arahants from such-and-such a king. You do not give this and that to the Saṅgha. If the king or the great ministers hear about your conduct, they will not be pleased. Come now, do this and that.' He makes them hold hoes and baskets and makes them perform necessary tasks in the tanks and channels. Having brought many crops into the monastery, he informs the Saṅgha of his helpfulness through the park-keepers. The Saṅgha then says, 'This young monk is very helpful; give him a hundred or two hundred,' and causes it to be given. Thus, this monk, growing wealthy from here and there with the Saṅgha's property, is bound by the twenty-one kinds of improper search (anesanā) outside the Dispensation. He is unable to enter the Noble Path and reach the ocean of Nibbāna while sitting on the raft of concentration.
78: One should recognize a lazy and gluttonous person as being like a tree that has fallen and become rotten, covered by sand. Regarding such a person—whose eyes are fixed on material gains, who is greedy for requisites, who has abandoned the duties toward teachers and preceptors, and who is devoid of the study of the Pāḷi texts, the commentaries, and systematic attention—the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) speak in essence as if saying, 'Friends, to whom shall we go?' Then, Sloth and Torpor (thina-middha) arises and says, 'Why do you not see? This lazy person living in such-and-such a monastery goes to such-and-such a village, swallows gruel upon gruel, cake upon cake, and rice upon rice. When he returns to the monastery, he abandons all duties, remains devoid of study and so forth, and approaches his bed, thus creating an opportunity for me.' Then, Sensual Desire (kāmacchanda) arises and says, 'Friend, when an opportunity is made for you, it is also made for me. Right now, after sleeping, he will wake up with a mind followed by defilements and will think thoughts of sensual pleasure.' Then, Ill-will (byāpāda) arises and says, 'When an opportunity is made for you all, it is also made for me. Right now, when he wakes up from sleep and is told, "Perform your major and minor duties," he will say, "Friends, these monks do not do their own work but are concerned with us," and thus speaking various harsh words, he will go about with protruding eyes.' Then, Restlessness (uddhacca) arises and says, 'When an opportunity is made for you all, it is also made for me. A lazy person has a restless mind like a mass of fire fanned by the wind.' Then, Remorse (kukkucca) arises and says, 'When an opportunity is made for you all, it is also made for me. A lazy person is indeed oppressed by remorse. He perceives what is unallowable as allowable and what is allowable as unallowable.' Then, Doubt (vicikicchā) arises and says, 'When an opportunity is made for you all, it is also made for me. Indeed, such a person develops great doubt in eight areas.' In this way, the five hindrances overwhelm, bite, and oppress the lazy and gluttonous person, just as fierce dogs and others overwhelm and bite an old ox with broken horns. That person, too, though entering the stream of the Noble Path and sitting on the raft of concentration, is unable to reach the ocean of Nibbāna. One should recognize a person possessed of wrong views (diṭṭhigatika) as being like a tree standing with its roots planted between two large rocks. He holds such views as: 'There is matter in the formless realm; mind occurs in the non-percipient realm; the supramundane path consists of many thought-moments'...
79:
## 
“Latent tendencies (anusaya) are dissociated from the mind, and only those beings wander and roam through Saṃsāra.” One who says this wanders about like the monk Ariṭṭha and the novice Kaṇṭaka. Furthermore, such a person is one of divisive speech, wandering about creating rifts between preceptors and their pupils. Even if such a person descends into the stream of the Noble Path and sits upon the raft of concentration, they are unable to reach the ocean of Nibbāna.

Just as a tree standing in an open field, filling the sky and firmly bound by creepers, gets soaked only once or twice when a great flood arrives after a year or two, so should one understand the person who ordains in old age and lives in a remote area, where seeing the Saṅgha and hearing the Dhamma are rare. Some, having ordained when old, receive higher ordination within a few days. After five years, they master the Pātimokkha. After ten years, while studying the Vinaya in the presence of a Vinaya-expert elder, they sit with a peppercorn or a piece of yellow myrobalan in their mouth, covering their face with a fan and dozing off. Thus, becoming a so-called Vinaya expert only by pretense, they take their bowl and robes and go to a remote region. There, people respect that monk, and because seeing a monk is rare, they say, “Venerable Sir, please reside right here,” and build a monastery for him. They plant trees laden with flowers and fruits and have him reside there.

Later, learned monks from a monastery similar to the Mahāvihāra, thinking, “We shall return after dyeing robes and such in the countryside,” arrive there. Seeing them, the resident monk is delighted and performs various duties for them. The next day, he takes them into the village for alms and says to the devotees, “This elder is an expert in the Suttas, this one is an expert in the Abhidhamma, this one is an expert in the Vinaya, and this one is a master of the Three Pitakas. When will you ever find such noble elders again? Listen to the Dhamma from them.” The lay devotees, saying, “We shall listen to the Dhamma,” clear the path to the monastery, bring ghee, oil, and so on, approach the Great Elder, and say, “Venerable Sir, we wish to hear the Dhamma; please arrange for the Dhamma preachers.” They return the next day to listen to the Dhamma.

The resident elder spends the day inside the chamber, tidying up the bowls and robes of the visiting monks. When the daytime Dhamma preacher finishes and leaves, the Sarabhāṇaka (intoner) recites the intoned verses like a pot pouring out water and then leaves.
80:
## 
The resident monk does not know that (intoned recitation) either. Even though the nighttime preacher speaks throughout the night, as if agitating the ocean, and then leaves, the resident monk does not know that Dhamma either. Even though the dawn preacher speaks and leaves, he does not know that Dhamma either. Rising early in the morning and washing his face, he offers the bowls and robes to the elders. When they go for alms, he asks the Great Elder: “Venerable Sir, which Jātaka did the daytime preacher speak? Which Sutta did the Sarabhāṇaka recite? Which Dhamma talk did the nighttime preacher give? Which Jātaka did the dawn preacher speak? How many are the aggregates (khandhas)? How many are the elements (dhātus)? How many are the bases (āyatanas)?”

A person of such nature, even if they get to see monks and hear the Dhamma for a year or two, is like a tree that is only moistened once or twice by water when a flood comes. Such a monk, living far away and withdrawing from seeing the Saṅgha and hearing the Dhamma, even if he were to enter the Noble Path and sit on the raft of concentration, would be unable to reach the ocean of Nibbāna.

One should understand the person who preaches the Dhamma with a sweet voice to be like a tender tree growing on a small island in the middle of the Ganges. Such a monk learns well-known Jātakas like the Vessantara and goes to remote areas where seeing a monk is rare. There, being supported by people whose hearts are inspired by his Dhamma talk, he lives in a monastery built for him, filled with trees bearing flowers and fruits, as delightful as the Nandana Grove. Then, monks who are “bearers of the burden” (bhārahāra), hearing news of him, think: “It is said that such a monk lives with a mind attached to his supporters. A wise monk is capable of learning the Word of the Buddha or practicing meditation. Let us bring him and study the Dhamma with him in the presence of such-and-such an elder, or practice meditation in the presence of such-and-such an elder.” They then travel to that place.

The resident monk performs duties for the visiting monks. In the evening, when they come out to walk around the monastery, they ask, “Friend, did you build this cetiya?” He replies, “Yes, Venerable Sirs, I built it.” They ask, “Did you prepare this Bodhi tree, this pavilion, this Uposatha hall, this fire-room, and this walkway? Did you plant these trees and create this monastery as delightful as the Nandana Grove?” He replies, “Yes, Venerable Sirs, I did.”

In the evening, he goes to attend to the elders, bows, and asks, “Venerable Sirs, for what reason have you come?” They reply, “Friend, we have come to take you to the presence of such-and-such an elder...”
81:
"Venerable sirs, we have come for this reason: to learn the Dhamma from such-and-such an elder, to learn meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) from such-and-such an elder, and to practice the recluse's Dhamma (samaṇadhamma) together in such-and-such a forest," they said. "Venerable sirs, it is well. You have indeed come for my benefit. I too have become weary of staying here for so long. Venerable sirs, I will follow you; let me first take my bowl and robes," he replied. "Friend, the young monks and novices are exhausted from the journey. Let us rest here today and depart tomorrow after the meal," they said. He replied, "Venerable sirs, it is well," and on the following day, he entered the village for alms together with those monks. The villagers, saying, "Our master has come bringing many visiting monks," prepared seats and offered rice gruel. After listening to their pleasant conversation while sitting comfortably, they offered the main meal. The elders said, "Friend, you should come after giving the blessing (anumodanā). We will go ahead and finish our meal duties at a place where water is easily available," and they departed first.

After hearing the anumodanā, the villagers asked, "Venerable sir, where have those elders come from?" "Lay followers, these elders are my teachers and preceptors (ācariya-upajjhāya), fellow disciples of the same preceptor, and close, familiar friends," he replied. They asked again, "Why have they come?" "They have come because they wish to take me with them," he said. "Do you also wish to go, venerable sir?" they asked. "Lay followers, I will go," he replied. "Venerable sir, what are you saying? For which venerable one did we build and offer the Uposatha hall, the refectory, the fire-room (aggisālā), and so on? To which venerable one shall we go for all our auspicious and inauspicious occasions?" they pleaded. The great female lay devotees also sat right there, shedding tears and weeping. The young monk thought, "If you are in such distress, what would I do by going? I will just let the elders go," and he returned to the monastery.

The elders, having finished their meal duties and taken their bowls and robes, were sitting there when they saw the young monk. They said, "Friend, why are you delayed? It is late in the day; let us go." "Venerable sirs, it is well. You are at ease (free from bonds). The foundation of such-and-such a house still remains as it was. The painting work and so on of such-and-such a house are still there. Therefore, even if I go, my mind will be distracted. Please go ahead, venerable sirs. At such-and-such a monastery, please proceed with washing and dyeing robes and so forth. I will come to that monastery later," he said. Those elders, realizing the young monk's desire to withdraw, said, "You may come later," and they departed.

After seeing the elders off, the monk returned to the monastery. Looking at the refectory and other buildings, and seeing the pleasantness of the monastery, he thought: "It is very good that I did not go. If I had gone, some Dhamma preacher might come, captivate the minds of all the villagers, and take this monastery as the property of his own group. Furthermore, as a latecomer, I would have to live eating the alms-food that he receives." Later, that monk thought: "Those monks, having learned the Buddha's word (Buddhavacana) wherever they went, have become commentators (aṭṭhakathā-cariya) and masters of the Vinaya (vinayadhara). They are now traveling with retinues of hundreds and thousands. The elders who went to practice the recluse's Dhamma, by applying their minds to meditation (kammaṭṭhāna)..."
82:
A certain preacher might come, captivate the minds of everyone, and make this monastery the property of his own sect. In that case, I, being a latecomer, would have to live following him, eating the alms-food he receives. Later, he hears: 'Those monks, wherever they went, have learned the Word of the Buddha in terms of one Nikāya, two Nikāyas, one Piṭaka, two Piṭakas, and so on; they have become teachers of the Commentaries (Atthakathā), masters of the Vinaya (Vinayadhara), and travel with a retinue of a hundred or a thousand. Those who went there to practice the recluse's Dhamma (samaṇadhamma), through their striving and exertion, have become Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), Once-returners (Sakadāgāmi), Non-returners (Anāgāmi), and Arahants, and have attained Parinibbāna with great honor.' Then he thinks: 'If I too had gone, such success would have been mine as well. But now, being unable to give up this place, I have declined greatly.' This person, because of his own softness, being unable to give up that place, is unable to enter the Noble Path (Ariyamagga), sit on the raft of concentration (samādhi), and reach the ocean of Nibbāna.

One should understand the person of stagnant conduct (olīnavuttiko) as being like a tree that has fallen across the Ganges River and, being covered with sand, has become like a bridge between two islands, thus being of service to many; such a person remains having learned one of the practices such as the Rathavinīta, the Mahā-ariyavaṃsa, or the Candopama Suttas. Having learned the Dhamma related to that practice, and being naturally sweet-voiced, he goes to a great place like Cittalapabbata and performs duties such as the service of the stupa courtyard (cetiyangaṇavatta). Then, the visiting young monks who have arrived at the place for hearing Dhamma request him, 'Please preach the Dhamma.' He explains and preaches the Dhamma and the practice he has well learned. Then all the monks—senior, middle-aged, and junior—such as the forest-dwellers (paṃsukūlika) and alms-food eaters (piṇḍapātika), are delighted, thinking, 'Oh, what a good man!'

Teaching some only the introduction (nidāna), some half a verse, and some a full verse, he gathers the young monks and novices as if binding them with an iron band. Approaching the senior elders (Mahātheras), he asks, 'Venerable sirs, this is an ancient monastery; is there any produce from the lands here?' The elders reply, 'What are you saying, friend? There is produce from as much as twenty-four thousand karīsas of land.' 'Venerable sirs, though you say so, not even a fire burns in the hearth.' 'Friend, the requisites received by the residents of the Mahāvihāra are destroyed in this way; no one can maintain them.' 'Venerable sirs, why do you allow these requisites, donated by ancient kings and used by the Arahants, to be destroyed?' 'Friend, it can only be achieved if a preacher like you manages it.' 'Venerable sirs, do not say so; we are preachers who point out the practice (paṭipatti). You seem to want to make me a monastery steward (saṅghakuṭumbika).' 'Friend, is this improper? If spoken by someone like you, gains will arise for us.' 'Venerable sirs, if that is the case, when the monastery attendants (ārāmikas) come, let them handle my burden; I will speak a proper way (kappiyadvāra) to them.' Having learned one or two Nikāyas...
83:
'Requisites that are received are indeed destroyed in this way; no one can maintain them,' they said. 'Venerable sirs, why are these requisites, donated by ancient kings and accepted by the Arahants, being destroyed?' he asked. 'Friend, it would be possible to obtain them only through a preacher like you,' they replied. 'Venerable sirs, do not say so; we are only preachers who point out the practice. You wish to make me a "wealthy steward of the Sangha" and a "monastery attendant" by thinking of me as such,' he said. 'Friend, is this improper? If someone like you speaks, gains will arise for us,' they said. 'Venerable sirs, if that is the case, when the monastery attendants come, carry out my burden; I will tell them a proper way (kappiyadvāra).'

Going early in the morning and standing in the assembly hall, when the monastery attendants arrived, he said, 'Lay devotees, where is the share from such-and-such a field? Where is the money (kahāpaṇa) from such-and-such a field?' and so on. Taking the field of one, he gave it to another. In this way, by gradually prohibiting some and giving to others, he acted such that people came only to him, carrying gruel, cakes, rice, oil, honey, molasses, ghee, and so on. The entire monastery became a single uproar; the virtuous monks, becoming disgusted, departed.

He also filled the monastery by giving dependence (upajjha) to many difficult-to-admonish persons who had been rejected by their teachers and preceptors. Visiting monks, standing at the monastery gate, would ask, 'Who lives in the monastery?' and upon hearing, 'Monks of such a kind live here,' they would depart from the outside. This person, because he lies across (obstructing) the Sasana, though he has become a source of requisites for the many, is unable to enter the Noble Path, sit on the raft of concentration, and reach the ocean of Nibbāna.
