'He said this to the Blessed One' means that, knowing the Dhamma teaching was concluded with the phrase 'tending towards Nibbāna' (nibbānapabbhāra), and being skilled in the sequence of connections (anusandhi), he spoke these words beginning with 'How is it, Bhante?' For the Tathāgata, sitting in this assembly, concluded the teaching at this point for the purpose of giving an opportunity to that monk, thinking, 'There is a monk skilled in connections; he will ask me a question.'

Now, in the internal sense bases (ajjhattikāyatana) and so on, mentioned by the method beginning with 'the near shore' (orimaṃ tīraṃ), the following ways of approaching and not approaching should be understood. One who delights in the clarity of the eye, thinking, 'My eye is clear; I can see even a minute form,' is one who finds pleasure in the clarity of the eye as described in various ways.
84:
"I can penetrate and see the form-object." One who, relying on this clarity, finds delight in the eye, or one who, because the sensitive matter (pasāda) is destroyed by cataracts, bad winds, and so on, falls into dejection, thinking, "My eye is unpleasant; it cannot make even a large form-object clear"—such a person is said to "approach" (upagacchati) the eye-base (cakkhāyatana). However, one who practices insight (vipassanā) by way of the three marks—impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anattā)—is said not to approach it. The same method applies to the ear-base and so on.

Regarding the mind-base (manāyatana): One who finds delight, thinking, "How pleasant is my mind! It takes everything correctly without taking anything wrongly," or "There is nothing that I cannot obtain by thinking with my mind," or one who gives rise to dejection, thinking, "My mind, having thought badly, tends to take things wrongly"—such a person is said to "approach" the mind-base. One who gives rise to lust (rāga) for a pleasant form or aversion (paṭigha) for an unpleasant form is said to "approach" the form-base (rūpāyatana). The same method applies to the sound-base and so on.

In the phrase "Nandīrāgassetam adhivacanam" (This is a designation for delight and lust), the explanation is: Just as a log that has sunk in the middle of a river and is covered by fine and coarse sand cannot raise its head again, even so, a person bound by delight and lust falls into the four great woeful planes and is covered by great suffering. That person cannot raise his head again even for many thousands of years. Therefore, it is said, "Nandīrāgassetam adhivacanam."

In the phrase "Asmimānassetam adhivacanam" (This is a designation for the conceit 'I am'), the explanation is: Just as a log placed on dry land, being moistened by the water of the Ganges from below and by rain from above, gradually becomes covered with moss so that it might be called either a stone or a stump, even so, a person puffed up with the conceit "I am" acts as a rag-robe wearer in the place of rag-robe wearers, a Dhamma preacher in the place of Dhamma preachers, a quarreler in the place of quarrelers, a physician in the place of physicians, and a slanderer in the place of slanderers. Falling into various kinds of improper search and being entangled by various offenses (āpatti), he reaches a state where it might be asked, "Is there still virtue (sīla) within this person, or has his virtue vanished and his training ended?" Therefore, it is said, "Asmimānassetam adhivacanam."

In the phrase "Pañcannetam kāmaguṇānam adhivacanam" (This is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure), the explanation is: Just as a log that has fallen into a whirlpool is smashed and broken into pieces by rocks and so on within it, even so, a person who has fallen into the whirlpool of the five cords of sensual pleasure...
85:
...is repeatedly and continuously oppressed by the sufferings of punishment, hunger, thirst, and so on in the four woeful planes, and for a long time comes to be smashed into pieces. Therefore, it is said, "Pañcannetam kāmaguṇānam adhivacanam."

*Dussīlo* means one without virtue. *Pāpadhammo* means one of evil nature. *Asuci* means one who is impure. *Saṅkassarasamācāro* means one whose conduct is such that others suspect him, thinking, "I think this deed belongs to this person." Alternatively, it means one who, through his own suspicion, reflects on the behavior of others. For when he sees two or three people talking, he thinks, "I think they are talking about my faults," and thus his mind runs with suspicion toward their behavior; hence, *saṅkassarasamācāro*.

*Samaṇapaṭiñño* (one who claims to be a recluse) refers to one who, when a count is started during the distribution of voting tickets (salāka) and so on, asking "How many recluses are there in the monastery?", gives his claim, saying, "I too am a recluse, I too am a recluse," and accepts the voting tickets and so on. *Brahmacāripaṭiñño* (one who claims to be a celibate practitioner) refers to one who, during the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies, enters those acts by claiming, "I too am a celibate practitioner." *Antopūti* (rotten within) means one who is rotten inside because his virtues have decayed, even if his internal organs like the kidneys and heart are not rotten. *Avassuto* means one who is moist with lust. *Kasambujāto* means one who has become like rubbish due to defilements such as lust.

"He addressed this speech" means that after making the herd of cows face the bank of the Ganges and standing at the edge of the assembly, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma desanā from beginning to end, he thought: "The Teacher says that one can fulfill the practice by not approaching the near bank and so on. If it is possible to fulfill it in this way, I shall ordain and fulfill it." Thinking thus, he spoke these words: "Venerable Sir, I..." and so on.

*Vacchagiddhiniyo* means that the cows, having affection for their calves and with milk flowing from their udders, will go on their own out of love for the calves. "Only after handing them over" means only after they have been delivered. For if the cows have not been handed over, the owners of the cows will come and wander behind you, saying, "One cow is not seen, one bull, one calf is not seen," and thus it will be unpleasant for you. This state of a monk is not suitable for one with debt; the Buddha and other noble ones praise only the ordination of one who is debt-free. To show this, he spoke thus. *Niyyātā* means they have been handed over. In this sutta, the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the escape from the round (vivaṭṭa) are taught.
86:
## 5. Commentary on the Second Wood-pile Simile Sutta (Dutiyadārukkhandhopama Sutta)

In the fifth sutta, "Kimilāyaṃ" means in the city named Kimilā. "Saṅkiliṭṭhaṃ" means that it is not that there is no defiled offense from the time it was concealed; rather, it refers to such a defiled offense. "Na vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati" means that emergence from the offense through probation (parivāsa), penance (mānatta), and rehabilitation (abbhāna) is not seen.

## 6. Commentary on the Avassutapariyāya Sutta

In the sixth sutta, "navaṃ santhāgāraṃ" means a newly constructed assembly hall or a large public hall. Indeed, during times of military expeditions and such, kings would stand there and organize the troops, saying, "Let this many soldiers go to the front, this many to the rear, this many on both sides; let this many mount elephants, this many horses, and let this many stay in chariots." In this way, they make an arrangement (santham) and establish boundaries; therefore, that place is called an assembly hall (santhāgāra).

Alternatively, it is called an assembly hall because kings rest (santharanti) there for two or three days after returning from the battlefield while their houses are being prepared with applications of fresh cow dung and the like. It is also called an assembly hall because it is the house where those kings collectively consult on state affairs. Since they are republican kings (gaṇa-rājā), matters that arise are not decided by the will of a single person; it is necessary to obtain the consensus of all. Therefore, they all assemble and consult there. For that reason, it is said, "The house where state affairs are collectively consulted is called an assembly hall."

Furthermore, it is called an assembly hall because those kings assemble there to discuss household matters, such as, "At this time, it is proper to plow; at this time, it is proper to sow." Thus, they lay out and discuss various household affairs there. "Acirakāritaṃ" means it has just been completed, well-prepared like a celestial mansion with brickwork, plastering, and painting. In the phrase "samaṇena vā" (or by a recluse), because deities take possession of their dwelling places as soon as the house site is acquired, it is not said "by a deity," but rather "by a recluse, or a brahmin, or any person who is a human being."
87:
"They approached where the Blessed One was" means that upon hearing the assembly hall was finished, they went to see it. Having looked at everything starting from the gateway, they thought, "This assembly hall is exceedingly delightful and glorious. If someone were to use it first, for whose sake would it lead to our long-term welfare and happiness?"

They decided, "Even if it were given first to the noblest of our relatives, it is only fitting for the Teacher. Even if it were given by way of an offering to one worthy of gifts, it is only fitting for the Teacher. Therefore, we will let the Teacher use it first and invite the Saṅgha of monks. When the Saṅgha of monks arrives, the Tipiṭaka, the word of the Buddha, will also have arrived. We will have the Teacher preach the Dhamma to us for the three watches of the night. After it has been used by the Triple Gem in this way, we will use it later. Doing so will lead to our long-term welfare and happiness." Having made this resolution, they approached.

"They approached where the new assembly hall was" means that on that day, although the assembly hall was well-prepared and decorated like a celestial mansion for the royal families to see, it had not yet been arranged in a manner suitable for the Buddha. This is because Buddhas have an inclination for the forest and delight in the forest; it was not known whether he would stay within the village or not. Therefore, thinking, "We will prepare it only after knowing the Blessed One's mind," they approached the Blessed One. Now, having gained his consent and wishing to prepare it, they approached the assembly hall.

"Having spread the whole assembly hall" means having the hall spread so that it was completely covered. First of all, saying "The application of cow dung is endowed with all auspiciousness," they had even the plastered floor smeared with fresh cow dung. Knowing it was well-dried, they had it smeared with four types of perfumes just enough for footprints to appear where stepped upon. Then, they had multi-colored mats spread on top. On top of those mats, starting with large carpets (large enough for sixteen dancers), they had all the suitable areas spread with various colored rugs, such as elephant rugs, horse rugs, lion rugs, tiger rugs, moon-patterned rugs, sun-patterned rugs, and ornate rugs. Therefore, it is said, "Having spread the whole assembly hall."

"Having prepared seats" means that first, having prepared a noble Buddha-seat leaning against the auspicious pillar (maṅgalathambha) in the center, they spread soft and delightful coverings in various places. They placed large red bolsters on both sides and hung a magnificent canopy decorated with golden stars above, adorning it with garlands of perfume, flowers, and fragrant leaves. Furthermore, they had flower nets made in the surrounding area of about twelve cubits and surrounded a thirty-cubit area with curtains. Leaning against the back wall, they prepared thrones, benches with backrests, and benches without backrests for the Saṅgha of monks, spreading white cloths on top. Leaning against the east wall, they spread large carpets for themselves and placed delightful large cotton pillows. They prepared these, thinking, "If arranged this way, we can listen to the Dhamma all night without fatigue." This arrangement...
88:
"Preparing the seats" means first preparing the seat of the Blessed One, which is fit only for the noble ones, leaning against the auspicious pillar in the center. In various places, soft and delightful coverings were spread, and large cushions, red on both sides and pleasant to look at, were placed. Above, a canopy decorated with gold and silver stars was fastened, and it was adorned with garlands of scents, flowers, and leaves. Furthermore, flower nets were made in the surrounding area of about twelve cubits, and an area of about thirty cubits was enclosed with cloth curtains. Leaning against the back wall, couch-like seats, seats with backrests, and plain seats were arranged for the community of monks, and they were covered with white cloths. Leaning against the eastern wall, large carpets, upon which sixteen dancers could dance, were spread for themselves, and delightful pillows stuffed with swan feathers and the like were placed, with the intention: "In this way, we shall listen to the Dhamma all night without fatigue." It is in reference to this that it is said, "having prepared the seats."

"Having set up a water jar" means setting up a large-bellied water pot. With the intention: "In this way, the Blessed One and the community of monks may wash their hands or feet, or rinse their faces as they desire," they filled them with emerald-colored water in various places, added various flowers and scented powders for fragrance, covered them with banana leaves, and set them up. It is in reference to this that it is said, "having set up a water jar."

"Having lit the oil lamps" means causing oil lamps to be lit in lampstands made of gold, silver, etc., and in gold and silver lamp-bowls held in the hands of figures of Greeks, Kirātas, and so on. "They approached where the Blessed One was": here, those Sakyan kings did not only decorate the assembly hall; they also had the main streets of the city of Kapilavatthu, which was a league in circumference, swept, flags and banners raised, and full jars and banana trees placed at the doors of houses. They made the whole city like a cluster of shimmering stars with rows of lamps. They had a drum beaten to announce: "Let those who are nursing infants give them milk; feed the young children quickly and put them to sleep; do not make loud noises; tonight the Teacher will stay within the village; Buddhas desire quietness." Then, holding torches themselves, they approached where the Blessed One was.
89:
Then the Blessed One, having dressed and taking his bowl and robes, went with the community of monks to where the new assembly hall was. When the time was announced, "Venerable Sir, it is now time for the Blessed One to depart," the Blessed One dressed in his double-layered under-robe, which was as red as if sprayed with lac-dye, well-covering the three circles (the two knees and the navel) as if cutting a lotus with scissors. He tied his waistband, which was like a streak of lightning, as if binding a bundle of lotuses with a golden band. He donned his noble rag-robe (paṃsukūla), which was the color of a young banyan shoot, as if covering an elephant's forehead with a red woolen cloth, or as if casting a coral net over a golden pagoda a hundred cubits high, or as if putting a red woolen tunic on a golden pagoda, or as if a red cloud were covering the moving full moon, or as if pouring well-cooked lac-dye on the peak of a golden mountain, or as if wrapping the peak of Mount Cittakūṭa with a streak of lightning—causing the earth, together with the Cakkavāḷa, Mount Sineru, and Mount Yugandhara, to tremble. He emerged from the door of the Gandhakuti like a lion king emerging from a golden cave, or like the full moon appearing from the peak of the Sunrise Mountain. Having emerged, he stood in front of the Gandhakuti.

While he stood there, rays of light emerged from the Blessed One's body like streaks of lightning from within a cloud, beautifying the garden trees in the vicinity with their leaves, flowers, fruits, and branches, as if they were being drenched with a stream of liquid gold. At that very moment, the great community of monks took their bowls and robes and surrounded the Blessed One. Those monks standing in attendance were of such nature: having few desires, contented, secluded, not mingling with crowds, energetic, speakers of Dhamma, patient of instruction, admonishers, blamers of evil, endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Surrounded by those monks, the Blessed One shone like a golden mass surrounded by red woolen cloths, or like a golden boat in the middle of a red lotus forest, or like a golden palace surrounded by coral railings. The great elders, such as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna, also donned their rag-robes the color of dark rain clouds and surrounded him like great noble elephants adorned with jewel-studded breastplates. Those great elders were those who had vomited out lust, destroyed the defilements, untangled the tangle of defilements, cut the bonds of craving, and were unattached to family or group.

Thus, the Blessed One, being himself free from lust, was surrounded by Arahants free from lust; being himself free from hatred, was surrounded by Arahants free from hatred; being himself free from delusion, was surrounded by Arahants free from delusion; being himself free from craving, was surrounded by Arahants free from craving; being himself free from defilements, was surrounded by Arahants free from defilements; being himself the Buddha (the Knower of the Four Noble Truths), was surrounded by the "lesser Buddhas" (Arahants) of great learning. Like a filament surrounded by petals, like the center of a lotus, like the Chaddanta elephant king surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like the Dhataraṭṭha swan king surrounded by ninety thousand swans, like a Cakkavatti king surrounded by his army, like Sakka surrounded by the host of devas, like Mahābrahmā surrounded by the host of Brahmas, and like the full moon surrounded by the stars, he proceeded on the journey to the city of Kapilavatthu with the incomparable appearance of a Buddha and the infinite splendor of a Buddha.
90:
The Blessed One, who is himself free from lust, hatred, delusion, craving, and defilements, and is surrounded by Arahants who are likewise free, set out on the journey to Kapilavatthu with incomparable Buddha-form and immeasurable Buddha-grace. He appeared like a filament surrounded by petals, like a pericarp surrounded by filaments, like Chaddanta the elephant king surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like Dhataraṭṭha the swan king surrounded by ninety thousand swans, like a Cakkavatti king surrounded by his army, like Sakka the king of devas surrounded by the host of devas, like Hārita Mahābrahmā surrounded by the host of Brahmas, and like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars.

As he journeyed, golden rays issued from the front of the Blessed One's body and spread to a distance of eighty cubits. Similarly, golden rays issued from the back, the right hand, and the left hand, spreading to a distance of eighty cubits. From the tips of the hair and all the hair-curls, rays the color of a peacock's neck issued and spread eighty cubits into the sky. From the soles of the feet, coral-colored rays issued, penetrating the thick earth and spreading to a distance of eighty cubits. Thus, the six-colored Buddha-rays, flashing and quivering within a range of eighty cubits, radiated like flames rising to the sky from golden torches, or like streaks of lightning emerging from a great cloud that covers the four continents. All directions shone as if strewn with golden campaka flowers, as if sprinkled with streams of liquid gold poured from golden jars, as if draped in spread-out golden cloths, or as if covered with the dust of Kiṃsuka and Kaṇikāra flowers blown by the Veramba wind.

The Blessed One's body, radiant with the eighty minor marks, the fathom-long radiance, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, shone like the sky adorned with stars, like a lotus thicket in full bloom, or like a Pāricchattaka tree a hundred yojanas in size in full blossom. He surpassed the glory of thirty-two moons, thirty-two suns, thirty-two Cakkavatti kings, thirty-two Sakkas, and thirty-two Mahābrahmas placed in order. This splendor was due to his having perfectly fulfilled and adorned himself with the thirty Perfections—the ten Perfections (Pāramīs), the ten Higher Perfections (Upapāramīs), and the ten Ultimate Perfections (Paramatthapāramīs). The dāna given, the sīla kept, and the meritorious deeds performed over four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons seemed to find no room to ripen in this single existence, as if crowded together. It was like the time when the cargo of a thousand ships is loaded onto a single ship, or the cargo of a thousand carts is loaded onto a single cart, or when the waters of twenty-five Ganges rivers converge at the river mouth. As the Blessed One journeyed, shining with Buddha-glory, many thousands of torches were raised in front of him. Likewise, they were raised behind him, and to his left and right sides. A rain of flowers—including Jātisumana, jasmine, campaka, kaṇikāra, red lotus, blue lotus, and sinduvāra—along with fragrant powders of various colors like blue and yellow, were scattered like currents of water poured from a great cloud covering the four continents. The sounds of five-fold music and the voices of praise concerning the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha also filled all directions...
91:
...It was like the currents of twenty-five Ganges rivers converging and forming a single mass at the river mouth. In front of the Blessed One, who was shining with this Buddha-glory, many thousands of torches were raised; likewise behind him, to his left side, and to his right side. Jātisumana, jasmine, campaka, kaṇikāra, red lotus, blue lotus, bakula, and sinduvāra flowers, along with fragrant powders of various colors like blue and yellow, were scattered like currents of water poured from a great cloud raining over the four continents. The sounds of five-fold music and the voices of praise concerning the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha filled all directions. The eyes of devas, humans, Nagas, Garudas, Gandhabbas, Yakkhas, and others were as if they had obtained the drink of immortality (Amata). Standing at this point, it is appropriate to praise his manner of walking with a thousand verses. Of those, this is merely the introduction:

Endowed with all limbs, shaking the earth, without harming any living beings, the Guide of the World proceeds.

The Bull among Men, endowed with glory, supreme among bipeds, lifts his right foot first as he walks in splendor.

As the Excellent Buddha walks, his soft soles touch the ground evenly, and he is not soiled by dust.

When the Lord of the World walks, low places rise and high places become level; even the inanimate earth acts as if conscious.

Stones, pebbles, potsherds, stumps, and thorns—all clear away from the path when the Lord of the World walks.

He lifts his foot not too far and sets it down not too near; he proceeds without his knees or ankles knocking against each other.

The Sage, perfect in conduct, walks neither too fast nor too slow; he proceeds with a composed mind.

He does not walk looking up, down, sideways, or at the various directions; he looks only a yoke's length ahead.
92:
That Exalted One, the Victor, has a gait like that of a noble elephant; He is graceful when He walks. The Foremost of the World, the Buddha, walks gracefully, bringing joy to the world including the devas.

Graceful like the moon and like a four-legged Kesari lion king, that Exalted One, bringing joy to many beings, arrived at the noble city of Kapilavatthu.

Regarding 'Vaṇṇakāla' (the time for praise): at such times, in praising the physical beauty or the virtues of the Buddha, the capability of the Dhamma preacher is the only measure. One should speak as much as possible, whether in prose (cuṇṇiyapada) or in verse (gāthā). It should not be said that 'it is poorly spoken.' For the Buddhas are endowed with immeasurable virtues. Even the Buddhas themselves are unable to describe their own virtues without remainder; how much less can other beings do so? Having entered the royal city of the Sakyans, which was adorned and prepared with such splendor, the Exalted One, being worshipped with scents, incense, and fragrant powders by the people with devoted hearts, entered the assembly hall (santhāgāra). Therefore, it is said: 'Then the Exalted One, having dressed and taken His bowl and robes, went to the new assembly hall together with the Saṅgha of monks.'

'With the Buddha alone at the head' means placing the Buddha in front. There, the Exalted One, sitting in the midst of the monks and the lay devotees, having bathed with scented water, dried with a roll of fine cloth (dukūla), and rubbed with natural vermilion (jātihiṅgulaka), shone exceedingly like a solid red-gold statue placed on a seat draped with a red blanket. In this regard, the ancient teachers' way of praising His virtues is as follows:

Having gone to the circular pavilion, He whose gait is like a noble elephant’s stride, the Foremost of the World, sat upon the noble seat, illuminating the surroundings.

Sitting there, the Trainer of those to be tamed, the God above gods, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits, the Buddha shines in the midst of the Buddha-seat like a golden coin on a crimson blanket.

Like a pure Jambonada gold coin placed on a crimson blanket, He shines like a radiant gem.
93:
Like a great Sal tree in full bloom, like the adorned Mount Meru, king of mountains, having an appearance like a golden pillar, and like a red lotus called Kokanada.

Like a fire burning on a mountain top, like a great radiant lamp-tree, and like the devas’ Pāricchattaka tree in full bloom, which is a hundred yojanas wide, He shines exceptionally.

In the passage 'teaching the Dhamma at night together with the devas among the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu,' the term 'Dhamma talk' (dhammakathā) should be understood as a miscellaneous discourse related to the blessing of the new assembly hall. At that time, the Exalted One preached a miscellaneous discourse that brought welfare and happiness to the Sakyans living in Kapilavatthu, as if bringing down the celestial Ganges (Ākāsagaṅgā), as if drawing out the essence of the earth, as if shaking a great Jambu tree by its top, or as if pressing a honeycomb of one yojana with a machine to let them drink the honey. 'Great King, this gift of a dwelling is indeed great. Your dwelling has been used by Me, and it has been used by the Saṅgha of monks. When it is used by Me and the Saṅgha, it is indeed used by the Dhamma Jewel; thus, it is said to be used by the Triple Gem. When the gift of a dwelling is given, all gifts are indeed given. Even the benefit of a small leaf-roofed hut built on the ground or a branch-roofed pavilion cannot be measured. By the power of the gift of a dwelling, even if one is reborn in various lives, there is no dwelling in a cramped womb; like an inner chamber of twelve cubits, the mother’s womb is not cramped but spacious.' Having thus preached a long Dhamma discourse, diverse in many ways:

A monastery wards off cold and heat, as well as wild beasts, snakes, scorpions, and insects, and also mosquitoes and rain in the cold season.

Furthermore, it wards off the fierce wind and sun that arise. It is for the purpose of shelter, for comfort, for meditation, and for practicing insight.

The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha is praised by the Buddha as the highest. Therefore, a wise person, seeing his own benefit, should have pleasant monasteries built and have learned monks dwell there.

To those monks, one should offer food, drink, clothing, and lodgings.
94:
One should give with a clear mind to those who practice uprightly.
They teach him the Dhamma that dispels all suffering.
Having understood that Dhamma in this life, one attains Nibbāna, free from taints. (Cūḷavagga 295)

In this manner, saying "This too is a benefit of donating a dwelling, this too is a benefit of donating a dwelling," he spoke extensively on the benefits of dwellings during the night for more than a watch and a half. Among those teachings, only these verses were included in the Council; the miscellaneous Dhamma teachings, however, were not included. Terms such as "Sandassetvā" have the meanings already mentioned.

"Abhikkantā" means that two watches have passed. "Yassa dāni kālaṃ maññatha" means "If you think it is now the time for you to go, then depart." Why did the Blessed One dismiss them? Out of compassion. For those Sakyans are delicate; if they spent all three watches of the night sitting, illness might arise in their bodies. Also, the Saṅgha of monks is large, and it is proper for that assembly to have the opportunity for standing and sitting; thus he dismissed them out of compassion for both.

"Vigatathinamiddho" means that the monks there, whether standing or sitting for two watches, did not nod. Some teachers say, "In the last watch, because the food was digested, the Saṅgha of monks became free from sloth and torpor," but this is not the reason. Indeed, for one listening to the Dhamma of the Buddhas, physical and mental distress do not occur, and lightness of body and mind arises. Therefore, for those monks who were listening to the Dhamma while standing or sitting for two watches, sloth and torpor were dispelled; even when the last watch arrived, they remained free from it. Thus it is said, "Vigatathinamiddho."

"Piṭṭhi me āgilāyati" (My back is aching)—why did he say this? While the Blessed One was practicing the great exertion for six years, intense physical suffering occurred. Later, in his old age, a wind-ailment causing back pain arose. Or rather, this is not the sole reason. The Blessed One is able to suppress the arisen pain and sit in a single cross-legged posture for one or even two weeks. However, he wished to make use of the Santhāgāra hall with all four postures. There, by walking from the place of washing the feet to the Dhamma-seat, the walking posture was accomplished. By standing for a moment upon reaching the Dhamma-seat, the standing posture was accomplished. By sitting on the Dhamma-seat for two watches, the sitting posture was accomplished. This much...
95:
...the standing posture was completed, and the sitting posture was also completed. Now, by lying down for a while on the right side, the reclining posture will be accomplished—thus he wished to make use of the four postures. It cannot be said that pain does not occur in the body, which is a heap of grasped matter (upādinnaka-rūpa); therefore, referring to the slight pain arisen from sitting for a long time, he spoke thus.

"Saṅghāṭiṃ paññāpetvā" (having spread the outer robe): It is heard that on one side of the Santhāgāra hall, those kings had a cloth screen drawn, a proper couch prepared, and spread with a proper coverlet. Above it, they hung a canopy adorned with gold stars, perfumes, and flower garlands, and lit scented oil lamps. They thought, "Perhaps the Teacher, having risen from the Dhamma-seat and resting for a while, might lie down here. If so, this Santhāgāra hall of ours will have been used by the Blessed One in all four postures, which will lead to our welfare and happiness for a long time." With this in mind, they lit the lamps. The Teacher, intending only their welfare and happiness, spread his outer robe there and lay down. "Uṭṭhānasanyaṃ manasi karitvā" means having placed in his mind the perception of rising, thinking, "I shall rise after this much time has passed." He did this while not falling asleep but listening to the Dhamma talk of the Elder Moggallāna.

"Avassutapariyāyaṃ" means the reason for being sodden with defilements. "Adhimuccati" means one enters into it by letting the mind go towards the object through defilement; one becomes greedy. "Byāpajjati" means one becomes of a corrupt mind through the power of ill-will. "Cakkhuto" means by way of the eye. "Māro" refers to both the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra) and the Māra as a deity (devaputta-māra). "Otāraṃ" means an opening (opportunity). "Ārammaṇaṃ" means a cause. Like a reed-hut or a grass-hut, the sense bases that are associated with indulgence are like a grass-torch, objects fit for the arising of defilements. Just as a charcoal fire burns wherever a grass-torch is placed, when an object comes into range, defilements arise. Therefore, it is said, "Māra might gain an opening."

In the wholesome side (sukka-pakkha), like a gabled mansion (kūṭāgāra) plastered with thick, smooth clay, the sense bases that are free from indulgence are like the aforementioned objects. Just as a grass-torch is extinguished without burning when placed [on such a surface], when an object comes into range of the sense bases free from indulgence, the fever of defilements does not arise. Therefore, it is said, "Māra cannot gain an opening."
96:
## 7. Dukkhadhammasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "dukkhadhammānaṃ" refers to the states that cause suffering. If the five aggregates exist, various forms of suffering such as cutting, killing, and binding arise; therefore, because they are the cause of the arising of suffering, those five aggregates are called "dukkhadhamma."

"Tathā kho panassa" means "of him in that manner." "Yathāssa kāme passato" means "of him who sees sensual pleasures in such a manner." "Yathā carantaṃ" refers to one who wanders and lives continuously in such a manner.

"Aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā diṭṭhā honti" means that sensual pleasures are seen as things that burn intensely like a pit of glowing coals, by virtue of the suffering rooted in seeking (pariyeṭṭhi) and the suffering rooted in rebirth (paṭisandhi). For those seeking sensual pleasures, great burning suffering arises through the power of seeking, such as entering the great ocean by ship, traveling on goat-paths (ajapatha) or spike-paths (saṅkupatha), and entering battlefields arrayed on both sides. For those enjoying sensual pleasures, great burning suffering arises through the power of rebirth given in the four lower realms due to the intention of enjoying sensual pleasures. Thus, by virtue of these two kinds of suffering, they are seen as things that burn intensely like a pit of glowing coals.

"Dāyaṃ" refers to a forest. "Purato pi kaṇṭako" refers to a thorn situated nearby as if wishing to prick from the front. The same method applies to terms like "pacchato" (from behind). Below, however, the thorn is near the place where the foot treads, not exactly on the spot being trodden. In this way, it would be as if that person had entered a thicket of thorns. "Mā maṃ kaṇṭako" means "May a thorn not prick me," which is the act of guarding against being pricked by a thorn.

"Dandho, bhikkhave, satuppādo" means, "Monks, the arising of mindfulness itself is slow; however, as soon as it arises, certain defilements are already suppressed and are unable to persist." When greed and so forth arise at the eye-door, one knows by the second javana (impulsion) that "defilements have arisen in me," and in the third javana, only the javana of restraint (saṃvara) occurs. It is not surprising that a practitioner of insight (vipassanā) can suppress defilements in the third javana. When a desirable object appears at the eye-door, after the bhavanga has turned and advertence (āvajjana) and so forth have arisen, one prevents the defilement-javana that would arrive immediately after the determining (votthabbana) and produces only wholesome states. This is the benefit for those who have begun insight meditation, being established in the repeated reflection of their development (bhāvanā).
97:
"Abhihatthuṃ pavareyyaṃ" means to invite by personally bringing the seven treasures or by saying, "Take as much as you want from our wealth," just as the invitations were made to the Elder Sudinna or the clansman Raṭṭhapāla. "Anudahanti" means causing burning heat and repeatedly burning because of being wrapped around the body, or it means sticking to a sweating body. In the phrase "Monks, that mind...", it is because if the mind does not return [to the household life], there is no such thing as the returning of that person. A mind of such a nature does not return to the world. Therefore, in this sutta, only the power of insight (vipassanā) is illustrated.

## 8. Kiṃsukopamasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, "dassana" (vision) is a designation for the first Path (sotāpatti-magga). The first Path is called "dassana" because it sees Nibbāna first while performing the task of abandoning defilements. Although the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) sees Nibbāna before the Path, it is not called "dassana" because it lacks the function of abandoning defilements. Alternatively, all four Paths are also "dassana." Why? Because at the moment of the Stream-entry Path, vision is purified, and at the moment of the Fruit, it is already purified. Hearing the monks who spoke thus—that vision is purified at the moments of the Once-returner Path, Non-returner Path, and Arahant Path, and is already purified at their respective Fruit moments—that monk thought, "I too will purify my vision, and while standing in the Fruit of Arahantship, I will dwell having realized Nibbāna purified by vision." He then approached that monk and questioned him.

That monk was one whose meditation subject was the sense-bases of contact (phassāyatana); he had reached Arahantship by discerning materiality and mentality (rūpa-arūpa) through the power of the six sense-bases of contact. Here, the first five bases are materiality (rūpa), and the mind-base (manāyatana) is mentality (arūpa). Thus, he taught only the Path he himself had attained.

"Asantuṭṭho" (unsatisfied) means he was unsatisfied because the teaching was given while standing on limited formations (saṅkhāra). It is said that he thought: "This monk teaches while standing on limited formations. Is it possible to reach Nibbāna purified by vision while standing on limited formations?" Then he asked him, "Friend, do you alone know this Nibbāna purified by vision, or are there others who know it?" The reply was, "Friend, there are; in such-and-such a monastery, there is an Elder of such-and-name." He approached and questioned him as well. In this manner, he questioned others and still others.
98:
Among these four monks, the second monk was one who practiced the meditation on the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha). By way of the material aggregate (rūpakkhandha), he defined matter (rūpa), and by way of the remaining mental aggregates (nāmakkhāndha), he defined mind (nāma); thus, having distinguished mind and matter (nāmarūpa), he reached the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala) in due course. Therefore, he too spoke only of the path (magga) he himself had attained. However, this [questioning] monk, being dissatisfied, thinking, "The words of these monks do not agree with one another; the first monk spoke while established in limited formations (sappadesa-saṅkhāra), while this [second] monk spoke while established in unlimited formations (nippadesa)," questioned him in the same way and then departed.

The third monk was one who practiced the meditation on the great elements (mahābhūta). Having grasped the four great elements both briefly and in detail, he reached the fruition of Arahantship. Therefore, he too spoke only of the path he himself had attained. However, this monk, being dissatisfied, thinking, "The words of these monks do not agree with one another; the first monk spoke while established in limited formations, the second monk in unlimited formations, and the third monk while established in very limited formations (atisappadesa)," questioned him in the same way and then departed.

The fourth monk was one who practiced the meditation on the three planes (tebhūmaka). It is said that his elements were balanced, his body was healthy and strong, and all meditation subjects were suitable for him. Whether they were past formations, future, or present; whether they belonged to the sensuous plane (kāmāvacara), the fine-material plane (rūpāvacara), or the immaterial plane (arūpāvacara)—all were suitable. There was no such thing as an unsuitable meditation subject. Even regarding times, whether before the meal or after the meal, or during the first watch, etc., there was no such thing as an unsuitable time. Just as a great elephant that has descended into its feeding ground might pull up with its trunk food that should be taken with the trunk, or strike with its feet food that should be taken with the feet; in the same way, that monk, having grasped all things of the three planes as a group and contemplating them, reached the fruition of Arahantship. Therefore, he too spoke only of the path he himself had attained.

However, this monk, being dissatisfied, thinking, "The words of these monks do not agree with one another; the first monk spoke while established in limited formations, the second monk in unlimited formations, the third monk again in limited formations, and the fourth monk only in unlimited formations," asked him: "Friends, is this Nibbāna, called the purification of vision (dassanavisuddhi), known by you through your own nature, or was it told to you by someone?" The monks replied, "Friend, what can we know? But there is a Fully Enlightened Buddha (Sammāsambuddha) in the world with its devas; it is by depending on that Buddha that we have known this." Then that monk thought, "These monks are unable to speak by understanding my inclination. I will ask the All-Knowing Buddha himself and become free from doubt." Thus, he approached the Blessed One.
99:
The Blessed One, having heard the words of that monk, did not harass him with such words as: "Those four monks who answered your question are all ones whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava); they have spoken well, but you, because of your own extreme foolishness, do not notice the meaning." Instead, knowing his state as a doer (one who strives), and thinking, "This monk is a seeker of meaning; I will make him understand only through a Dhamma discourse," he brought forth the simile of the kiṃsuka tree. In that simile, the meaning should be explained by making a factual story: It is said that in a great city, there lived a wise brahmin physician who was a master of all texts. Then, a man suffering from jaundice (paṇḍuroga) who lived in a village at the eastern gate of the city came to that physician, paid homage, and stood there. The wise physician, after exchanging pleasantries with him, asked, "Good man, for what purpose have you come?" "Sir, I am afflicted by a disease; please give me a prescription." "In that case, friend, go, cut a kiṃsuka tree, dry it, burn it, take the alkaline water (khārodaka) from that wood, mix it with such and such medicines, make a medicinal decoction (ariṭṭha), and drink it. By drinking that, you will be cured and at ease." That man did as instructed and became free from disease, strong, and of a pleasing appearance.

Then, another man living in a village at the southern gate, being afflicted by the same disease, heard that "such and such a person has become free from disease by using medicine," approached him and asked, "Friend, by what means were you cured?" "By the kiṃsuka decoction; you go and make it too." He also did so and became like the first man.

Then, another man living in a village at the western gate... (and so on)... a man living in a village at the northern gate, being afflicted by the same disease, heard that "such and such a person has become free from disease by using medicine," approached him and asked, "Friend, by what means were you cured?" "By the kiṃsuka decoction; you go and make it too." He also did so and became like the first man.

Then, a man living in the borderlands, who had never seen a kiṃsuka tree before, being afflicted by the same disease, treated it with various medicines for a long time, but the disease did not subside. Hearing that "a man living in a village at the eastern gate of the city has become free from disease by using medicine," he thought, "I too will go and make the medicine made by him." Leaning on a staff, he went to that man in due course and asked, "Friend, by what means were you cured?" "Friend, it was by the kiṃsuka decoction," he replied.
100: What is the nature of that Kiṃsuka tree? It is like a charred stump standing in a burnt-out village. In this way, that man described the Kiṃsuka tree according to the manner in which he himself had seen it. For at the time he saw it, the Kiṃsuka tree was seen during the season when its leaves had fallen and it was a stump; therefore, it was indeed of such a nature. However, that man (the forest-dweller), being one who was inclined to take omens from what he heard, thought: "This man says, 'It is like a charred stump in a burnt village'; this is inauspicious. Even if I prepare this medicine, the disease will not be cured." Being dissatisfied with that explanation, he asked him: "Friend, do you alone know the Kiṃsuka tree, or is there someone else?" "Friend, in the village of the South Gate, there is a person named so-and-so," (he replied). He approached that villager of the South Gate and inquired; that person, having seen it when it was in bloom, said according to his own vision: "The Kiṃsuka tree is red in color." He thought: "This man says the opposite of the first; black and red are very far apart." Being dissatisfied with that explanation as well, he asked: "Friend, is there anyone else who has seen the Kiṃsuka tree before?" When told, "In the village of the West Gate, there is a person named so-and-so," he approached that person and inquired as well. That person, having seen it when it was fruiting, said according to his own vision: "The Kiṃsuka tree is like tattered rags hanging down, or like someone holding a scabbard." Indeed, when the Kiṃsuka tree bears fruit, it has hanging fruits like tattered rags, or like a scabbard held facing downwards, or like the pods of a Sirīsa tree. He thought: "This man says the opposite of the previous ones; his words cannot be accepted." Being dissatisfied with that explanation as well, he asked: "Friend, is there anyone else who has seen the Kiṃsuka tree before?" When told, "In the village of the North Gate, there is a person named so-and-so," he approached that person and inquired as well. That person, having seen it when it was covered with leaves, said according to his own vision: "The Kiṃsuka tree has thick foliage and dense shade." Sandacchāyo (dense shade) refers to shade formed by overlapping leaves. He thought: "This man also says the opposite of the previous ones; his words cannot be accepted." Being dissatisfied with that explanation as well, he said to him: "Friend, do you know the Kiṃsuka tree by your own nature, or did someone tell you?" "Friend, how could we know? In the great city..."
101: "In our midst is our teacher, the wise physician; it is through him that we know," (they said). Thinking, "If so, I too will approach the teacher and become free from doubt," he approached that wise physician, paid homage, and stood there. The wise physician greeted him pleasantly and asked: "O auspicious-faced one, for what purpose have you come?" "Venerable sir, I am afflicted by a disease; please prescribe medicine for me," he requested. "Friend, if so, go, cut a Kiṃsuka tree, dry it, burn it, take the alkaline water from that wood, mix it with such-and-such medicines, make a medicinal tonic (ariṭṭha) and drink it. By this, you will find relief," he instructed. He did as told and became free from disease, strong, and pleasant to look at. In that simile, the great capital city should be understood as the city of Nibbāna. The wise physician should be understood as the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha). It is also said: "Sunakkhatta, 'physician' and 'surgeon' are names for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One" (Majjhima Nikāya). The four disciples of the physician at the four village gates should be understood as the four Arahants (khīṇāsavas) who have attained the purification of vision (dassanavisuddhi). The first man from the borderlands should be understood as the monk who asks the question. The time when the border-dweller, dissatisfied with the words of the four physician's disciples, approaches the teacher himself to ask, should be understood as the time when this monk, dissatisfied with the words of the four Arahants who have attained purification of vision, approaches the Teacher (the Buddha) to ask. "Yathā yathā adhimuttānaṃ" means: according to the manner in which they are inclined. "Dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ" means: the vision of Nibbāna is perfectly pure. "Tathā tathā kho tehi sappurisehi byākataṃ" means: those virtuous ones have answered you in those very ways. How so? Just as the one who said "The Kiṃsuka tree is black in color" was not speaking of something else, but spoke of the Kiṃsuka tree itself according to the manner he had seen it; in the same way, the Arahant who has attained purification of vision by way of the six sense bases (cha-phassāyatana), when answering this question, does not speak of something else, but speaks only of Nibbāna, which is the purification of vision attained through his own path. Just as the one who said "The Kiṃsuka tree is red, or has cracked bark, or has thick leaves" was not speaking of something else, but spoke of the Kiṃsuka tree itself according to the manner he had seen it; in the same way, the Arahant who has attained purification of vision by way of the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandha), or by way of the four great elements (caturmahābhūta), or by way of the phenomena of the three planes (tebhūmaka-dhamma), when answering this question...
102:
In answering this problem, he does not answer anything else; he answers only regarding Nibbāna, which is the purification of vision (dassana-visuddhi) attained through the path he himself has reached.

In that simile, for the person who sees the Kiṃsuka tree when it is charred (black), that vision is true and real; that person has not seen anything else, but has seen only the Kiṃsuka tree. In the same way, the vision of an Arahant who has reached the purification of vision by way of the six bases of contact (phassāyatana) is also true and real; that Arahant does not speak of anything else, but speaks only of Nibbāna, which is the purification of vision attained through the path he himself has reached. Furthermore, the vision of one who sees the Kiṃsuka tree during the time it is red, or when the bark is parched and peeling, or when it is covered with thick foliage, is also true and real; that person has not seen anything else, but has seen only the Kiṃsuka tree. In the same way, the vision of an Arahant who has reached the purification of vision by way of the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandha), the four great elements (mahābhūta), or the things of the three planes (tebhūmaka-dhamma) is also true and real; that venerable one does not speak of anything else, but speaks only of Nibbāna, which is the purification of vision attained through the path he himself has reached.

Why was this simile started: "Monks, suppose there were a king's frontier city..."? If that monk understood the point shown by the simile of the Kiṃsuka tree, then it was started for the sake of his Dhamma teaching. If he did not understand, then it was started for the sake of illustrating and making clear that same meaning of the purification of vision for that monk through this city simile. In that city simile, the reason is that in the middle country (majjhima-desa), whether the walls and so forth of a city are firm or weak, or even if they do not exist at all, there is no fear of thieves. Because there is no such fear of thieves, the Buddha did not take a city of the middle country but said "a frontier city" (paccantimaṃ nagaraṃ). "Daḷhuddāpaṃ" means having firm inner walls. "Daḷhapākāratoraṇaṃ" means having firm outer walls and firm gate-pillars. Indeed, gate-pillars (toraṇa) as high as a man are made for the sake of decorating the city, and they also serve the purpose of warding off thieves. Alternatively, the name "toraṇa" is a name for the door-frame, so it should be understood as meaning having firm door-frames. "Chadvāraṃ" (six gates) means that a city may have one gate, two, a hundred, or a thousand. However, in this simile, the Teacher said this because He wished to show a city with six gates. "Paṇḍita" (wise) means endowed with wisdom. "Byatta" (skilled) means endowed with proficiency and having clear knowledge. "Medhāvī" (intelligent) means endowed with intelligence characterized by quick-wittedness in various matters.

In the passage beginning with "Puratthimāya disāya" (In the eastern direction), having established the evident meaning, the following meaning should be understood: It is said that in a prosperous great city, a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) endowed with the seven treasures rules the kingdom. This frontier city of that King is devoid of a governor appointed by the King. Then the people...
103:
(The citizens) came and petitioned, "Your Majesty, there is no governor appointed by you in our city. Please grant us some governor." The King handed over one of his sons and commanded, "Go, take this son of mine, anoint him in that city, establish places of judgment (courts) and so forth, and dwell there." They did as commanded. Because of associating with evil friends, within a few days the prince became a drunkard; he abandoned all administrative duties such as the places of judgment, and surrounded by rogues in the middle of the city, he spent his time drinking liquor and indulging in delights such as dancing and singing. Then, they came and informed the King of the matter.

The King commanded a wise minister, "Go, admonish the prince, make him perform the administrative duties of the courts, and after anointing him once more, return." The minister replied, "Your Majesty, it is not possible to admonish the prince; the violent prince might even kill me." Then the King commanded a powerful warrior, "You go with this minister, and if that prince does not abide by the admonition, cut off his head." Thus, that pair of swift messengers—the minister and the warrior—went to that city and asked the gatekeeper, "Friend, where is the prince, the lord of the city?" (The gatekeeper) said, "This prince is sitting in the central junction of the city, surrounded by rogues, drinking liquor and enjoying delights such as singing." Then that pair of messengers went there, and the minister first petitioned, "My Lord, please perform the administrative duties of the courts and rule the kingdom well." The prince sat as if he did not hear. Then the warrior grabbed the prince by the head and, drawing his sword from its scabbard, said, "If you follow the command of the Great King your father, then do so; if not, I shall strike off your head right here." The attendant rogues fled in all directions at that very moment. The prince, being terrified, accepted the command. Then they anointed the prince in that very city, raised the white umbrella, and after delivering the truthful words spoken by the King, "Rule the kingdom properly," they returned by the same path they had come. To make this meaning clear, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with "Puratthimāya disāya."

In that simile, the comparison is as follows: The prosperous great city should be understood as the city of Nibbāna. The Universal Monarch endowed with the seven treasures should be understood as the Sammāsambuddha, the King of Dhamma, who is endowed with the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). The frontier city should be understood as the city of the self-identity (sakkāya). The deceitful prince in that city should be understood as the arising of deceitful thoughts in this monk. The time when the deceitful prince was surrounded by rogues should be understood as the time when this monk is possessed by the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). The two swift messengers should be understood as the meditation subject of tranquility (samatha) and the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā). The time when the prince's head was grabbed by the great warrior should be understood as the time when the mind is held firmly and unshakeably by the concentration of the first absorption (pathamajjhāna). Just as the rogues fled in all directions and became distant when the warrior grabbed the head, so too in the first absorption, the hindrances...
104:
The period of holding the mind steadily and immovably with the concentration of the first jhāna should be understood like the time a great warrior holds a head. Just as drunkards flee in all directions and become distant as soon as the warrior grabs the head, the distancing of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) as soon as the first jhāna arises should be understood. The time of emerging from jhāna should be understood like the time one is released just by acknowledging, 'I will follow the King's command.' The time of developing the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna) by making the mind workable through concentration should be understood like the time a minister reports the King's command. Just as the raising of the white umbrella and the performance of the consecration (abhisheka) by those two messengers in that very city, the raising of the white umbrella of liberation (vimutti) for the monk who has reached Arahatship based on the meditation subjects of calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) should be understood.

In the passages such as 'Monks, "city" is a designation for this body consisting of the four great elements,' the meaning of terms like 'consisting of the four great elements' (cātumahābhūtika) has been explained in detail below. However, because it is the residence of the prince of consciousness (viññāṇa), the body is called a 'city' here. Because they are like the gates of that body, the six sense bases (āyatana) are called 'gates.' Because mindfulness (sati) is always well-established at those gates, it is called the 'gatekeeper.' Because they are sent by the King of Dhamma who explains the meditation subject, calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are called the 'swift pair of messengers.' Here, calm should be understood like the great warrior, and insight like the wise minister.

'Crossroads in the middle' means the crossroads in the middle of the city. 'Of the great elements' means the great elements which are the support for the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu). This mention of the four great elements is made only to show the cause of the physical base (vatthu-rūpa). Like that prince in the middle of the city, the prince of insight-consciousness (vipassanā-viññāṇa) who sits at the crossroads of the heart-base in the middle of the body and is to be consecrated with the consecration of Arahatship by the messengers of calm and insight should be understood. Because Nibbāna has a true nature and possesses indestructible sovereignty, it is called the 'true word.' Because the Noble Path (ariya-magga) is similar in nature to the preceding insight path and is endowed with eight factors, it is called the 'path as it came.' This is the comparison with the simile brought here for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.

To clarify that very meaning, in the part brought for comparison: Here, the simile of the six gates is brought to show the Arahant who has reached the purification of vision (dassana-visuddhi) by way of the six sense bases of contact...
105:
...to show the Arahant who has reached the purification of vision, the simile of the six gates is brought by way of the six sense bases of contact, the simile of the lord of the city by way of the five aggregates, the simile of the crossroads by way of the four great elements, and the simile of the city by way of the phenomena belonging to the three planes. In brief, however, only the Four Noble Truths are taught in this sutta. By way of the entire city structure (the teaching on the six gates), only the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) is spoken of. By the term 'true word,' the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) is spoken of; by the 'path as it came,' the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Craving, which produces suffering, is called the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca). At the conclusion of the teaching, the monk who asked the question was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).

## 9. Vīṇopama Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth, the Vīṇopama Sutta, the Teacher spoke these words, 'Monks, for whatever monk or nun,' with the following simile: For example, it is like a great householder who, after engaging in extensive farming and when the crops have been produced, builds a pavilion at the door of his house and gives alms to the Sangha of both sides (monks and nuns). Although he started the alms-giving intending it for the Sangha of both sides, after satisfying the two assemblies, he also satisfies the remaining people. In the same way, the Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand eons, having attained omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) at the seat of enlightenment (bodhi-maṇဍa), and having set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, while residing in the Great Jeta Grove Monastery, wishing to give a great gift of Dhamma to the assembly of monks and the assembly of nuns, undertook (preached) the Vīṇopama Sutta. Although that sutta was undertaken with the two assemblies in mind, it is not forbidden for all four assemblies. Therefore, it should be heard and believed by all gods and humans; having delved into it, the essence of its meaning (attharasa) should be experienced.

In that sutta, among the terms such as 'chanda' (desire), the initial weak craving is called 'chanda'; that chanda is not able to cause attachment. However, the strong craving that arises repeatedly is called 'rāga' (lust); that rāga is able to cause attachment. The initial weak anger that is unable to perform acts such as taking up a stick is called 'dosa' (hate). The strong anger that arises repeatedly and is able to perform acts such as taking up a stick is called 'paṭigha' (aversion). 'Moha' (delusion) is the ignorance (aññāṇa) that arises by way of bewildering and complete delusion. Thus, by these five terms, the three unwholesome roots (akusala-mūla) are included. When those three unwholesome roots are included, all defilements rooted in them are also included. By the two terms 'chanda rāga,' the eight types of consciousness associated with greed are included; by the two terms 'dosa paṭigha,' the two types of consciousness associated with displeasure are included; by the term 'moha,' the two types of consciousness associated with restlessness and doubt are included. In this way, all twelve unwholesome types of consciousness are indeed shown. 'Sabhaya' (fearful) means being with fear because it is the dwelling place of defilement-thieves. 'Sappaṭibhaya' (dangerous) means being with danger because it is the cause of killing and binding. 'Sakaṇṭaka' (thorny) means being thick with the thorns of lust and so on. 'Saganahana' (dense/wild) means being thick with wild beasts of lust and so on that seize and devour. 'Ummugga' (emergence) means, for one going to the deva world, the human world, or Nibbāna, it causes one to reach Nibbāna, the state free from death.
106:
By the two words "doso paṭigha," the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure (domanassasahagata cittuppāda) are taken. By the word "moha," the two types of consciousness accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca) and doubt (vicikicchā), which are free from greed and hatred, are to be taken. In this way, all twelve types of unwholesome consciousness are shown.

"Sabhayo" means a journey with danger because it is the dwelling place of the thieves of defilements (kilesa). "Sappaṭibhayo" means a journey with peril because it is the cause of killing, binding, and so forth. "Sakaṇṭako" means a journey thick with thorns, such as lust (rāga) and other thorns. "Sagahano" means a journey thick with defilements such as lust, which are like tigers and lions that seize and devour. "Ummaggo" means a wrong path, not the path for one going to the deva world, the human world, or Nibbāna. "Kummaggo" means a bad path because it leads to the states of deprivation (apāya), like a narrow foot-wide path leading to a loathsome place. In the word "duhitiko," "ihiti" means movement; a journey where movement is painful is called "duhitiko." Just as in a journey where there are no roots, fruits, or other food to eat, traveling is very painful and one cannot reach the desired place, so too, if one follows the path of defilements, one cannot reach a prosperous existence (sampatti-bhava); thus the path of defilements is called "duhitiko." There is a variant reading "dvīhitiko," but the meaning is the same. "Asappurisasevito" means a path frequented by ignoble persons such as Kokālika.

"Tato cittaṃ nivāraye" means one should restrain the mind that arises through the power of desire and lust for those forms cognizable by eye-consciousness, by means of methods such as reflecting on foulness (asubha), and so forth. When lust arises due to an agreeable object at the eye-door, the mind of one reflecting on foulness turns away. When hatred arises due to a disagreeable object, the mind of one reflecting on loving-kindness (mettā) turns away. When delusion arises due to a neutral object, the mind of one reflecting on learning the Pali, questioning the commentaries, and living under a teacher turns away. If one is still unable to do so, one should repeatedly reflect on the greatness of the Buddha, the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, and the good conduct of the Saṅgha. The mind of one reflecting on the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha also turns away from the unwholesome; therefore it is said, "one should restrain it by means of methods such as reflecting on foulness, etc."

"Kiṭṭhaṃ" refers to the crops growing in a field. "Sampannaṃ" means being fully developed or abundant. "Kiṭṭhādo" refers to an ox that eats the crops. "Evameva kho": In this context, the five strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa) should be understood as the abundant crop. The crooked mind should be understood as the ox that eats the crop. The time when the monk wanders having abandoned mindfulness (sati) at the six doors should be understood as the time when the crop-watcher is negligent. Just as the farmer does not enjoy the benefit of the crop because the ox eats the budding crops due to the watcher's negligence, so too, it should be understood that for a monk who abandons the mindfulness that should be guarded at the six doors, the crooked mind that delights in the five strands of sensual pleasure destroys the crop of wholesome states, and thus he no longer attains the fruits (phala) which are the benefit of monkhood. "Uparigīvāyaṃ" means pressing firmly on the neck between the two horns and with a stick instantly... "Monks, that ox..."
107:
Just as the owner of the field does not obtain the benefit of the crop because of the ox, so too, it should be understood that a monk cannot obtain the fruits (phala) which are the benefit of monkhood because the wholesome side is destroyed by the mind that delights in the five strands of sensual pleasure, having come to be separated from the mindfulness that guards the six doors.

"Uparighaṭāyaṃ" means between the two horns. "Suniggahitaṃ niggaṇheyya" means one should restrain it by firmly and securely holding the nose-rope attached to the neck. "Daṇḍena" means with a thick stick similar to a club (muggara). Monks, in this way, if that ox, relying on the negligence of the crop-watcher, wishes to descend into the field at any moment, it is an ox that is brought to the state of avoiding the opposite (the field) by being restrained and beaten in those moments and then released.

"Evameva kho": In this Sutta as well, the five strands of sensual pleasure should be understood as the abundant crop. The crooked mind should be understood as the ox that eats the crop. This monk's not letting go of mindfulness at the six doors should be understood as the crop-watcher's diligence. The Suttanta discourses should be understood as the striking stick. Just as the ox is beaten with a stick when it faces the field, so too, when the mind faces various external objects, one should reflect on various discourses such as the Anamataggiya Sutta, Devadūta Sutta, Āditta Sutta, Āsīvisūpama Sutta, and Anāgatabhaya Sutta, thereby restraining the arising of the mind from various objects and making it descend into its original meditation subject (mūla-kammaṭṭhāna). Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"Having heard the well-spoken Dhamma, the mind becomes clear;
It tames that mind, and one finds joy (pīti) and happiness (sukha).
Then his mind stands firm in the object,
Just like the crop-eating ox threatened by the stick."

"Udujitaṃ" means threatened and restrained. "Sudujitaṃ" means well-threatened and restrained; it also has the meaning "sujitaṃ." The terms "udu" and "sudu" are merely particles (nipāta). "Ajjhattaṃ" means within one's own meditation object (gocara-ajjhatta). In the words "santiṭṭhati," etc., it stands well by the power of the first jhāna; it settles down well by the power of the second jhāna; it becomes unified (ekodi) by the power of the third jhāna; it is well-concentrated by the power of the fourth jhāna. Alternatively, all of this should be understood by the power of the first jhāna. By this sequence of words, the Blessed One has taught the virtue of sense restraint (indriyasaṃvara-sīla) protected by serenity (samatha).

"Rañño vā" means of some king of a border region. "Saddaṃ suṇeyya" means hearing the sweet sound of a lute played by a skilled lutenist upon waking at dawn. In the words "rajanīyo," etc., it is called "rajanīya" because it dyes (excites) the mind.
108:
It is called 'kamanīya' because it is desirable. It is called 'madanīya' because it intoxicates the mind. It is called 'mucchaniya' because it acts as if to stupefy the mind. It is called 'bandhanīya' because it binds and holds firmly. Seeing the shape of the lute and not desiring it, he says, "Enough with this lute for me, friends!" 'Upadhāraṇe' refers to the belly or case of the lute. 'Koṇa' refers to the four-cornered plectrum made of heartwood.

That King said, "Bring that lute here, I will see its sound." Taking the lute, he would first split it into ten pieces. Even after splitting it, not seeing the sound, he would split it into a hundred pieces. Still not seeing it, he would break it into splinters. Still not seeing it, he would burn it with fire, thinking, "The splinters will burn, but the sound will come out and flee; then I shall see it." Still not seeing it, he would winnow it in a strong wind, thinking, "The light charcoal dust will be blown away by the wind, but the sound will fall at my feet like solid grain; then I shall see it." Still not seeing it, he would float it in a river with a swift current, thinking, "The charcoal dust will go with the water, but the sound will come out and cross over like a man going to the other bank; then I shall see it."

Searching with all these means and not seeing it, he would say to those people: "This lute is indeed hollow (without essence)," meaning this lute is inferior. 'Asatī' is a synonym for inferior. To prove this, the Blessed One said:
"In this world, those called women are not virtuous, they are only inferior;
There is no limit or shore (of shame and fear) for those women;
They are intensely lustful and bold,
Like the all-consuming fire."

It is meant that not only is the lute inferior, but just as this lute is, so too is any other stringed instrument—all are inferior. In this simile, the five aggregates should be understood as the lute, and the practitioner (yogāvacara) should be understood as the King. Just as that King, searching from the time he split the lute into ten pieces, did not see the sound and thus had no need for the lute; likewise, the practitioner, when contemplating the five aggregates and not seeing any essence to be grasped as 'I' or 'mine,' has no more need for the aggregates. To show that contemplation of the aggregates, the Blessed One taught the words: "He investigates form, he searches the entire range (gati) of form, he thoroughly searches form, he searches the entire range of form," and so on. In that passage, 'samanvesati' means he searches. 'Yāvatā rūpassa gati' means as far as the range of form extends. Those ranges are many, such as: gatigati, sañjātigati, salakkhaṇagati, bhavagati, vibhavagati, and sambhedagati.

Among those, form is defined from the Avīci hell below to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm above, and it wanders within these five destinies (gati). These five destinies—hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas—are called the 'gatigati' of that form. Furthermore, this physical body (karajakāya) does not appear in a fragrant lotus chamber or among white or blue lotuses. Instead, it arises between the stomach and the lower intestine, in thick darkness, where foul odors circulate, in an extremely repulsive place, like a worm born in rotting fish. This place of origin of form is called the 'sañjātigati' of form.
109:
To show the contemplation of the aggregates, the Blessed One said: "He investigates form, he searches the entire range (gati) of form," and so on.

In that passage, 'samanvesati' means he searches. 'Yāvatā rūpassa gati' means as far as the range of form extends. In that context, there are five kinds of gati: (1) gatigati, (2) sañjātigati, (3) salakkhaṇagati, (4) vibhavagati, and (5) bhedagati. Among these five, the wandering and changing of this form within the range from the Avīci hell below to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm above is called the 'gatigati' of this form.

This body (kāya) does not arise in a lotus chamber, nor in white or blue lotuses; rather, it arises between the stomach and the lower intestine, in thick darkness where foul odors circulate, in an extremely repulsive place, like worms arising in rotting fish. This is called the 'sañjātigati' of form.

The characteristics (lakkhaṇa) of form are of two kinds: the individual characteristic (paccatta-lakkhaṇa) known as 'being molested/deformed,' as stated in: 'Monks, it is called form because it is deformed (ruppati),' and the general characteristic (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) consisting of impermanence and so on. This is called the 'salakkhaṇagati' of form.

As it is said:
"The range of wild beasts is the forest,
The range of birds is the sky,
Cessation (vibhava) is the range of phenomena,
Nibbāna is the range of the Arahants."
In accordance with this, the non-existence (cessation) of form is called 'vibhavagati.' The breaking up of form is called 'bhedagati.' The same method should be understood for the mental aggregates such as feeling (vedanā). The difference is that their 'sañjātigati' should be understood as extending up to the peak of existence (bhavagga). In 'salakkhaṇagati,' their individual characteristics should be understood through the functions of feeling, perceiving, constructing, and cognizing.

'Tampi tassa na hoti' means that the three graspings (gāha)—view (diṭṭhi), craving (taṇhā), and conceit (māna)—which are expressed as 'I,' 'mine,' or 'I am' regarding form and so on, no longer exist for that Arahant (khīṇāsava). This is stated according to the sequence of the sutta. Therefore, it is said in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā:
"Virtue is taught at the beginning,
Development of concentration in the middle,
And Nibbāna at the end;
This is the discourse with the lute simile."
110:
The three attachments (gāha)—namely, view (diṭṭhi), craving (taṇhā), and conceit (māna)—no longer exist for that Arahant. Thus, although it appears in the Sutta by way of sequence, it is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakatha: "In the beginning, virtue (sīla) is taught; in the middle, the development of concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā); and at the end, Nibbāna. This is the teaching with the simile of the lute." This concludes the commentary on the ninth sutta.

## 10. Chappāṇakopamasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the tenth sutta (Chappāṇakopama Sutta): 'Arugatto' refers to one whose body is covered with sores and ulcers, like a wood-apple. Because those sores are festering, he is called 'pakkagatto' (one with a festering and putrid body). 'Saravanaṃ' refers to a thicket of reeds (or a forest of sharp grass) with thorns as sharp as arrows. By the phrase 'evameva kho', an immoral (dussīla) person should be understood as being like the man with sores. Just as that man suffers extreme bodily and mental pain from being pierced by grass-thorns and reed-stumps, and being scratched by reed-leaves which are like sword-blades, so too should be understood the suffering of an immoral person who is rebuked and blamed by his fellow practitioners in various places, saying, "This is the one who commits such and such evil deeds."

'Labhati vattāraṃ' means finding an accuser. 'Evaṃkārī' refers to one who performs such things as medical work, acting as a messenger, and so on. 'Evaṃsamācāro' refers to one whose conduct involves frequenting improper places such as the houses of widows. 'Asucigāmakaṇṭako': he is called 'asuci' (impure) because of his lack of purity, and 'gāmakaṇṭako' (village thorn) because he pricks and harasses the villagers by accepting their alms without possessing virtue. Thus, it means one who is like an impurity and a thorn to the villagers.

'Pakkhiṃ' refers to the elephant-trunk bird (hatthisoṇḍa-sakuna). 'Ossajjeyya' means one should let go. 'Āviñcheyyuṃ' means they would pull or drag. 'Pavekkhāmi' means "I will enter." 'Ākaāsaṃ ḍessāmi' means "I will fly into the sky."

Among those six creatures, the snake desires to enter an anthill, thinking, "I will sleep coiled up." The crocodile desires to enter the water, thinking, "I will enter a hole and sleep." The bird desires to fly into the sky, thinking, "I will roam happily in the open sky." The dog desires to enter a village, thinking, "I will scratch the ashes at the hearth and sleep, taking in the warmth." The jackal desires to enter a cemetery, thinking, "I will eat human flesh and sleep with my back stretched out." The monkey desires to enter the forest, thinking, "I will climb high trees and leap in all directions."

'Anuvidhāyeyyuṃ' means they would follow along. There is also a variant reading 'anuvidhiye-yyuṃ'. It means they would have to follow where the strongest creature goes. In this simile, the six sense bases (āyatana) should be understood as the six creatures. Craving (taṇhā) should be understood as the strong rope. Ignorance (avijjā) should be understood as the knot in the middle. Whichever door the object is strongest at, that sense base pulls towards that object. The Buddha brought forth this simile to show this identical nature.
111:
The Blessed One brought forth this simile either by way of similarity or by way of showing the diversity of the sense bases. Among these two, in the case of similarity, there is no separate task of application; it is already applied in the Pali text itself.
