However, in showing the diversity of the sense bases, the application is as follows: A snake does not delight in an external place that has been sprinkled with water and swept; it delights only when it has entered and lies in places like rubbish heaps, grass, thickets of leaves, and anthills, where it attains one-pointedness of mind. In the same way, this eye has a diverse (uneven) inclination; it does not delight in smooth golden walls and the like, and does not even wish to look at them; it delights only in places variegated with pictures, flowers, vines, and so forth. Indeed, in such places, when the eye cannot get enough of looking, one even desires to look with the mouth open.

A crocodile, too, when it goes out [on land], cannot see what is to be seized and moves with its eyes closed. But when it has dived into water about a hundred fathoms deep and lies in a hole, then its mind becomes one-pointed and it sleeps peacefully. In the same way, this ear is inclined towards holes, depending on space (ākāsa); its inclination is only within the ear-cavity. The space of the ear-cavity itself is the condition (upanissaya) for that creature's hearing of sound. The unobstructed open sky is also suitable. If one is reciting (paritta/scriptures) inside a cave, the sound cannot break through the roof of the cave to go outside; however, it goes out through the doors and windows, and striking the successive physical elements, it comes and strikes the ear-sensitivity (sotapasāda). At that time, those staying outside the cave know, "He is reciting such and such a text."

When the sound comes through the succession of elements in this way, it is the 'attainment of the object' (sampattagocara). If it is asked, "Does this ear take an object that has reached it?", the answer is "Yes, it does." If that is so, an objection might be raised: "When a large drum or the like is beaten far away, one would not be able to know that 'the sound is far away'." It is not that one does not know; one does. When the sound strikes the ear-sensitivity, there is a way of knowing according to the circumstances: "The sound is far, the sound is near, the sound is on the far bank or the near bank." This is simply the nature (dhammatā) of things, as stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakatha. How does it happen by this nature? Wherever there is a hole, hearing occurs from that direction, just like the seeing of the moon and the sun. Therefore, this ear is actually one that takes an object that has not reached it (asampattagocara).

A bird, too, does not delight in trees or on the ground. Only when it has flown past the distance of one or two stone-throws into the open sky does it attain one-pointedness of mind. In the same way, the nose also desires the open space; its object is the scent that comes depending on the wind.
112: Indeed, when it has newly rained, cows sniff the ground repeatedly and, facing the sky, inhale the air. Even when holding a ball of perfume with the fingers to smell it, if one does not inhale, one cannot know its scent. A dog, too, when wandering outside, does not see a place of safety and is harassed by clods, sticks, and so on. But when it enters a village, scratches the ashes near a fireplace, and lies down, it finds comfort. Similarly, the tongue is inclined toward the village and has the sense of taste based on the water element. This is true: even after practicing the Dhamma of a recluse throughout the three watches of the night, in the early morning, one must take the bowl and robes and enter the village. Furthermore, one cannot know the taste of dry food that is not moistened by saliva. A jackal, too, finds no delight when wandering outside; it only finds comfort when it eats human flesh in a cemetery and lies down. Similarly, the body is inclined toward the clung-to (upādiṇṇaka) matter and has the sense of touch based on the earth element. This is true: when they do not obtain another clung-to body, beings lie down placing their head on their own palm. Internal and external earth elements are the supporting conditions for the body to grasp an object. Whether it be a well-spread bed or the wooden planks beneath, one cannot know their hardness or softness without sitting on or pressing against them. In this way, internal and external earth elements are the supporting conditions for this body to know the object of touch. A monkey, too, does not delight in moving on the ground; it only finds comfort when it climbs a tree a hundred cubits high, sits in the fork of a branch, and looks around in all directions. Similarly, the mind is inclined toward various objects and has the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as its condition. It creates various desires even for objects previously seen. The original life-continuum is the supporting condition for that mind. This is just a summary here; the diversity of the sense bases (āyatana) is explained in detail in the 'Description of the Sense Bases' (Āyatananiddesa) of the Visuddhimagga. 'That eye no longer pulls' means that the sense-base creatures, bound by the rope of craving to the pillar of mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati), have reached a state of being free from fickleness and thus no longer pull. In this sutta, only preliminary insight (pubbabhāgavipassanā) is taught.
113:
## 11. Yavakālāpī Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eleventh sutta, the Yavakālāpī Sutta, 'yavakālāpī' refers to a heap of harvested barley. 'Byābhaṅgīhatthā' refers to those holding carrying poles in their hands. 'Six people should strike it with poles' means striking it with six flat carrying poles. 'Sattamā' (the seventh) means that after those six people have struck the barley heap, filled their bags, and left, another seventh person arrives. 'Suhatatarā assa' means that if any small amount of chaff or empty husks remains in that barley heap, it is struck even more thoroughly to collect them.

Similarly, in this Dispensation, the six sense bases should be understood as a four-way crossroads. A being should be understood as a bundle of barley placed at the crossroads. The eighteen types of objects—agreeable, disagreeable, and neutral—should be understood as the six people. The defilements that crave for existence should be understood as the seventh person. Just as the barley bundle at the crossroads is struck by six people, so too are these beings constantly oppressed and struck at the six sense bases by the sticks of the eighteen objects. Just as the seventh person strikes it even more thoroughly, so too are beings struck even more intensely than before by the defilements that crave for existence, while experiencing suffering rooted in existence.

Now, to show the defilements of craving for existence of these beings, He spoke the words beginning with 'Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave' (Once upon a time, O monks). There, the word 'tatra' is in the locative case, meaning 'at the gate of the Sudhammā assembly hall of the devas'. 'The devas are indeed righteous' is said with the intention: 'These devas are called righteous because, having captured an Asura lord like me, they did not inflict even the slightest harm of breaking my body.' 'The devas are unrighteous' means: 'These devas are called unrighteous because, having captured an Asura lord like me, they bind me with fivefold bonds, including the neck, like a pig that eats dung, and make me sit there.' 'Monks, the bond of Vepacitti is so subtle' means that the bond is as subtle as the fibers inside a lotus stalk or a spider's web. However, it is not possible to cut that bond with a billhook or an axe. Because one is bound only by the mind and can be freed only by the mind, it is called 'Vepacitti-bandhana' (the bond of Vepacitti).

'A subtler bond than that is the bond of Māra' means the bond of defilements, which is even subtler than Vepacitti's bond; it is not visible to the eye, nor does it obstruct one's posture. Beings bound by that bond of Māra, whether on the ground or in the sky, for a hundred leagues...
114:
(Beings bound by the bonds of Māra) go for even a thousand yojanas and come back. When this bond of Māra is cut, it is cut only by the knowledge of the Path, not by anything else. Therefore, it is also called "the bond that is released only by knowledge."

"Manyamāno" refers to one who conceives the five aggregates as "I" or "mine" through the power of craving (taṇhā), views (diṭṭhi), and conceit (māna). "Baddho mārassa" means bound by the bond of Māra. Alternatively, this genitive case "mārassa" expresses the sense of the instrumental (karaṇattha); meaning bound by the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra). "Mutto pāpimato" means released from the bond of Māra. Alternatively, this genitive case "pāpimato" is used only in the sense of the instrumental; meaning released from the bond of the evil defilements.

By the word "asmi" (I am), conceiving through craving is meant. By the phrase "ayamahamasmi" (this I am), conceiving through views is meant. By the word "bhavissanti" (they will be), conceiving through views by way of the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) is meant. By the phrase "na bhavissanti" (they will not be), conceiving through views by way of the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) is meant. The words "rūpī" (possessing form), etc., show the varieties of the eternalist view. "Tasmā" (therefore) means—because the act of conceiving (manyita) is an affliction, it is called a disease, a boil, and a dart, due to its power to oppress and destroy internal virtues; therefore (it is called a disease, etc.). The words "iñjitaṃ" (agitation), etc., are spoken to show the state of those beings who are agitated and trembling because of these defilements, who are bound by the proliferating tendencies (papañca) that prolong saṃsāra, and who have reached a state of heedlessness.

In the section on conceit (mānagata-vāra), the occurrence of conceit is called "mānagata." It means the manifestation of conceit (māna-pavattī). Just like the words "gūthagata" (excrement) and "muttagata" (urine), conceit itself is called "mānagata." In that section, the word "asmi" is spoken by way of conceit associated with craving. The phrase "ayamahamasmi" is spoken by way of views. If it is asked, "Is there not no conceit associated with views?"—the answer is: Yes, there is none. However, because conceit has not yet been abandoned, views arise. This is spoken with reference to views rooted in conceit. The rest of the meanings are clear everywhere.

115:
## 2. Vedanāsaṃyuttaṃ
## 1. Sagāthāvaggo
## 1. Samādhisuttavaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Sagāthāvagga of the Vedanāsaṃyutta, 'samāhito' means well-concentrated either by access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or by absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). 'Vedanā ca pajānāti' means knowing feelings distinctly by way of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). 'Vedanānañca sambhavaṃ' means knowing the cause (origin) of those feelings by way of the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca). 'Yattha cetā' means knowing that Nibbāna where these feelings cease by way of the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca). 'Khayagāminaṃ' means knowing the path leading to the destruction of those feelings by way of the truth of the path (magga-sacca). 'Nicchāto parinibbuto' means being quenched through the quenching of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna), having become free from craving. Thus, in this sutta, feelings as the domain of insight (vipassanā) are taught. In the verses, serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are taught by two words, and the four truths are taught by the remaining words. Thus, in this sutta, the definition of dhammas belonging to the four planes, which encompasses everything, is stated.

## 2. Sukhasuttavaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'adukkhamasukhaṃ saha' refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling together with pleasant and painful feelings. 'Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca' means within one's own continuity and in the continuity of others. 'Mosadhammaṃ' means having the nature of perishing. 'Palokinaṃ' means having the nature of being subject to disintegration. 'Phussa phussa vayaṃ passaṃ' means seeing the passing away by repeatedly contacting it with wisdom (ñāṇa). 'Evaṃ tattha virajjati' means thus becoming dispassionate towards those feelings. In this sutta also, feeling as the domain of insight is taught, and in the verses, contacting with wisdom is taught.

## 3. Pahānasuttavaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'acchecchi taṇhaṃ' means the complete cutting off of all craving. 'Vivattayi saṃyojanaṃ' means the uprooting of the ten fetters. 'Sammā' means by way of cause. 'Mānābhisamayā' means because of the realization of seeing conceit and the realization of abandoning it. Indeed, the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga) sees conceit well by way of its function.
116:
This is the realization through seeing (dassanābhisamaya) of that Path. That conceit, seen by the Path of Arahantship, is abandoned at the very moment of seeing, just as the life of those who have reached the Path of Stream-entry disappears upon being seen. This is the realization through abandoning (pahānābhisamaya) of that Path.

'He has made an end of suffering' means that because conceit has been seen and abandoned by the Path of Arahantship, he has made an end of the entire suffering of the round, which is called the fourth extreme. Among the four types of ends (anta)—namely, the final limit (antima-mariyādanta) described as 'it decays within the body-binding, or the green grass'; the lowest end (lāmakanta) described as 'Bhikkhus, this living by alms-gathering is the lowest among livelihoods'; the portion end (koṭṭhāsanta) described as 'the individual identity (sakkāya) is one end'; and the extreme end (koṭanta) described as 'this alone is the end of suffering through the destruction of all conditions'—he has made an end of the fourth extreme. This means he has made a boundary, a limit, and has made suffering remain only as the final physical body.

'He does not neglect clear comprehension' means he does not abandon the factor of clear comprehension (sampajañña). 'He does not come to a designation' means he no longer comes to the designation of being 'lustful,' 'hateful,' or 'deluded'; having abandoned such designations, he is called one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). In this discourse, the underlying tendency in the object (ārammaṇānusaya) is discussed.

## 4. Pātālasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth discourse, 'Pātāla' (the abyss) is so called because it is suitable for falling into, and because there is no foothold in it. 'False and non-existent' (asantaṃ avijjamānaṃ) means it is not real and not evident. 'Speaks such a word' refers to the statement 'There is an abyss in the great ocean.' This refers to the whirlpool in the world known as 'Balavāmukha,' where the powerful current of the great ocean rushes violently, strikes the Cosmos Mountain or Mount Sineru, rises up to one, two, or ten yojanas, and then falls back into the great ocean, appearing like a great hellish chasm where it falls.

In that Balavāmukha, there is a place for fish, turtles, devas, and asuras to stay and live happily. Therefore, the statement 'There is an abyss in the great ocean' is a false and non-existent word. Because all worldlings are unable to establish themselves in the face of bodily painful feeling, this bodily painful feeling itself is shown to be the 'Abyss' in the sense of being suitable for falling into. Thus, it is said: 'Bhikkhus, this bodily painful feeling (is called the abyss),' and so on. One finds no foothold in this great hellish chasm of bodily painful feeling, which falls without any resistance or restraint. 'He weeps and wails' means weeping while uttering inconsistent and distorted lamentations. 'Weak' (dubbala) means being weak in the power of wisdom. 'Of little strength' (appathāmaka) means having little strength because of the smallness of the strength of wisdom. In this discourse, 'noble disciple' (ariyasāvaka) refers to a Stream-winner (sotāpanna). Indeed, the Stream-winner is the primary focus here; however, a practitioner (yogāvacara) who possesses strong insight and sharp wisdom, and is able to stand firm without following the feeling that has arisen, is also suitable.

5. In the fifth discourse, 'should be seen as suffering' means it should be seen as suffering by way of its nature of change and destruction. 'As a dart' means painful feeling should be seen as a dart (salla) because it pierces and oppresses the individual identity. 'As impermanent' means neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling should be seen as impermanent (anicca) by way of its state of non-existence after having arisen. He saw (addā)...
117:
'He does not stand firm in the abyss' means he does not find a footing in the abyss. 'Foothold' (gādha) means a place to stand. 'He weeps' (akkandati) means he cries out while uttering inconsistent and distorted lamentations. 'Weak' (dubbala) means weak in wisdom. 'Of little strength' (appathāmaka) means one who has little strength due to the smallness of the strength of wisdom. In this discourse, 'noble disciple' (ariyasāvaka) refers to a Stream-winner (sotāpanna). This is because the Stream-winner is the primary focus here. Alternatively, a practitioner (yogāvacara) who has strong insight and sharp wisdom, and is able to stand firm without following the feeling that has arisen, is also suitable.

## 5. Daṭṭhabbasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth discourse, 'should be seen as suffering' (dukkhato daṭṭhabbā) means it should be seen as suffering by way of its nature of change and destruction. 'As a dart' (sallato) means it should be seen as a dart (salla) because of its sense of causing pain and piercing. 'As impermanent' (aniccato) means neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling should be seen as impermanent (anicca) by way of its state of non-existence after having arisen. 'Addā' means he saw (addasa). 'Peaceful' (santaṃ) refers to the nature of peace.

## 6. Sallasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth discourse, 'therein' (tatra) means among those two types of persons. 'He would pierce with a second dart' (anuviddhaṃ viddheyya) means a subsequent piercing in the vicinity of the same wound, within the distance of one or two finger-breadths. For one thus pierced, that subsequent piercing pain is more powerful than the first pain. Similarly, the mental pain (domanassa-vedanā) that arises later is more powerful than the preceding [bodily] pain. 'The escape from painful feeling' (dukkhāya vedanāya nissaraṇaṃ) refers to concentration (samādhi), the Path (magga), and the Fruit (phala), which are the means of escape from painful feeling. That person does not know this escape and knows only sensual pleasure (kāmasukha) as the escape. 'Of those feelings' (tāsaṃ vedanānaṃ) refers to those pleasant and painful feelings. 'He feels it yoked' (saññutto naṃ vedayati) means he feels that feeling while being conjoined with defilements (kilesa), not being disjoined from them. In the phrase 'yoked to suffering' (saññutto dukkhasmā), the ablative case is used in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇattha), meaning 'conjoined with suffering.' 'Of one who has understood the Dhamma' (saṅkhātadhammassa) means one who has distinguished and weighed the Dhamma. 'Of one who is learned' (bahussutassa) means one who is learned in the scriptures (pariyatti) and learned in realization (paṭivedha). 'He rightly understands, gone to the further shore of existence' means he has reached Nibbāna, the further shore of existence, and rightly understands that very Nibbāna. In this discourse as well, only the underlying tendency in the object (ārammaṇānusaya) is discussed. Among the noble disciples, the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is the primary focus here, but teachers say that the Non-returner (anāgāmī) is also suitable.
118:
## 7. Paṭhamagelanyasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh discourse, the phrase "yena gilānasālā tenupasaṅkami" (he approached the infirmary) means that even the Buddha, the supreme person in the world including the devas, went to the place where the sick are tended. He did so thinking, "The monks, believing and accepting this, will consider the sick as those who ought to be attended to, seeing that even the Tathāgata attends to them," and also, "I will speak on meditation topics to those monks there for whom meditation is suitable."

What should be said regarding "kāye kāyānupassī" (contemplating the body in the body) and so forth, I shall explain later (in the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta). "Aniccānupassī" means repeatedly contemplating impermanence. "Vayānupassī" means repeatedly contemplating decay. "Virāgānupassī" means repeatedly contemplating dispassion. "Nirodhānupassī" means repeatedly contemplating cessation. "Paṭinissaggānupassī" means repeatedly contemplating relinquishment.

What is shown by these words? It shows the path of practice to be attained by this monk. The foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) also belong only to the preliminary stage (of the supramundane path). In clear comprehension (sampajañña), these three contemplations—contemplation of impermanence, contemplation of decay, and contemplation of dispassion—also belong only to the preliminary stage. Contemplation of cessation and contemplation of relinquishment, these two are a mixture (of mundane and supramundane). By this much, the period of this monk's development of meditation (bhāvanā) is shown. The remaining words are just as previously explained.

## 2. Rahogata-vagga

## 1. Rahogata Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Rahogata-vagga, the phrase 'Whatever feeling is felt, all that is suffering' (yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ, taṃ dukkhasmiṃ) means that whatever feeling is experienced, all of it is called suffering. In the words beginning with 'the impermanence of formations' (saṅkhārānaṃyeva aniccatanti), there is the nature of impermanence, the nature of exhaustion, the nature of dissolution, and the nature of change of formations. It is shown that the Buddha said 'Whatever feeling is felt, all that is suffering' with reference to this nature of impermanence, exhaustion, dissolution, and change of those formations. This is because the impermanence of formations is also the impermanence of feelings. Impermanence is indeed death (maraṇa), and there is no suffering greater than death. With this intention, all feelings are spoken of as suffering.

'Monks, I...' (atha kho pana bhikkhu mayā): This phrase is begun to show that 'I do not only designate the cessation of feelings, but I also designate the cessation of these states (dhammas).' Tranquillity (vūpasama) and serenity (passaddhi) are spoken of according to the disposition of the veneyya (those to be guided) who can understand through such a teaching. It should be understood that by the inclusion of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha), the four formless attainments (āruppa) are also included here.

## 9-10. Pañcakaṅga Sutta Ādi Vaṇṇanā

267-268. In the ninth sutta, 'Pañcakaṅga Thapati' is the name of that master carpenter. Indeed, he is known as 'Pañcakaṅga' because he is endowed with five tools: the adze, the axe, the chisel, the handle, and the measuring line (or mallet). 'Thapati' means the head carpenter. 'Udāyī' refers to the wise Elder Udāyī. 'Pariyāya' means the reason or method. 'Dvepānanda' means 'Ānanda, in one way there are also two [feelings].' Here, it should be understood as two feelings by way of body and mind; three by way of pleasant [painful, and neutral]; five by way of faculties such as the pleasure faculty (sukhindriya); six by way of eye-contact, etc., through the doors; eighteen by way of mental exploration (upavicāra) such as 'having seen a form with the eye, one explores the form that is a basis for joy,' and so on; and thus thirty-six, consisting of six worldly joys, six renunciation joys, six worldly sorrows, six renunciation sorrows, six worldly equanimities, and six renunciation equanimities. These are thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future, and thirty-six in the present; thus, it should be understood that there are one hundred and eight feelings.

'Ānanda, these five are the cords of sensual pleasure': this statement is a separate connection (anusandhi). The Blessed One did not only designate feelings as two and so on; in one way, he also spoke of feeling as one. Desiring to show that, he began this teaching to support the view of Pañcakaṅga the head carpenter. 'Abhikkantatara' means more excellent. 'Paṇītatara' means more sublime. In this teaching, the neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling from the fourth jhāna onwards is also called 'pleasant' (sukha) because of its peaceful sense and its sublime sense. The attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is called 'pleasant' by way of unfelt pleasure (avedayita-sukha). Indeed, the pleasure arising by way of the five cords of sensual pleasure and the eight attainments is called 'felt pleasure' (vedayita-sukha). The attainment of cessation is called 'unfelt pleasure' (avedayita-sukha). Thus, whether it be felt pleasure or unfelt pleasure, it is truly pleasant because of the sense of pleasure characterized by the state of being free from suffering.

'Yattha yattha' means in whatever place. 'Sukhaṃ upalabbhati' means felt pleasure or unfelt pleasure is obtained. The Blessed One designates all that as pleasure because of the state of being free from suffering. In this sutta, the Blessed One brings the attainment of cessation to the peak of the teaching and concludes the teaching with the summit of the fruit of Arahantship according to the disposition of the neyya person.

## 3. Aṭṭhasatapariyāya Vagga

## 1. Commentary on the Sīvaka Sutta

In the first sutta of the third vagga, in the name "Moḷiyasīvaka," Sīvaka is his name. Because he has a topknot (cūḷā), he is called Moḷiyasīvaka. "Paribbājaka" means a clothed wandering ascetic. "Bile-originated" refers to feelings that have bile as their cause. "Vedayita" refers to feelings. Among those eight causes, three types of feelings arise due to bile. How? Some person thinks, "My bile is disturbed, and life is indeed difficult to know," and so gives gifts, undertakes the precepts, and performs the Uposatha duties; thus, wholesome feeling arises in him. Another person thinks, "I will prepare medicine for the bile," and so kills living beings, takes what is not given, speaks falsehood, and commits the ten types of misconduct; thus, unwholesome feeling arises in him. Another person thinks, "Even with this much medical treatment, my bile is not calmed; let whatever happens, happen," and being indifferent, he lies down enduring the bodily feeling; thus, indeterminate feeling arises in him.

"Known by oneself" (sāmampi kho etaṃ) means that by seeing that particular bile disorder, one should know this feeling for oneself. "Agreed as true" (saccasammataṃ) means accepted as a fact. Even the world, seeing the signs of bile disorder such as spots or discoloration on his body, knows, "His bile is disturbed." Therefore, because they overreach what is known by oneself and what is agreed as true by the world, it is said "tasmā" (therefore). The same method applies to phlegm-originated feelings and so on. Here, "produced by conflict of humors" (sannipātikāni) refers to those arising from the disturbance of all three: bile, phlegm, and wind. "Produced by change of season" (utupariṇāmajāni) refers to those born from an unsuitable climate. For those living in a dry jungle region (jaṅgala), an unsuitable climate arises when they stay in a well-watered region (anupadesa), and for those living in a well-watered region, it arises when they stay in a dry jungle region; thus, climatic unsuitability also arises by way of the Malaya region, the seacoast, and so on. Those born from that are called "produced by change of season."
122:
Feelings born from improper care and lack of restraint of the body are called visamaparihārajā vedanā. These feelings arise due to carrying excessively heavy and large loads, or from [improper] sleeping, sitting, and so on; or from being pricked by thorns, falling into pits, etc., while wandering at improper times. Opakkamikā vedanā (feelings born of assault) are those that arise due to the effort of being seized and tortured with sticks or clubs up to the knees, [under the accusation] "This person is a thief" or "This person is an adulterer." When subjected to such external assault, some perform wholesome deeds as mentioned, some perform unwholesome deeds, and some lie down enduring it. Kammavipākajā vedanā (feelings born of karmic result) arise solely from karma that produces bad results, without depending on external assault. When these karmic feelings arise, some perform wholesome deeds, some unwholesome, and some lie down enduring it, in the same manner as described. Thus, in all instances, feelings are of three types.

Among those eight causes, bodily feelings born of the first seven causes—bile (pitta), phlegm (semha), wind (vāta), internal imbalance (sannipāta), climate (utu), improper care (visama), and assault (upakkama)—can be prevented or removed. However, bodily feelings born of karma that produces bad results cannot be removed even by all kinds of medicines or all kinds of protective chants (paritta). In this sutta, worldly parlance is spoken.

## 2-10. Commentary on the Aṭṭhasata Sutta and Others

270-278. In the second sutta, "aṭṭhasatapariyāyaṃ" means the sequence of Dhamma which is the cause for knowing the one hundred and eight feelings. "Dhammapariyāyaṃ" means the cause of the Dhamma. In the phrase "kāyikā ca cetasikā ca" (bodily and mental), bodily feelings are found only in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), while mental feelings can occur in all four planes. Regarding "sukhā" etc., pleasant feeling (sukha vedanā) does not exist in the formless-sphere (arūpabhūmi); it is found in the remaining three planes. Painful feeling (dukkha vedanā) occurs only in the sense-sphere; the remaining equanimity feeling (upekkhā vedanā) occurs in all four planes. In the group of five, the faculties of pleasure (sukhindriya), pain (dukkhindriya), and grief (domanassindriya) occur only in the sense-sphere. The faculty of joy (somanassindriya) occurs in three planes. The faculty of equanimity (upekkhindriya) occurs in four planes. In the group of six, feelings occurring at the five [sense] doors are only in the sense-sphere; feelings at the mind-door occur in all four planes. In the group of eighteen, they are called "somanassūpavicāra" (mental explorations accompanied by joy) because one explores with joy regarding the six desirable objects. The same method applies to the remaining two: domanassūpavicāra and upekkhūpavicāra. Thus, although this teaching comes by way of exploration (vicāra), here eighteen feelings should be understood by way of joy (somanassa) and so on, which are associated with that exploration.

In the passage beginning with "six household-based joys" (gehasita somanassa): joy arises for one who obtains, or perceives the obtaining of, visible forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasant, charming, and connected with worldly baits; or for one who recollects such forms previously obtained in the past, which have now ceased and changed. Whatever joy is of this nature,
123:
this is called 'household-based joy' (gehasita somanassa). In this way, the six types of joy based on the cords of sensual pleasure at the six doors are called the 'six household-based joys.'

Having known the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation, joy arises for one who sees this impermanence as it really is with insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā): 'All these forms, whether in the past or at present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.' Whatever joy is of this nature is called 'renunciation-based joy' (nekkhamma-sita somanassa). In this way, for one who is able to establish insight by way of impermanence etc. when a desirable object appears at the six doors and can strive towards the path, the six types of joy that arise thinking 'My insight has reached the path' are called the 'six renunciation-based joys.'

Grief arises for one who does not obtain visible forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasant, charming, and connected with worldly baits; or for one who recollects such forms previously obtained in the past, which have now ceased and changed. Whatever grief is of this nature is called 'household-based grief' (gehasita domanassa). In this way, the six types of grief based on the cords of sensual pleasure that arise for one who thinks at the six doors, 'I no longer enjoy the desirable object; alas, I do not enjoy it,' are called the 'six household-based griefs.'

Having known the impermanence of forms, and seeing their change, fading away, and cessation, one sees with insight-wisdom as it really is: 'All these forms, whether in the past or at present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,' and then develops a longing for the unsurpassed liberations (vimokkha—the fruit of Arahantship): 'When shall I attain and abide in that fruit of Arahantship, in which the Noble Ones now attain and abide?' Thus, for one who develops longing for the unsurpassed liberations, grief arises due to that longing. Whatever grief is of this nature is called 'renunciation-based grief' (nekkhamma-sita domanassa). In this way, when a desirable object appears at the six doors, for one who develops longing for the Noble Fruits called the unsurpassed liberations, but is unable to strive in insight by way of impermanence etc. to attain that fruit, the six types of grief that arise for one who repeatedly grieves, 'Though I have striven in insight for this week, this month, this whole year, I have not been able to reach the stage of the Noble Ones,' are called the 'six renunciation-based griefs.'

Equanimity (aññāṇupekkhā) arises for an unlearned worldling who is overwhelmed by greed, hatred, and delusion, who is confused, who has not overcome the limits of defilements, who has not overcome [karmic] results, who does not see the danger, and who lacks great learning, upon seeing a visible form with the eye-sensitivity. Whatever equanimity is of this nature exists. That equanimity cannot transcend the visible form. Because it cannot transcend it, that equanimity is called 'household-based equanimity' (gehasita upekkhā). In this way, the six types of equanimity based on the cords of sensual pleasure that arise at the six doors, being attached only to those forms without being able to transcend them, are called the 'six household-based equanimities.' Having known the impermanence of forms, and knowing their change, fading away, and cessation, equanimity arises for one who sees with insight-wisdom as it really is: 'All these forms, whether in the past or at present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.' Whatever equanimity is of this nature exists.
124:
For a worldling who is overwhelmed and bewildered by greed, hatred, and delusion, who has not overcome defilements and their results, who does not see faults, and who lacks knowledge, there arises such a kind of equanimity (ignorant equanimity). This equanimity does not transcend the form (object); because it does not transcend it, this equanimity is called 'household-based equanimity (gehasita-upekkhā).' Thus, when a pleasant object appears at the six doors, like a fly stuck to a lump of molasses, not transcending the forms and so on, being stuck and attached right there, the six types of equanimity based on the cords of sensual pleasure that arise are called 'gehasita-upekkhā.'

'Having known the impermanence of forms, and having known their change, fading away, and cessation, both formerly and now, for one who sees this as it really is with right insight-wisdom—"All these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change"—equanimity arises. Such a kind of equanimity transcends the form; because it transcends it, this equanimity is called "renunciation-based equanimity (nekkhammasita-upekkhā)."' Thus, when pleasant and other objects appear at the six doors, for one who is not attached to the pleasant, not offended by the unpleasant, and not bewildered in improper observation, the six types of equanimity associated with insight-knowledge that arise are called 'nekkhammasita-upekkhā.' In this sutta, the classification of dhammas occurring in the four planes, which encompasses everything, is taught. The third sutta and others have very clear meanings.

## 11. Nirāmisa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, 'sāmisa' means being with the 'āmisa' (bait/carnal) of defilements. 'Nirāmisatara' means being even more free from 'āmisa' than the spiritual rapture of jhāna. One might ask: 'In the two jhānas, rapture is both lofty (mahaggata) and supramundane (lokuttara), whereas reviewing rapture (paccavekkhaṇā-pīti) is purely mundane (lokiya); why then is that mundane reviewing rapture more free from āmisa?' It is more free from āmisa because it arises by virtue of reflecting on the peaceful and sublime Dhamma. For example, a young favorite attendant of the king, when entering the palace freely as he pleases, does not care even if he accidentally kicks or touches great wealthy merchants or generals. Why? Because he serves in close proximity to the king. Thus, just as that young attendant surpasses those merchants and generals, this reviewing rapture should be understood as surpassing even supramundane rapture because it arises by virtue of reflecting on the peaceful and sublime Dhamma. The same method applies to the remaining sections on pleasure (sukha) and equanimity (upekkhā).

In the section on liberation (vimokkha-vāra), however, liberation connected with form is called 'sāmisa' by virtue of the carnal form (rūpāmisa) which is its own object. Liberation connected with the formless is called 'nirāmisa' due to the absence of carnal form.

## 4. Jambukhādakasaṃyuttaṃ
## 1. Nibbānapañhā Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the Jambukhādakasaṃyutta, the wanderer named Jambukhādaka is the wanderer Channa, who is the nephew of the Elder Sāriputta. In the passage, "Friend, the destruction of lust is Nibbāna," lust is destroyed because Nibbāna is reached and realized through the Noble Path; because it is the place and cause for the destruction of lust, Nibbāna is called the destruction of lust (rāgakkhaya). The same method applies to the destruction of hatred (dosakkhaya) and the destruction of delusion (mohakkhaya).

If someone were to say, based on this Jambukhādaka Sutta, that Nibbāna is merely the destruction of defilements, they should be asked: "Whose destruction of defilements is it? One's own or that of others?" They will certainly say, "One's own." Then they should be further asked: "What is the object of change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa)?" If they are knowledgeable, they will say, "It is Nibbāna." If asked, "At the moment of change-of-lineage knowledge, are the defilements already destroyed, being destroyed, or will they be destroyed?" one should not say they are "already destroyed" or "being destroyed," but only that they "will be destroyed." Then it should be asked: "In that case, while those defilements are not yet destroyed, does change-of-lineage knowledge take the destruction of defilements as its object?" When asked thus, that proponent of a different view (paravādī) will certainly be unable to answer.

This point should also be applied to Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). At the moment of the Path, one should not say defilements are "already destroyed" or "will be destroyed," but only that they are "being destroyed." Furthermore, the destruction of defilements cannot be the object while the defilements are not yet destroyed. Therefore, it should be accepted that Nibbāna is that reality which, when realized and reached, causes lust and so forth to be destroyed. Moreover, because Nibbāna is included under the term "immaterial states" (arūpino dhammā) in the dyads (duka-mātikā) such as "material states, immaterial states" (rūpino dhammā, arūpino dhammā), it is not merely the destruction of defilements.

## 6. Moggalānasaṃyuttaṃ

## 1-8. Paṭhamajhānapañhā Sutta Vaṇṇanā

332-339. In the Moggalānasaṃyutta, "kāmasahagata" means occurring together with the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). For the Elder Mahāmoggalāna, when he emerged from the first jhāna, the five hindrances appeared to him in a subtle manner. Because of the appearance of those hindrances, his first jhāna became what is called "partaking of decline" (hānabhāgiya). Knowing that lapse, the Blessed One gave the exhortation, "Do not be negligent." The meaning should be understood in this same way for the second jhāna and so forth. Here, "sahagata" (accompanied by) refers only to being accompanied by the object.

## 9. Animittapañhā Sutta Vaṇṇanā

"Animitta cetosamādhi" (signless concentration of mind) is said with reference only to insight-concentration (vipassanā-samādhi) which occurs after abandoning the signs of permanence (nicca-nimitta), etc. "Nimittānusāri viññāṇaṃ hoti" (consciousness follows the sign) means that while one is dwelling in this insight-concentration, the insight-knowledge is sharp and courageous like a double-edged sword as it performs its function. For example, if a woodcutter cutting a tree with a sharp axe frequently looks at the axe blade, thinking, "My axe is working very well indeed," the task of cutting will not be completed. Similarly, for the Elder, the attachment (nikanti) arose toward his insight, thinking, "My knowledge is working courageously indeed." At that time, he was unable to complete the task of insight. It is with reference to the arising of such attachment that it is said, "consciousness follows the sign." By not attending to all signs of permanence, pleasure, and self, he dwelt having attained the signless concentration of mind associated with insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā), as well as the concentration of the higher paths and fruits which has Nibbāna as its object.

## 10-11. Sakkasutta Vaṇṇanā

341-342. "Aveccappasādena" means with unwavering confidence. "Dasahi ṭhānehi" means by ten reasons or grounds. "Adhigaṇhanti" means they surpass or stand excelling. The rest of the terms have clear meanings in all the suttas.

## The Commentary on Moggalānasaṃyutta is finished.
130:
## 7. Citta Saṃyutta
## 1. Saṃyojana Sutta Vaṃṇanā

In the first sutta of the Citta Saṃyutta, "Macchikāsaṇḁe" means in the forest grove named Macchikāsaṇḁa. "This conversation arose" means that the ancient elders did not usually engage in tiracchānakathā (pointless talk that hinders the Path and Fruit); instead, at every place they stayed, they would raise problems, where those who did not know would ask and those who knew would answer. Thus, this conversation arose among those elders. "Migapathakaṁ" refers to his own village of wealth and property named Migapatha. It is said that this village is located behind the Ambāṭakārāma monastery. "Approached those elders" means he approached with the thought, "By answering the elders' questions, I will make them dwell comfortably." "In the profound word of the Buddha" means in the word of the Buddha which is profound both in meaning (attha) and in the text (dhamma). It means the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu) enters, functions, and arises.

## 2. Paṭhamaisidatta Sutta Vaṃṇanā

In the second sutta, "Venerable Elder" refers to the Mahāthera who was the most senior among those elders. "Remained silent" means that even though he knew the answer, he said nothing because of a lack of confidence (avisārada). "Venerable sir, I will answer" means he thought, "This Mahāthera neither answers himself nor invites others to answer. The lay devotee is as if bothering the Saṃgha by asking repeatedly. I will answer this question to make them dwell comfortably." Thus, he rose from his seat, went to the elder, and asked for permission. After receiving permission, he sat back in his place and answered.

"With his own hand" means personally. "Satisfied" means giving as much as desired and making them well-filled. "Invited (refused)" means causing them to refuse by saying "Enough, enough" with both hand gestures and words. "Those who had removed their hands from the bowls" means those who had removed the bowls from their hands, washed them, put them into bags, and hung the bowls on their shoulders.

## 3. Dutiyaisidatta Sutta Vaṃṇanā

In the third sutta, "In Avanti" means in the Avanti country in the southern region (Dakkhiṇāpatha). "Good words were spoken" means speaking with the intention: "Lay devotee, the words you said about attending and serving with the four requisites are indeed faultless and good words."
131:
## 4. Mahakapaṭihāriya Sutta Vaṃṇanā

In the fourth sutta, regarding the phrase "Discard the remains" (sesakaṁ vissajjetha), it should be noted that the householder, together with the elders, polished the bronze bowls, served the milk-rice (pāyāsa), and gave it to them. After eating the milk-rice, the householder, wishing to go along with the elders, thought: "At home, the female lay devotee manages the remains. But here, if I do not tell these servants, they will not manage them. If so, this excellent milk-rice will go to waste." Thus, he spoke this to give them permission. "Kuthitaṁ" means extremely sharp heat due to the hot sand below and the heat of the sun above. This term is an unmixed word (asambhinnapada) in the Buddha's word of the Tipiṭaka. "Paveliyamānena" means shrinking (like wax softened by fire). "It is well, venerable sir" (sādhu khvassa bhante) was said by Venerable Mahaka with the thought, "I will make these elders dwell comfortably."

"Performed a feat of psychic power" (iddhābhisaṃkhāraṁ abhisaṃkhari) means he performed psychic power by determination (adhiṭṭāna-iddhi). Here, various preparations (parikamma) such as "Let a cool breeze blow gently, let the rain-god make a cloud-pavilion and drop rain drop by drop," and a single determination (adhiṭṭāna) such as "Let it rain with wind," can occur together. Or a single preparation such as "Let it rain with wind" and various determinations such as "Let a cool breeze blow gently, let the rain-god make a cloud-pavilion and drop rain drop by drop" can occur. In the same manner, there can be various preparations with various determinations, or a single preparation with a single determination. For one who performs it in this way, after rising from the basic jhāna (pādakajjhāna) and completing the preparation, the psychic power succeeds immediately after the preparation through the lofty (mahaggata) mind of determination. "Okāsesi" means he scattered or spread it out.

## 5. Paṭhamakāmabhū Sutta Vaṃṇanā

In the fifth sutta, "Nelaṁgo" means faultless. "Setapacchādo" means having a white covering or being pure and clean. "Anīghaṁ" means free from suffering. "Remaining silent for a moment" (muhuttaṁ tuṇhī hutvā) means remaining silent for a moment to investigate the meaning of that verse, as if moving the three Piṭakas like an earring in the ear, reflecting, "This is the meaning of this word, that is the meaning of that word." "Vimuttiyā" means by the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala-vimutti). In answering this question, the lay devotee performed a difficult task. The Blessed One indeed said, "Monks, do you see this monk?"...
132:
The Blessed One spoke according to what he saw with his omniscience regarding the monk who was approaching—fair-skinned, slender, and with a prominent nose. Citta the Householder, however, by way of inference, said: "This is a name for an Arahant."

## 6. Commentary on the Second Kāmabhū Sutta

In the sixth sutta, the words "Venerable sir, how many formations (saṅkhāra) are there?" are heard. It is said that this householder, Citta, was accustomed to the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); therefore, thinking, "I will ask about the formations that are the basis for the attainment of cessation," he spoke thus. The Elder, knowing the householder's intention, although there are many formations such as meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so on, wishing to explain only bodily formations and the like, said: "Householder, there are three formations," and so forth. In that explanation, because it is connected with the body and is conditioned or produced by the body, it is called "bodily formation" (kāyasaṅkhāra). Because it conditions or produces speech, it is called "verbal formation" (vacīsaṅkhāra). Because it is connected with the mind and is conditioned or produced by the mind, it is called "mental formation" (cittasaṅkhāra).

Why is it asked here, "Venerable sir, what is the bodily formation?"—These formations are mixed with one another, confused, not clear, and difficult to demonstrate. Indeed, the twenty volitions (cetanā)—comprising eight sense-sphere wholesome volitions and twelve unwholesome volitions—which arise by causing taking, grasping, releasing, and moving at the body-door, as well as in-breaths and out-breaths, are called simply "bodily formations." The aforementioned twenty volitions, as well as thought-conception (vitakka) and discursive thinking (vicāra), which arise by causing the movement of the jaw and the breaking into speech at the speech-door, are called simply "verbal formations." The twenty-nine wholesome and unwholesome volitions that arise in one who is sitting in seclusion and thinking without reaching movement in the body-door or speech-door, as well as these two states—perception (saññā) and feeling (vedanā)—are called simply "mental formations." Thus, these formations are mixed, confused, unclear, and difficult to demonstrate; thinking, "I will have them explained clearly," he asked the question.

"Venerable sir, why (is it called bodily formation?)"—here he asks for the meaning of the terms such as "bodily formation." In the answer to that, "kāyappaṭibaddhā" means they are dependent on the body. If the body exists, they exist; if the body does not exist, they do not exist. "Cittappaṭibaddhā" means they are dependent on the mind. If the mind exists, they exist; if the mind does not exist, they do not exist.
133: Now, wishing to know, "Does this Venerable Kāmabhū enjoy the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling or not? Does he have mastery (vasībhāva) in that attainment or not?" he asked, "Venerable sir, how does the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling come to be?" In the answer to that, the period of the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is spoken of by the two words "samāpajjati" (enters) and "samāpajji" (entered). The period within the attainment of cessation is spoken of by the word "samāpanno" (has entered). Likewise, the period with mind is spoken of by the first two words, and the period without mind is spoken of by the last word. . . "The mind has been previously developed in such a way" means that even during the time of determining the duration before entering the attainment of cessation, the mind is developed to determine, "I shall remain without mind for this much time." The mind thus developed leads that person to the state of being without mind. "The verbal formation ceases first" means that it ceases first among the remaining formations, even in the second jhāna. Then the bodily formation ceases in the fourth jhāna. Then the mental formation ceases within the attainment of cessation. "Āyu" (life) is the material life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya). "Viparibhinnāni" means destroyed or perished. . . In this matter, some teachers say: "Because it is said of one who has entered the attainment of cessation that 'the mental formation has ceased,' the mind itself has not yet ceased; therefore, this attainment must be one with mind." To them, it should be replied: "If, because it is said 'his verbal formation has also ceased,' speech has not yet ceased, then one who has entered the attainment of cessation should remain sitting while preaching the Dhamma or performing recitations. Also, for one who is dead and passed away, because it is said 'the mental formation has ceased,' the mind would not have ceased; if that were so, one who cremates deceased parents or Arahants would be committing an anantariya-kamma (a grave crime)." Thus, one should not cling merely to the phrasing (byañjana) but should investigate the meaning (attha) by standing in the method of the teachers. For the meaning is the refuge, not the phrasing. . . "The faculties are exceptionally clear" means that while performing bodily and verbal actions, the faculties become tired when they strike against external objects; they become like a mirror placed at a crossroads, soiled by the dust raised by the wind and so forth. However, a mirror that is placed in a bag and kept in a chest or the like...
134: It shines only within; thus, for a monk who has entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), the five clear sense-bases (pasāda), such as the eye-base, shine exceedingly within the cessation. Therefore, it is said: "The faculties are very clear."  By the two words "vuṭṭhahissaṃ" and "vuṭṭhahāmi", the period within the attainment of cessation is spoken of; by the word "vuṭṭhito", the time of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) is spoken of. Similarly, by the former two words, the mindless period (acittaka) is spoken of; by the latter word, the period with mind (sacittaka) is spoken of. "The mind was previously developed in such a way" means that even during the time of delimiting the duration before the attainment of cessation, the mind that delimits the duration is developed, thinking: "For this much time I shall be mindless, and thereafter I shall have mind." "The mind which leads to that state" means that the mind thus developed leads that person to the state of having mind. Thus, the time of entering the attainment of cessation was taken below; here, the time of emerging from cessation is taken.  Now is the time to speak the discourse on cessation (nirodhakathā). That discourse on cessation should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga, where it is explained in all its aspects, having established the table of contents (mātikā): "The wisdom of mastery in the attainment of cessation, due to being endowed with two powers, the tranquilization of the three formations, sixteen types of knowledge-conduct, and nine types of concentration-conduct, is knowledge." What is this cessation? It is the non-occurrence of the four aggregates through reflective knowledge. For what purpose do they enter this attainment? Being weary of the occurrence of formations, they enter it for this purpose, thinking: "We shall live happily for seven days without mind; this cessation is indeed Nirvana in this very life."  "The mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra) arises first" means that for one emerging from the attainment of cessation, the mind of the attainment of fruition arises first. Referring to the perception (saññā) and feeling (vedanā) associated with that fruition-mind, it is said: "The mental formation arises first." After that, at the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra) arises.  Does the attainment of fruition not cause the in-breaths and out-breaths to arise? It can cause them to arise. However, for this person, the attainment of fruition associated with the fourth jhāna does not cause those in-breaths and out-breaths to arise. In any case, whether the attainment of fruition is associated with the first jhāna, or the second, third, or fourth jhāna, for the monk who has emerged from the peaceful attainment, the in-breaths and out-breaths...
135: ...the in-breaths and out-breaths are unmanifest (abbhohārika). The unmanifest nature of those in-breaths and out-breaths should be understood through the story of the Elder Sañjīva. For the Elder Sañjīva, having emerged from the attainment, while walking and treading upon embers without flames, like the flowers of the Butea monosperma (kiṃsuka), not even a thread of his robe was burnt, nor was there even the appearance of heat. This is said to be the power of the attainment. In this same way, it should be understood that it is said only with reference to the moment of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) that the in-breaths and out-breaths of a monk who has emerged from the attainment of fruition are unmanifest.  "Then the verbal formation (vacīsaṅkhāra)" means that after that life-continuum, at the time of using the sequence that produces bodily and vocal actions, the verbal formation arises. If it is asked, "Does the life-continuum not cause initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) to arise?", the answer is: it can. However, the initial and sustained thoughts arising because of that life-continuum are not able to process speech. Therefore, the arising of this verbal formation is spoken of only with reference to the time of using the sequence that produces bodily and vocal actions.  "Void contact" (suññato phasso) and so forth should be explained both by way of their own quality and by way of their object. First, speaking by way of its own quality, the attainment of fruition is called "void" because it is void of lust and so on. Referring to the contact co-arisen with that attainment of fruition, it is called "void contact". The same method applies to the signless (animitta) and the undirected (appaṇihita). By way of the object, however, Nibbāna is called "void" because it is void of lust and so on; it is "signless" because of the absence of the signs of lust and so on; it is "undirected" because of the absence of the longing (paṇidhi) called lust, hatred, and delusion. The contact associated with the attainment of fruition that has arisen making the void Nibbāna its object is called "void". The same method applies to the signless and the undirected.  There is another discourse called the traditional discourse (āgamanīyakathā). Insight (vipassanā) is also called void, signless, and undirected. Therein, when a monk grasps formations as impermanent, sees them as impermanent, and emerges from them as impermanent, his insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) is called "signless". When one grasps them as suffering, sees them as suffering, and emerges from them as suffering, it is called "undirected". When one grasps them as non-self, sees them as non-self, and emerges from them as non-self, it is called "void". Therein, the path of signless insight is called "signless"; the fruition of the signless path is called "signless"; when the contact co-arisen with the signless attainment of fruition touches, it is said: "signless contact touches." The same method applies to the undirected and the void. If it were spoken by way of the traditional discourse, there would be a distinction (vikippa) between void contact, signless contact, or undirected contact. Therefore...
136:
It is spoken of by its own quality and by its object. In this way, the statement "the three contacts touch" is consistent.

In the terms "vivekaninna" and so forth, Nibbāna is called "viveka" (seclusion). Bending towards that viveka is "vivekaninna". Standing like a tree that does not go to other objects but leans only towards viveka is "vivekapoṇa". Standing as if falling towards viveka is "vivekapabbhāra".

## 7. Godattasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "different in meaning and different in phrasing" means that their phrasing is different and their meaning is also different. Among these two, the difference in phrasing is obvious. As for the meaning: "appamāṇā cetovimutti" (limitless deliverance of mind) is, by plane, a sublime (mahaggata) state of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and by object, it has the concept of beings (satta-paññatti) as its object. "ākiñcaññā" (nothingness) is, by plane, a sublime state of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), and by object, it has a concept that cannot be described (as limited or sublime) as its object. "suññatā" (emptiness) is, by plane, a state of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), and by object, it has formations (saṅkhāra) as its object. Here, insight (vipassanā) is intended as "suññatā". "animittā" (signless) is, by plane, a supramundane (lokuttara) state, and by object, it has Nibbāna as its object.

In the words "Venerable sir, lust is a maker of limits" and so forth, there is an analogy: at the foot of a mountain, water containing rotten leaves and debris appears dark black; to those looking at it, it seems a hundred fathoms deep, but when measured with a stick or rope, it is not even deep enough to cover the top of the foot. Similarly, as long as defilements such as lust do not arise, it is impossible to know a person as they truly are, and they may appear like a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner. But when lust and so forth arise in them, then they are clearly known as "one with lust", "one with hate", or "one with delusion". Thus, because these defilements arise while showing the limit of the person, saying "this person is only this much", they are called "pamāṇakaraṇa" (limit-makers).

The phrase "Venerable sir, as many as there are limitless deliverances of mind" means how many are there that are called limitless deliverances of mind? There are twelve: the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), the four paths, and the four fruits. Among these twelve, the divine abodes are "limitless" because of the limitlessness of their pervasion of objects. The others (paths and fruits) are "limitless" because of the absence of defilements that make limits. Nibbāna is also limitless, but since it is not a deliverance of mind (cetovimutti), it is not included here. "Akuppā" (unshakable) refers to the deliverance of mind of the fruit of arahantship. Because it is the eldest and most excellent among those deliverances of mind, it is called "akuppā" (that which cannot be shaken).
137:
Therefore, it is said to be "declared the foremost". "Venerable sir, lust is an impediment (kiñcana)" means that when lust arises, it crushes, oppresses, and obstructs the person; therefore, it is called "kiñcana". It is said that when people make oxen tread the threshing floor, they say, "Tread, O Kapila (white ox)! Tread, O Kālaka (black ox)!" In this way, the meaning of "crushing/treading" should be understood as the meaning of "kiñcana". The same method applies to hatred and delusion.

"Ākiñcaññā cetovimutti" (deliverance of mind through nothingness) refers to nine states: the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) and the four paths and four fruits. Among these nine, the sphere of nothingness is called "ākiñcañña" because it has not even a slight object. The paths and fruits are called "ākiñcañña" because of the absence of defilements called "kiñcana" which crush and oppress. Nibbāna is also called "ākiñcañña", but since it is not a deliverance of mind, it is not included here.

In the words "Venerable sir, lust is a maker of signs (nimittakaraṇa)" and so forth, there is an analogy: there are two similar calves belonging to two different families. As long as they have not been branded with a mark, it is impossible to distinguish, "This calf belongs to such-and-such a family, and this calf belongs to such-and-such a family." But when they are branded with a mark such as a trident (trisūla) and so forth, then they can be known. Similarly, as long as lust does not arise in a person, it is impossible to distinguish, "Is this a noble one (ariya) or a worldling (puthujjana)?" But when lust arises in that person, it arises as if making a sign for recognition, "This person is one with lust." Therefore, it is called "nimittakaraṇa" (sign-maker). The same method applies to hatred and delusion.

"Animittā cetovimutti" (signless deliverance of mind) refers to thirteen states: insight (vipassanā), the four immaterial states (āruppa), the four paths, and the four fruits. Among these thirteen, insight is called "signless" because it removes the sign of permanence (nicca-nimitta), the sign of happiness (sukha-nimitta), and the sign of self (atta-nimitta). The four immaterial states are called "signless" because of the absence of the sign of form (rūpa-nimitta). The paths and fruits are called "signless" because of the absence of defilements that make signs. Nibbāna is also signless, but since it is not a deliverance of mind, it is not included here. If it is asked, "Why is the emptiness deliverance of mind (suññatā cetovimutti) not taken separately?" Because of the word "empty of lust" and so forth, it is already included in all states; therefore, it is not taken separately.
138:
“Ekattā” means having a single meaning by way of the object. Indeed, all these names—“immeasurable (appamāṇa), nothingness (ākiñcañña), emptiness (suññata), and signless (animitta)”—are names for Nibbāna alone. Thus, in this sense, they have a single meaning. However, in another context, it is immeasurable; in another, nothingness; in another, emptiness; and in another, signless. In this sense, they are different in phrasing.

## 8. Nigaṇṭhanāṭaputta Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, “tenupasaṅkami” (approached him): Why did an Anāgāmī noble disciple, who has mastered the scriptures and realized the Teaching himself, approach a naked and ungraceful Nigaṇṭha? It was to free himself from blame and to establish a debate. It is said that the Nigaṇṭhas criticized, “The disciples of the ascetic Gotama are like hard khadirā stumps; they do not even engage in friendly conversation with anyone.” He approached to free himself from that blame and with the thought, “I will establish a debate with him.”

“Venerable sir, I do not go in this matter out of faith in the Blessed One”: One who has not realized it through knowledge might go out of faith in another, thinking, “It is said to be so.” But I have realized this through knowledge; therefore, I do not go in this matter out of faith in the Blessed One—he said this to show this point.

“Ulloketvā” (looking up) means looking up while raising the body, protruding the belly, and stretching the neck, surveying all directions.

“Bādhetabbaṃ maññeyya” (should be considered obstructed) means it should be considered as being prevented or bound so that it cannot break through and escape. 

“Sahadhammikā” means with reasons and logic. 

“Then bring me before the Nigaṇṭha assembly” means, “When the meaning of those questions is known, then come to me with the Nigaṇṭha assembly; having come to me, let me know of your arrival.” 

“Eko pañho” (one question) means one line of questioning or the seeking of one question. 

“Eko uddeso” (one summary): “What is one?”—this is the one summary. 

“Ekaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ” (one explanation): “All beings subsist on nutriment”—this is the one explanation. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.
139:
## 9. Acela Kassapa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, “kīvaciraṃ pabbajitassa” means how long has it been since he went forth?

“Uttari manussadhammā” (beyond human states): “Human states” refers to the ten wholesome courses of action; it means beyond those human states. 

“Alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso” (a distinction in knowledge and vision sufficient for nobility): It is a distinction in knowledge and vision called “sufficient for nobility” (alamariya) because it is capable of making one a Noble One (ariya). 

“Naggeyyā” is due to the state of nakedness. 

“Muṇḍeyyā” is due to the state of being shaven-headed. 

“Pavāḷanipphoṭanāyā” is due to the shaking off of clinging dust. It means using just a bundle of peacock feathers held for the purpose of shaking off the dust, grime, and sand clinging to the buttocks of one who sits on the ground.

## 10. Gilānadassana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, “ārāmadevatā” refers to deities dwelling in flower gardens and fruit gardens. 

“Vanadevatā” refers to deities dwelling in forest groves. 

“Rukkhadevatā” refers to deities dwelling in various trees, like Vessavaṇa and other deities during the time of King Mattarāja. 

“Osadhitiṇavanappatīsu” refers to deities dwelling in medicinal plants such as myrobalan and gallnut, in grasses such as muñja and pabbaja, and in great forest trees.

“Saṅgamma” means having assembled. 

“Samāgamma” means having come together from various places. 

“Paṇidhehi” means set or establish by way of aspiration. 

“Ijjhissati sīlavato cetopaṇidhi” means the mental aspiration of a virtuous person will be fulfilled. 

“Dhammiko” refers to one endowed with the ten wholesome qualities and free from the four biases (agati). 

“Dhammarājā” is a synonym for that term “dhammika.” Alternatively, he is a “Dhamma-king” because the kingship was obtained righteously. 

“Tasmā” (therefore) is because they said, “Young master, if so, then please advise us too.” 

“Appaṭivibhattaṃ” (undivided) means it will be shared in common with the monks, without dividing it as “I will give this to the monks, and I will use this myself.”

## The Explanation of the Citta Saṃyutta is Finished.

The commentary on the Citta Saṃyutta has ended.
140:
## 8. Gāmaṇi Saṃyutta

## 1. Commentary on the Caṇḍa Sutta

In the first sutta of the Gāmaṇi Saṃyutta, "Caṇḍa Gāmaṇi" refers to a village headman named Caṇḍa by the Elders who recited the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka). "Pātukaroti" (He manifests) means he makes his anger manifest by quarreling back with one who quarrels, reviling back one who reviles, and striking back one who strikes. "Na pātukaroti" (He does not manifest) means he does not perform any opposition even when reviled or struck.

## 2. Commentary on the Tālapuṭa Sutta

In the second sutta, "Tālapuṭa" is the name of such a person. It is heard that his facial complexion was very clear, like the color of a ripe palmyra fruit fallen from its stalk; therefore, they named him Tālapuṭa. He was a person in his final birth (pacchimabhavika), endowed with the resolution (abhinīhāra). "Saccālikena" means by truth and by falsehood. "Tiṭṭhatetaṃ" means "Let this talk be/set this aside." The hell named Pahāsa does not exist as a separate hell apart from the eight great hells. Thus, in this sutta, only the teaching of the Dhamma with respect (sakkacca) is mentioned. For the Buddhas, there is no such thing as teaching the Dhamma without respect. The Buddhas have a practice similar to a lion. Just as a lion king exerts the same speed and effort whether to catch a great rutting elephant or to catch small creatures like rabbits and cats, even so, the Buddhas teach with respect whether they are teaching a single person, or two, or a large assembly of monks, or an assembly of nuns, laymen, and laywomen, or even ascetics. Because the four assemblies listen with faith and conviction, the teaching for them is called 'sakkacca-desanā' (teaching given with respect).

In the phrase "mettāya cetovimuttiyā," when "mettā" is said, both access concentration (upacāra) and absorption (appanā) are applicable. But when "cetovimutti" is said, only absorption is applicable. "Yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ" refers to sense-sphere kamma (kāmāvacara-kamma). "Appamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ" refers to fine-material sphere kamma (rūpāvacara-kamma). That kamma is called "appamāṇakata" because it is performed by transcending limits and developing it through pervading the directions, whether specifically or non-specifically.

"Na taṃ tatrāvasissati, na taṃ tatrāvatiṭṭhati" means that sense-sphere kamma does not remain or persist in that fine-material or immaterial sphere kamma. What is meant? It means that sense-sphere kamma is unable to get stuck or remain in the midst of that fine-material or immaterial sphere kamma, nor can it overwhelm the fine-material or immaterial sphere kamma to exhaust it and take its own place to persist. Rather, just as a great flood overwhelms a small amount of water, exhausts it, and persists by making its own space, even so, the fine-material or immaterial sphere kamma alone overwhelms the sense-sphere kamma, exhausts it, and persists by making its own space. It blocks the result of that sense-sphere kamma and itself leads one to the company of the Brahmas. Thus, this sutta, having arisen by way of defilements at the beginning and being concluded by way of the Brahma-vihāras at the end, proceeds according to a proper sequence (anusaṃdhi).

## 12. Commentary on the Rāsiya Sutta

In the twelfth sutta, "Rāsiya" is the name given by the Elders who recited the Dhamma because he asked questions by making a heap (rāsi). "Tapassī" refers to one who relies on ascetic practices that heat the body. "Lūkhajīvī" refers to one who has a harsh livelihood. "Antā" means portions or sides. "Gāmmā" or "Gammā" means the low practice which is the conduct of villagers. "Attakilamathānuyoga" means the repeated exertion in tiring oneself, the act of causing suffering to the body.

Why are devotion to sensual pleasure (kāmasukhallikānuyoga), devotion to self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga), and the middle way (majjhimā paṭipadā) taken up in this sutta? Devotion to sensual pleasure is taken to show those who enjoy sensual pleasures. Devotion to self-mortification is taken to show those who rely on asceticism (tapanissitaka). The middle way is taken to show the three grounds for the wearing away [of kamma] (nijjara-vatthu). What is the benefit of showing these? The Tathāgata, the Blessed One, having abandoned these two extremes, attained Supreme Enlightenment through the middle way. That Blessed One does not criticize all those who enjoy sensual pleasures, nor does he praise them all. He also does not criticize all those who practice asceticism.

He does not praise everyone; He blames only those who deserve blame and praises only those who deserve praise. This answer should be understood as a clarification of this meaning.

Now, wishing to clarify that matter, He said: "Gāmaṇi, there are these three types of sensual pleasure seekers," and so forth. In that passage, 'sāhasena' means by acts of violence and oppression. 'Saṃvibhajati' means not sharing with friends and companions. 'Na puññāni' means not performing meritorious deeds that serve as support for future lives. 'Dhammena' means acquiring by both righteous and unrighteous means. 'Thānehi' means by causes. 'Sacchikaroti': In what way can one realize it while tormenting oneself? One can realize it by the power of fourfold energy and by the power of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). In the phrase "three things that wear away defilements in this very life," even a single Path is called "threefold wearing away" (nijjara) because it utterly abandons the three defilements of greed, hatred, and delusion.

147: The four paths along with insight (vipassanā) are called concentration of mind (citta-samādhi). Alternatively, the five qualities called joy (pāmojja), rapture (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), happiness (sukha), and concentration (samādhi), as taught in the passage: "Joy arises; for one who is joyful, rapture arises," are called concentration of the Dhamma (dhamma-samādhi). Concentration of mind, however, refers specifically to the four paths along with insight. Alternatively, the ten courses of wholesome action (kusala-kammapatha) and the four sublime abodes (brahma-vihāra) are called concentration of the Dhamma; the one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) that arises in one who fulfills that concentration of the Dhamma is called concentration of mind. "In this way, you should abandon this state of doubt" means that if, while established in the aforementioned variety of concentration of the Dhamma, you obtain such concentration of mind, you will certainly be able to abandon that doubt. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as explained in all other places. ## The Explanation of the Gāmaṇisaṃyutta is finished.
148: ## 9. Asaṅkhata-saṃyutta ## 1. Pathama-vagga ## 1-11. Commentary on the Kāyagatāsati-sutta and others 366-376. In the Asaṅkhata-saṃyutta, "Asaṅkhata" (the Unconditioned) refers to Nibbāna, which is not created. "Hitesinā" means by one who seeks welfare. "Anukampaka" means by one who is compassionate. "Anukampā upādāya" means having grasped with a compassionate mind; it is also said to mean "depending on [compassion]." "That task has been done by me for you" means that I, the Buddha, have done what should be done for you by teaching this Unconditioned and the path to the Unconditioned. Indeed, the only duty of a compassionate teacher is the teaching of the Dhamma without distortion. Beyond this, practice is the duty of the disciples. Therefore, he said: "Monks, these are the roots of trees... this is our instruction." By this, he shows the dwelling at the root of a tree. By the words "empty huts" (suññāgāra), he shows a place secluded from people. With both terms, he points out a dwelling suitable for meditation and hands over the inheritance. "Meditate" (jhāyatha) means: through meditation on an object, meditate on the thirty-eight objects; and through meditation on characteristics, meditate on the aggregates, sense bases, etc., by way of impermanence and so forth. It means "develop tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā)." "Do not be negligent" means do not be heedless. "Do not be those who regret later" means: those who, in the past—when young, when healthy, when endowed with the seven types of suitability (sappāya), and when in the presence of the Teacher—were devoid of wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and, becoming food for bedbugs day and night, were negligent while enjoying the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of drowsiness. Later, in old age, in sickness, at the time of death, at the time of ruin, and when the Teacher has attained Parinibbāna, they remember that past life of negligence and, seeing the heaviness of the transition to a future rebirth, they become full of regret. Showing "Do not be such people," he said, "Do not be those who regret later." "This is our instruction to you" means "This is the instruction and advice for you from our presence, saying 'Meditate, do not be negligent.'"
