In the terms beginning with "anataṃ": It is called "anata" (the non-inclined) because of the absence of "nati" (inclination), which is craving. It is called "anāsava" (the taintless) because of the absence of the four taints (āsavas). It is called "sacca" (the truth) because it is the ultimate truth. It is called "pāra" (the far shore) in the sense of being beyond the round of suffering (vaṭṭa). It is called "nipuṇa" (the subtle) because of its subtle nature. It is called "sududdasa" (the very difficult to see) because it is extremely hard to perceive. It is called "ajajjara" (the undecaying) because it is not worn out by aging. It is called "dhuva" (the stable) because of its permanence. It is called "apalokita" (the non-disintegrating) because it does not perish. It is called "anidassana" (the invisible) because it cannot be seen by eye-consciousness. It is called "nippapañca" (the non-proliferated) because of the absence of the proliferations (papañca) of craving, conceit, and views.

It is called "santa" (the peaceful) because of its peaceful nature. It is called "amata" (the deathless) because of the absence of death. It is called "paṇīta" (the sublime) because of its exalted nature. It is called "siva" (the auspicious) because of its cool and peaceful nature. It is called "khema" (the secure) because it is free from danger and affliction. It is called "taṇhakkhaya" (the destruction of craving) because it is the cause for the ending of craving.

It is called "acchara" in the sense of causing wonder; it is called "acchariya" (the marvelous) as it is worthy of snapping one's fingers in amazement. It is called "abbhuta" (the astounding) because it exists as something that has never occurred before, or because it appears without having arisen before. It is called "anītika" (the free from calamity) because of the absence of suffering. It is called "anītikadhamma" (the state free from calamity) because its nature is free from suffering. It is called "nibbāna" (extinction) because of the absence of craving, which is called "vāna". It is called "abyābajjha" (the non-afflicted) precisely because of the absence of anxiety. It is called "virāga" (dispassion) because it is the cause for the attainment of the fading of lust. It is called "suddhi" (purity) because of its ultimate purity. It is called "mutti" (liberation) because it is liberated from the three planes of existence. It is called "anālaya" (the attachment-less) because of the absence of the dwellings of craving (kāmālaya). It is called "dīpa" (the island) in the sense of being a foundation. It is called "leṇa" (the cave) in the sense of being a place to be relied upon. It is called "tāṇa" (the protection) in the sense of guarding against danger. It is called "saraṇa" (the refuge) in the sense of being a refuge from fear; the meaning is that it destroys fear. It is called "parāyaṇa" (the final destination) because it is the supreme goal and support. The remaining words in this Saṃyutta are to be understood in the same manner as already explained.

150: ## 1. Commentary on the Khemā-sutta ## 10. Abyākata-saṃyutta In the first sutta of the Abyākata-saṃyutta, "Khemā" refers to the Great Elder Nun (Mahātherī) who, as a laywoman, was a female lay follower (upāsikā) of King Bimbisāra and later ordained with faith in the Dispensation. As the Blessed One declared, "Monks, among my female disciples who possess great wisdom, Khemā is the foremost," she was placed in the position of the foremost disciple (aggasāvikā) in terms of great wisdom. "Paṇḍitā" means being endowed with wisdom. "Viyattā" means being endowed with proficient and clever wisdom. "Medhāvinī" means being endowed with retentive wisdom. "Bahussutā" means being endowed with both the learning of the scriptures (pariyatti-bāhusacca) and the learning of realization (paṭivedha-bāhusacca). "Gaṇaka" means one skilled in continuous counting. "Muddika" means one skilled in counting by finger-marks. "Saṅkhါyaka" means one skilled in counting by groups. "Gambhīra" means being eighty-four thousand yojanas deep. "Appameyya" means immeasurable by being measured with a bushel (āḷhaka). "Duppariyogāha" means difficult to fathom for the purpose of taking a measurement. By whatever form (rūpa) one might designate the Tathāgata—described as a being—as long, short, dark, or fair, that aforementioned form has been abandoned in the Omniscient Tathāgata through the abandonment of its origin (samudaya). "Released from the category of form" (rūpasaṅkhāya vimutto) means being liberated from the designation of form because form will no longer arise in the future, and because the conventional usage of saying "one is of such a nature" by way of the groups of form and non-form has ceased. "Gambhīra" means deep due to the depth of intention and the depth of virtues. For the Omniscient Tathāgata who is thus deep in virtues, the designation "Tathāgata" described as a being occurs depending on the aggregates; since those aggregates no longer exist, for one who sees the absence of that designation, the statement "This Tathāgata, described as a being, exists after death" is not appropriate, nor are statements such as "He does not exist after death" appropriate. "Saṃsandissati" means it will be one. "Samessati" means it will be without interval. "Na virodhayissati" means it will not be a contradictory term. "In the foremost word" (aggapadasmiṃ) means in the teaching. Here, the teaching (desanā) is intended as the "foremost word."

## 9. Kutūhalasālāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, "kutūhalasālāyaṃ": there is no specific hall named "Kutūhalasālā" (Hall of Curiosity). However, because it is a place where wanderers and brahmins of various sects engage in various kinds of talk, and where many people create a stir and commotion asking, "What is this one saying? What is that one saying?", it is called the "Hall of Curiosity."

"Dūrampi gacchati" means it goes as far as the Ābhassara Brahma realm. "Imañca kāyaṃ nikkhipati" means one casts off this body with the death-consciousness (cuti-citta). "Anupappanno hoti" means because the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) has not yet arisen at the very moment of death, one is not yet reborn.

## 10. Ānandasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, "tesametaṃ saddhiṃ abhavissa" means this statement of "self" (attā) would have been in accordance with their view. "Anulomaṃ abhavissa ñāṇassa uppādāya sabbe dhammā anattā" means: for the arising of the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that "all phenomena are non-self," would [my answer] have been suitable for the arising of that knowledge? This is the meaning.
152:
## 11. Sabhiyakaccānasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, regarding the phrase "Etamettakena ettakameva": Friend, for whoever can explain within this much time that "when there is a cause, the designation 'possessing form' (rūpī) occurs; when there is no cause, it does not occur," even this much [knowledge] is a great deal for that person. Regarding "Ko pana vādo atikkante": What need is there to speak of the method of Dhamma teaching that surpasses this and is exceedingly delightful? There is nothing more to say; the discussion is concluded.
